The CoA has set targets to reduce its emissions to 20 percent below 2009 levels by 2020, and 40 percent below 2009 levels by 2030. The Hartsfield-Jackson Airport has pledged to reach net zero by 2050 under the department of aviation (CoA) Additionally, this plan also utilizes business as usual forecasts based on expected future trends using the 2013 Georgia Power (main utility) Integrated Resource Plan (IRP).

column23: Over the last decade, agencies and organizations across Atlanta have produced a range of reports and frameworks establishing a vision for the future of the city. Resilient Atlanta builds on these efforts by bringing together decades of planning and applying a resilience lens to projects previously identified or already underway. This Strategy sets specific Visions, Targets, and Actions in order to ensure that our future Atlanta is a more equitable, connected, transparent, and sustainable city. The Resilient Atlanta development process revealed that recurring themes related to social equity, culture and identity, and climate remain priorities for Atlantans. Rather than putting each of these topics in their own silo, we have included equity, culture and identity, and climate throughout the Resilient Atlanta Visions and, in doing so, intend to address these priorities, and elevate their importance, from multiple angles. This includes the 2015 Climate Action Plan, which has been integrated across 3 out of 4 visions .

column23: Wording straight from Clean Energy Atlanta States: \'Atlanta has an imperative to act to reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change. The global community has called for a reduction in carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions to avoid warming the planet 2°C above its current temperature, a target that was selected by the scientific community to represent the highest temperature increase permissible before catastrophic effects of climate change become more likely. This target was commemorated in the 2015 Paris Agreement, which is the first international accord to establish a common cause for all nations, undertaking ambitious efforts to reduce CO2 emissions and adjusting behaviors and policies to prepare for unavoidable climate change impacts. Atlanta was one of the few cities from the American South represented at the 2015 United Nations Climate Change Conference and joined 109 other U.S. cities to commit to the targets commemorated in the Agreement to keep greenhouse gas emissions from causing a warming increase of more than 2°C. Key City of Atlanta sustainability plans incorporate energy goals, such as the Resilient Atlanta Strategy and the Climate Action Plan, but Clean Energy Atlanta is the first to focus exclusively on achieving Atlanta's clean energy goals and to identify policy options for achieving them.\'

column30: Essex County Council (ECC) published the 'Essex Strengthening Adaptation & Resilience to Climate Change: Climate Adaptation Plan Framework' in 2024. The document aims to outline the immediate and long-term priorities and strategies for climate adaptation in Essex and was developed jointly with multiple teams across the Council. As part of the plan's development process the council updated its previous identification and prioritization of climate hazards and undertook an assessment of climate risks. Adaptive measures to tackle climate change and improve the environment were identified for each of the function areas of the council. Functions assume responsibility and are accountable for actions and ongoing reviews. They can action any updates to current, new, or amended actions guaranteeing that the action plan stays pertinent to the provision of ECC services. There isn't an estimate for the total cost of implementation for this adaptation plan since it is a mixture of strategic plans; and the risks and actions identified in this document are integrated into the BAU (business as usual) service provision of the Council, where appropriate. These sit alongside specific resilience projects such as Tree and Woodland planting, Local Nature Recovery and Flood Resilience Programme (capital works) where of course costs are itemised. ECC received £562,000 external funding up to 2025 to develop the Local Nature Recovery Strategy. Under the Essex flood capital programme, since 2015 ECC has invested a total of £28 million in flood resilience schemes, of which ECC have funded £16,750million and £11,250million has come from external funding Climate Adaptation is part and parcel of our overall climate approach, therefore detailed costing of most of the actions is set out in the integrated climate plan 'Essex Climate Action Plan (2021-2025)' published in November 2023 (refer to latest version of climate action plan once agreed.) \n

column30: The Essex Climate Action Commission (ECAC)'s report 'Net Zero: Making Essex Carbon Neutral' sets out recommendations to 2050 and recognises that Essex County Council (ECC) cannot tackle climate and environmental challenges alone. ECC's Climate Action Plan outlines the immediate actions ECC is taking directly and in concert with partners to drive effective progress against ECAC recommendations. It is structured following ECAC's report core themes with the addition of a new theme focused on local business-oriented projects. In its first version in 2021 the themes were: 1) Land Use and Green Infrastructure, 2) Energy; 3) Built Environment; 4) Transport, 5) Waste; and 6) Community Engagement; 7) Supporting Our Businesses. However, since original publication, there have been significant changes at regional, national, and international levels which have impacted Essex residents. Therefore, the plan has been reassessed and a second edition of the plan was launched in July 2023. This current version widened up the theme seven 'Supporting Our Businesses' to add just transition and green economy, renaming the theme as 'A Just Transition to Green Economy'. The third iteration of the Climate Action Plan is currently being finalised for adoption later in 2025. This will cover the period 2025/26-2027/28. \n

Manchester's overarching climate action plan is the Manchester Climate Change Framework 2020-2025, first adopted in 2020 and updated in 2022.
The Framework sets a citywide target to become zero carbon by 2038 and is fully aligned with the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) Five-Year Environment Plan to ensure consistency across the wider city region.

Current Progress and Challenges

The Framework requires a 13% annual reduction in direct emissions to remain within Manchester's science-based carbon budget and to meet the first milestone of a 50% emissions cut by 2025.
To date, the city has not reduced emissions at this required pace, placing the 2025 milestone at risk and underlining the urgency of accelerated action.

Purpose of the 2022 Update

The 2022 Update to the Framework:

Presents detailed modelling to identify granular targets for achieving a 50% reduction in direct emissions.

Provides an overview of work supporting adaptation and resilience objectives.

Recommends specific actions for delivery at local, regional, and national levels by government, businesses, the third sector, and communities.

Highlights the co-benefits of climate action—improved health and wellbeing, a more inclusive and productive economy, and enhanced environmental quality.

Embeds the principle of a just transition, ensuring the costs and impacts of change do not fall disproportionately on vulnerable residents.

Key Messages from the Update

Urgent action is needed to cut emissions from buildings and ground transport and to scale up renewable energy generation.

Decisive adaptation is required to strengthen the city's resilience—addressing infrastructure, buildings, economy, and community preparedness for climate impacts.

Collective responsibility is essential: individuals, organisations, and all levels of government must act and collaborate.

Private finance and innovative investment mechanisms are critical, as the transition cannot rely solely on public funding.

Climate action delivers wider benefits, including better health outcomes, reduced fuel and food poverty, job creation, and a greener urban environment.

Forthcoming 2025-2030 Update

Manchester is currently updating its Climate Change Framework and Action Plans for 2025-2030, with publication scheduled for October 2025.
This update will set out revised carbon budgets, new adaptation priorities, and mechanisms to accelerate emissions reductions, ensuring continued full alignment with the GMCA.

column23: This initial report from 2015 was the first from the newly created Office of Resilience and Sustainability and set forth a wide range of goals and activities, including climate adaptation, hazard mitigation, equity and economic development. This was done in collaboration with the Rockefeller 100 Resilient Cities Network. The city developed this strategy by researching the challenges facing New Orleans, gathering input from stakeholders with relevant knowledge and expertise, and sourcing best practices from around the world. The City of New Orleans investigated the city's shocks, stresses, and assets. We met with local organizations and stakeholders to understand how the city's resilience is perceived today, to gather local best practices, and to devise new approaches. Over 350 individuals participated throughout the process and provided valuable insight into what contributes to and detracts from the city's resilience, what local expertise and knowledge exist, and what specific needs are not being met. In addition, the Office of Neighborhood Engagement convened a summit of neighborhood leaders to solicit perspectives on city resilience. This research was then compiled in the Preliminary Resilience Assessment and grouped into focus areas. Working groups, composed of local and outside experts, met to further explore each focus area and propose potential approaches and solutions. This, in turn, led to a more detailed analysis of the opportunities within each focus area and resulted in more specific workshops on issues such as financing, risk modeling, and design. The proposals developed through this process directly inspired the actions set forth in this document.

Nottingham's Carbon Neutral target and associated carbon budget will reduce emissions within the time frames indicated by Paris Agreement and limit the total emissions to a level compatible with an equitable component of implementing a greater-than-even chance of keeping temperature below 2°C.

The carbon budget has been calculated by the Tyndall Centre and is based on translating the “well below 2°C and pursuing 1.5°C” global temperature target and equity principles in the United Nations Paris Agreement to a national UK carbon budget. The UK budget is then split between sub-national areas, to give Nottingham's 'fair' contribution towards the Paris Climate Change Agreement.

Nottingham's Carbon Neutral Charter (www.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/CN2028) recognised that tackling climate change needs to be done in a way that is fair and sustainable- improving and protecting our environment, economy and society. This sits at the heart of the city's approach. The city's Carbon Neutral action plan builds on the Carbon Neutral Charter by setting out high-level objectives in order to achieve a resilient and carbon neutral Nottingham by 2028, and actions to meet these objectives.

column23: When Oslo launched its budget in 2017, the city began tracking its carbon emissions alongside its finances. Oslo's Climate Budget is believed to be the first of its kind. It is a pioneering approach to mainstreaming climate into decision-making processes, which the city considers to be its most important tool for achieving its climate targets.Oslo's Climate and Energy Strategy outlines the city's ambitious climate goals, which include a 95% reduction in emissions by 2030 compared to 2009 - in line with the 1.5°C target of the Paris Agreement. The Climate Budget was created to ensure that the city implements actions to match these ambitions, allocating carbon dioxide (CO2) cuts to relevant sectors. The climate budget process is the responsibility of Oslo's finance department and is a fully integrated part of the regular financial budgeting process. The climate budget presents recent emissions levels and expected future trends, and a detailed breakdown of the measures planned to get there. The effect of new climate measures are estimated based on a baseline scenario with existing measures. The baseline scenario is an integral part of estimating the potential impacts of climate measures that are decided in the climate budget process.

HISTORY OF THE STRATEGY
Vancouver has recognized the need to respond to these impacts and has been taking action for over a decade through the Climate Change Adaptation Strategy (the Strategy), the first of its kind in Canada when approved in 2012. Now on its third iteration following an update in 2018, the Strategy aims to prepare Vancouver for the impacts of a changing climate. Proactively planning for change allows for a greater variety of implementation options, harnessing windows of opportunity and leading to significant avoided costs and losses in the future. Cities are at the forefront of climate impacts and also have many of the tools necessary to respond and adapt. Strong steps have been taken in Vancouver to prepare for climate change impacts, but continued momentum is needed. Public opinion polling indicates a high level of concern for climate change among residents, with extreme weather and disasters the top concern.

2024-25 UPDATE
This 2024-25 Strategy update is structured around the five main climate-related hazards facing Vancouver (extreme heat, poor air quality, drought, extreme rainfall, and sea level rise) and takes a risk-based approach to adaptation planning. The Strategy introduces updated climate projections, new objectives, and an action plan structured around the hazards plus enabling actions to support mainstreaming of climate adaptation across the City. It also has an increased focus on equity, prioritizing adaptation measures that support populations disproportionately impacted by climate change. An indicator and financial framework are included to support implementation. It is important to note that the funding needed to advance climate adaptation at the pace and scale required is beyond the City's capacity and will require long term, sustainable funding from senior levels of government. This is particularly the case for coastal adaptation, for which we know the infrastructure costs will be high and there is a history of senior funding to support.

Description: The Climate Emergency Action Plan is mitigation-focused, and contains 31 action recommendations (organized into six “Big Moves”) in line with efforts to limit global warming to 1.5ºC. CEAP sets a target of 50% reduction in community-wide greenhouse gas emissions reduction by 2030. CEAP adopts an existing goal of deriving 100% of energy used in Vancouver from renewable sources before 2050. It expands the 2050 target, by committing to achieving carbon neutrality in our community-wide greenhouse gas emissions before 2050. CEAP supersedes the previous Renewable City Action Plan (2017), and the greenhouse gas related goals in the Greenest City Action Plan (2011).
Governance: The Climate Emergency Directors Forum provides oversight at a working level, while the Climate Emergency Steering Committee provides oversight at a program level. The Sustainability Group tracks progress and reports to Council annually. Executive reports are also prepared as required. Staff provided an update on CEAP at the halfway of implementation in July 2025.The primary purpose of this plan is to reduce emissions in areas of jurisdiction the City has control or significant influence over. CEAP estimated a cost of approximately $500,000,000 to reach 2030 targets between 2021-2025. Updated modelling have helped the City to measure how a changing policy context provides opportunities to deepen climate action and meet the targets laid out in the plan, including opportunities to ensure that we are meeting our emissions reductions targets.

column23: To set science-based carbon reduction targets for an area, we take the total global level of emissions that the IPCC suggests gives us a 66% chance of limiting average levels of warming to 1.5ºC, and divide it according to the share of the global population living in the area in question. This enables us to set the total carbon budget for an area that is consistent with a global budget. To set targets for carbon reduction, we then calculate the annual percentage reductions from the current level that are required to enable an area to stay within its overall carbon budget. The plan was informed by the Resilience Strategy that highlighted the impacts of rising sea levels and temperatures (amongst other things) on the city.

Following on from The Climate Change Committees NI Advice Report in 2023 and NI's fourth Carbon Budget, the declaration of a climate emergency and subsequent research pieces (energy audits, feasibility studies), Belfast City Council recognised the need to adapt and mitigate against the changing climate. 

In line with global trends, the climate of Northern Ireland and Belfast is changing - temperatures are increasing, sea levels are rising and patterns of precipitation are changing. These changes are projected to continue and intensify with a wide range of impacts for Belfast and Belfast City Council. A summary of key climate and weather-related changes already observed and projected for Northern Ireland and the city of Belfast including- INCREASED TEMPERATURES (annual average temperatures have increased by 0.8 degrees C for the most recent decade compared to 1961-1990 baseline) - CHANGING RAINFALL PATTERNS - average annual rainfall has increased by 7% compared to the same baseline. INCREASED SEA LEVEL RISES AND TIDAL SURGES - sea levels have risen by 16.5cm around the UK and Belfast harbour has experienced 5 highest tidal surges on record since 1994.


After intensive consultation with all departments in the council, 71 actions across 5 themes were developed along with a Monitoring, Learning and Reporting framework that will track progress.
The purpose of this plan is to set out the practical steps Belfast City Council will take in the coming years across its own assets and operations to address the climate emergency, some of which are already underway. The aim is to adopt an integrated approach to tackling the climate and ecological emergency alongside other city priorities to maximise the co-benefits. 
Belfast City Council will mainstream these climate actions into our corporate planning and delivery processes. Each year, selected mitigation and adaptation actions from this plan will be imbedded into our Corporate Annual Delivery Plan and report on our progress in line with Northern Ireland's Public Body reporting requirements under the NI Climate Change Act. 
It will be updated regularly to add new actions and remove actions that have completed.

Carbon Free DC, the District's strategy to reach carbon neutrality by 2045, was released in 2023. Rooted in community priorities for improving health, affordability, accessibility, and economic opportunity, Carbon Free DC identifies key actions necessary to cut greenhouse gas emissions to achieve the District's 2045 commitment to an equitable and carbon free future.

Carbon Free DC is the next step in the District's leadership on equitable climate action. To reach carbon neutrality, the District must transform the drivers of emissions across all sectors—buildings, energy, transportation, and waste— focusing on ways to reduce wasted energy and use more clean, renewable power, while building a more resilient and livable city for all residents.

The District has already made tremendous progress toward carbon neutrality, cutting emissions by 36% between 2006-2021. However, that still leaves more than 7 million metric tons of carbon emissions per year that the District needs to eliminate to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045. Carbon Free DC sets the vision for meeting the 2045 target and charts a pathway to the key milestones and actions needed to achieve the goal. It also provides a guide for future policy and program conversations by turning community feedback into tools to incorporate equity into policy development, and highlights some possible policies for further exploration, including in the updates to Clean Energy DC, Climate Ready DC and Sustainable DC (see below).

Ernst and Young were commissioned to undertake detailed modelling and develop scenarios with associated emissions reductions mapped to 2025 and 2030. 

To inform the development of the strategy we analysed four scenarios:
1. Business as Usual (BAU)
2. Significant Action to reduce emissions
3. Accelerated Action to reduce emissions
4. Purchasing Offsets from 2020.

The City of Melbourne's preferred approach is to deliver the actions needed to achieve the Significant Action Scenario and pursue actions for the Accelerated Action Scenario where there is the opportunity to go further, as reflected in our Response to the Climate Change and Biodiversity Emergency Declaration (2020) This will require us to take bold action within our powers, collaborate and advocate for policy change from the Victorian and Australian Governments. Our approach aligns with the Paris Climate Agreement while acknowledging our limited
powers and financial resources.

Aligning to the science-based targets in the Paris
Climate Agreement requires a mix of delivery mechanisms: engaging, facilitating, collaborating and partnering. We will lead the delivery of actions within our powers and advocate for policy change and action from others.

Council's draft Council Plan 2025-29 includes a deliverable to explore a new Integrated Climate Change Strategy and Circular Economy Framework. Work is underway to develop this framework in alignment with C40's Climate Change Transition Framework.

column30: 都では、2050年の世界のCO2排出量実質ゼロに貢献するため、令和元（2019）年12月に「 ゼロエミッション東京戦略」を策定するとともに、「未来を拓くグリーンでレジリエントな世界都市・東京」の実現に向け、令和4（2022）年9月に「東京都 環境基本計画」を策定しました。 また、令和5（ 2023）年12月には「TOKYO強靭化プロジェクト upgrade Ⅰ 」を、令和6 （2024）年1月には都の長期計画である「『 未来の東京』戦略 version up 2024」をそれぞれ公表しました。一方、令和5（2023）年4月には、気候変動適応の一分野である熱中症対策を強 化するため、 熱中症特別警戒情報の創設や、 指定暑熱避難施設（クーリングシェルター）の指定等を盛り込んだ、改正気候変動適応法が国会で可決・成立しました。改定する新たな計画では、こうした動向やSDGs（ 持続可能な開発目標）の実現への寄与などの観点も踏まえつつ、 都民・事業者等との連携・ 協働の下、気候変動 の緩和と 適応の両面から 生命・ 財産を将来にわたって守る施策を展開し 、持続可能な発展を図ることを目的としています。（P2）\nIn order to contribute to the world's net zero CO2 emissions by 2050, Metropolitan Government formulated the \'Zero Emission Tokyo Strategy\' in December 2019 and formulated \'Tokyo Environmental Master Plan\' in September 2022 to realize \'A Green and Resilient Global City Tokyo Opens up a Future.\' In addition, \' TOKYO Resilience Project Upgrade I\' was announced in December 2023, and in January 2024, Metropolitan government's long-term plan, \''Future Tokyo' Strategy version up 2024,\' was announced. On the other hand, in April 2023, the Diet passed and established Revised Climate Change Adaptation Act to strengthen measures against heatstroke, which is a field of adaptation to climate change, including the creation of Special Heat Stroke Alert information and the designation of designated heat evacuation facilities (Cooling shelters). column23: 直面する気候危機を回避するため、2016年に発効したパリ協定では、世界の平均気温の上昇を産業革命前から2℃未満に抑えること、1.5℃未満に抑える努力をすることが共通目標として掲げられた。また、2018年10月に国連の気候変動に関する政府間パネル（IPCC）が公表した「1.5℃特別報告書」では、世界の平均気温の上昇を1.5℃に抑えるためには、世界の温室効果ガス排出量を2050年までに実質ゼロ、2030年までに約半減させることが必要と示された。2021年11月に英国グラスゴーで開催されたCOP26では、1.5℃に抑える努力を追求することが世界的に合意され、脱炭素化に向けた潮流は、世界中で大きな加速を見せている。しかしながら、IPCC が2021年8月に公表した第6次評価報告書第1作業部会報告書では、2021年から2040年までの間に1.5℃を超える可能性が非常に高いことが報告されている。（P7)　世界有数の大都市である東京は、エネルギーの大消費地としての責務を果たすとともに、脱炭素社会においてもレジリエントで持続可能な成長を実現する都市であり続けるため、気温上昇を1.5℃に抑えることを追求し、ゼロエミッション東京の実現を目指す。省エネや再エネ、水素等の活用によるCO2排出量の最小化、省資源化、再生資源の活用、ZEVの普及、フロン対策、さらには革新的なイノベーションの誘導など、あらゆる分野の取組を気候変動対策として進化させ、都内からのCO2排出量の実質ゼロを目指すとともに、都外でのCO2削減にも貢献していく。（P27)\nTo avoid the climate crisis facing us, the Paris Agreement, which came into effect in 2016, set a common goal of holding the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels. According to the Special Report on Global Warming of 1.5°C publicized by UN IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) in October 2018, limiting global average temperature rise to 1.5°C requires global greenhouse gas emissions to be approximately halved by 2030 and net zero by 2050. At COP26 held in Glasgow, UK in November 2021, it was agreed globally to pursue efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C, indicating that the trend toward decarbonization is significantly accelerated around the world. However, the Working Group I Contribution to the Sixth Assessment Report released by IPCC in August 2021 stated that the temperature rise is very likely to exceed 1.5°C between 2021 and 2040. (P7)As one of the world's largest cities, Tokyo aims to realize a Zero Emission Tokyo by pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C in order to fulfi ll its responsibility as a major energy consumer and continue to be a city that achieves resilient and sustainable growth in a decarbonized society. Tokyo will strive for achieving net zero CO2 emissions in itself and contributing to the reduction of CO2 in other regions by developing climate change measures based on efforts in a wide range of fi elds: Energy effi ciency, the use of renewable energy, minimizing CO2 emissions through hydrogen etc., resource effi ciency, the utilization of recycled resources, the spread of ZEVs, measures for fl uorocarbons, and the encouragement of revolutionary innovation. (P27)

column30: 都は、2016年3月に策定した環境基本計画の下、「世界一の環境先進都市・東京」の実現を目指し、幅広く環境施策に取り組んできた。　計画策定から6年、持続可能な社会の実現に対する関心が世界的に高まる中で、気候危機の一層の深刻化、生物多様性の損失、水・大気環境の変化など、環境を取り巻く状況は世界規模で大きな課題となっている。また、国連の推計によると、2030年までに世界の人口は85億人、2050年には97億人に増加し、世界人口のほとんどの増加は都市地域で発生すると予測されている。さらに、新型コロナウイルス感染症の感染拡大に加え、ウクライナ・ロシア情勢による資源やエネルギーへの影響等、未曽有の危機の最中にある。　欧州を中心に、気候危機への対処を図りながら、コロナ禍からの「より良い復興」を目指す「グリーン・リカバリー」の流れが生まれている。都は、持続可能な生活を実現する観点にまで広げた「サステナブル・リカバリー（持続可能な回復）」を進めている。グリーンかつレジリエントな「ゼロエミッション東京」を実現し、50年、100年先も、自然との共生や質の高い大気環境など、豊かさにあふれる持続可能な都市をつくるため、まさに今、行動を起こさなければならない。　都は、世界の主要都市の一員として、世界の、そして東京の未来を切り拓くため、都の環境施策を更に大胆に加速する、新たな環境基本計画を策定することとした。（P2）\nIn accordance with the Environmental Master Plan formulated in March 2016, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government (TMG) has been working on a wide range of environmental initiatives with the aim of realizing Tokyo as a world-leading, environmentconscious city.While interest in the realization of a sustainable society has increased worldwide in the six years since the formulation of the plan, the environmental situation is posing ever more serious issues on a global scale, such as further aggravated climate crisis, biodiversity loss, and changes in the water environment and air quality. The United Nations estimates that the world population will grow to 8.5 billion by 2030 and 9.7 billion by 2050, with almost all of the growth occurring in urban areas. In addition, we are in the midst of unprecedented crises, including the COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of the conflict between Ukraine and Russia on resources and energy.In European and other countries, there is a movement aiming for a green recovery to “build back better” from the COVID-19 crisis while coping with the climate crisis. TMG is promoting sustainable recovery that expands the perspective to include the realization of sustainable lifestyles. Now is the time to act for TMG to realize a green and sustainable Zero Emission Tokyo and create a sustainable city full of abundance, which will provide environmental symbiosis and an excellent air quality 50 or 100 years from now.As one of the major cities in the world, TMG determined to formulate a new Environmental Master Plan that will more boldly accelerate our environmental initiatives to open up the future of the world and Tokyo. (P2)

In 2022, Kaohsiung City's total GHG emissions reached 53.53 million metric tons of CO₂e. After deducting carbon absorption from forest carbon sinks, the net emissions were 52.35 million metric tons of CO₂e. According to Article 4 of the “Kaohsiung City Net-Zero Urban Development and Self-Government Ordinance,” the city aims to reduce GHG emissions by 30% by 2030 compared to 2005 levels, and to achieve net-zero by 2050, in pursuit of a sustainable and livable city.
A carbon budget refers to the upper limit of GHG emissions for each period, with each period spanning two years. The next period's budget must be proposed one year before the current period ends. Prior to formulation, the carbon budget must undergo a consultation process that includes public hearings or other appropriate means to gather opinions from relevant agencies, scholars, experts, and civil society groups. The draft budget is then submitted to the Kaohsiung City Sustainable Development and Climate Change Response Promotion Commission for review, followed by approval from the City Council.
In line with the National Development Council's (NDC) 2050 Net-Zero Roadmap, Kaohsiung City uses the national population growth rate projected by the NDC as a variable, and integrates data from approved Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) cases to project the city's future GHG emission trajectory based on economic development. Key factors include expansion of industrial parks, new building construction, and development of transportation systems. Kaohsiung City's first-phase carbon budget draws on the UK's carbon budgeting system and considers approved EIA cases between 2022 and June 2024 as a basis for evaluating potential increases in GHG emissions.

To achieve Kaohsiung City's net-zero target, the Kaohsiung City Government has drawn reference from the United Kingdom's carbon budgeting system. Through a bottom-up planning approach, the city has conducted a comprehensive assessment of mid- and long-term reduction potentials across sectors, while taking into account Kaohsiung City's natural environment, industrial characteristics, and social structure. Based on this, the city has planned its GHG reduction pathway and is establishing a carbon budget system.
A carbon budget refers to the upper limit of GHG emissions for each period, with each period spanning two years. The next period's budget must be proposed one year before the current period ends. Prior to formulation, the carbon budget must undergo a consultation process that includes public hearings or other appropriate means to gather opinions from relevant agencies, scholars, experts, and civil society groups. The draft budget is then submitted to the Kaohsiung Sustainable Development and Climate Change Adaptation Promotion Council for review, followed by approval from the City Council.
To ensure the alignment of economic growth with emission reductions, Kaohsiung City will regularly monitor and evaluate progress toward its reduction targets and make timely adjustments to its net-zero policies. With the vision of decoupling economic growth from GHG emissions, the city will steadily move toward its net-zero goal by developing and refining its carbon budgeting framework.

The City of Sydney local area is facing more challenges from the impacts of climate change and social and economic disruptions, which threaten the city's stability and prosperity. To address these challenges, The City developed a local resilience strategy that sets out a vision for a more adaptive and prosperous city.
The strategy's challenges and opportunities are described across 5 directions:
Direction 1: An equitable, inclusive and connected community - collaborate with partners and community to increase equity and create connected communities that are more resilient to shocks and stresses.
Direction 2: A climate resilient city - adapt to a changing climate by understanding risks and creating equitable solutions.
Direction 3: Places, buildings and infrastructure for resilience - strengthen infrastructure and assets to withstand shocks and stresses and build community resilience.
Direction 4: A robust local economy - improve community economic resilience through diversity, inclusivity and revitalising our city.
Direction 5: A prepared community - work with communities and government to prepare organisations, services and people to respond to and recover from shock events.
Our resilience strategy requires partnerships and collaboration between the City of Sydney and other levels of government, business and community organisations. We're prioritising action and investment in physical infrastructure, social systems, economic sustainability, and programs, people and existing initiatives.
By working together, we can create a more adaptive and thriving city for our communities to be better prepared for future challenges.

The review applied downscaled climate models (six AR5 global models, bias-corrected to 8×8 km resolution for Gauteng province).Scenarios were analysed for two timeframes: near-future (2021-2050) and far-future (2070-2099), relative to a 1961-1990 baseline. Both high emissions (worst-case) and strong mitigation (best-case) futures were considered.
Temperature:
Even under best-case mitigation, Gauteng warms by ~3°C.
Worst-case pathways (RCP8.5) show ~6°C warming, with devastating effects on agriculture, water security, and health.
Rainfall:
Most projections show a general drying trend, especially in southern and western Gauteng.
Some ensemble members allow for increases in rainfall, though these are less likely.
Extremes:
Multi-year droughts become much more frequent.
Extreme thunderstorms and flash floods may increase, even as overall rainfall declines.
Future “normal” years may be worse than Gauteng's 2015/16 drought.

Risk Framing:
Scenarios highlighted that Johannesburg must prepare for opposite extremes: severe droughts and intense storms. This directly informed the call for both a Drought Plan and a Flood Plan.
Priority Areas:
Scenario evidence underpinned the selection of three Key Risk Areas (KRAs): Governance, Water Security, and Heat/Health. These KRAs align with the projected risks of hotter, drier conditions and rising heatwave/health threats.
Planning Approach:
The review cautioned that rigid, “one-size-fits-all” approaches risk becoming maladaptive under shifting scenarios. Instead, it recommended flexible, reflexive planning, capable of adjusting as new scenario evidence emerges.
Equity and Resilience:
Scenario analysis emphasised the uneven burden of future climate extremes—especially on poorer communities—leading to stronger focus on just and inclusive adaptation.

Climate scenarios were developed for both adaptation and mitigation aspects of the CAP. 

For adaptation the methodology was employed: future climate change scenarios, called Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs), are based on potential levels of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. These scenarios, developed by the IPCC, predict different levels of radiative forcing by 2100: 2.4, 4.5, 6, and 8.5 W/m², depending on how much GHG emissions are reduced.

Key point:

RCPs: Trajectories of atmospheric GHG concentrations.

The Climate Action Plan (CAP) projects the impact of climate change on temperatures and rainfall in the City of Johannesburg by 2050, using the latest downscaled climate change scenarios. It focuses on:

RCP4.5: Requires ambitious global climate action.
RCP8.5: Likely without significant climate action.

In both scenarios, temperatures are projected to rise beyond 2 degrees by 2050. As for rainfall, while there is no clear trend, there are signs of more intense and frequent storms.

In addressing mitigation, the Business As Usual (BAU) baseline trajectory was developed, reflecting the City's projected economic and population growth up to 2050. Under this scenario, the City's emissions are projected to increase by 133%, from 20.9 million metric tons of CO2 equivalent (MtCO2e) in 2016 to 48.7 MtCO2e by 2050. The city also considered the C40's Deadline 2020 scenario analysis report. In this report, Johannesburg was categorized as an 'early peak city.' Johannesburg's proposed mitigation scenario includes room for some growth in emissions in the short term, but states that the City's GHG emissions should
peak by 2030 at no more than 28.9 MtCO2e, and then decline towards net-zero emissions by 2050. Thereafter the city developed two scenarios: Existing and planned and Ambitious scenarios. The 'Existing and planned scenario' demonstrates the
GHG emission reductions that may be achieved through implementation of policies and actions that are already in place. This includes policies and actions initiated by the City, provincial or national administrations that have already been planned or committed to, and that will impact future GHG
emissions. The objective of the 'Ambitious scenario 'is to explore opportunities to enhance and scale-up existing programmes and identify additional actions to deliver greater future emissions reductions and help the city move closer to meeting its targets.

The final CAP incorporates a mitigation planning process. This outlines sectoral GHG targets and details a range of mitigation actions the city will implement to achieve a carbon-neutral future.

The CAP employed an iterative and consultative process with stakeholders to prioritise actions. The prioritisation was informed by the following:
 
1. Evidence and Risk Assessments
The Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment and CSIR Green Book informed the prioritisation of adaptation actions. Areas with highest exposure to drought, flooding, and heatwaves (e.g., Soweto, Alexandra, Diepsloot, Orange Farm) were prioritised for resilience interventions.

2. Socio-Economic and Human Benefits
Actions were assessed using a Benefit-Cost Profile approach. Adaptation measures were prioritised based on their Human Benefit Indicator (HBI) - i.e., the number of people reached and the degree of improvement in health, wellbeing, and safety. Co-benefits such as job creation, poverty alleviation, and service delivery improvements influenced ranking.

3. Emission Reduction Potential
For mitigation, priority was given to actions with the greatest GHG reduction potential relative to Johannesburg's net-zero 2050 target.
Scenarios compared “existing and planned actions” with “ambitious actions,” and ambitious but realistic measures were prioritised to close the emissions gap.

4. Feasibility and Resources
Actions were filtered for technical feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and readiness for implementation.
“Early win” interventions that could be financed within existing budgets or through climate finance (e.g., green bonds, donor programmes) were ranked higher.

5. Policy Alignment
Prioritisation ensured actions aligned with the Joburg 2040 Growth and Development Strategy, national climate policies, the Paris Agreement, and C40 Leadership Standards. This alignment helps secure political support and financing.

6. Inclusivity and Equity
Actions were prioritised that advance climate justice, address the needs of vulnerable communities, and contribute to a just transition.
Stakeholder engagement (including youth and community organisations) was central to validating which actions should take priority.

Toronto's Resilience Strategy sets out a vision, goals, and actions to help Toronto survive, adapt and thrive in the face of any challenge, particularly climate change and growing inequities.

Actions are organized into three focus areas: People & Neighbourhoods, Infrastructure, and Leading a Resilient City. Each focus area contains a series of goals and specific actions, which are the most critical projects Toronto must undertake to achieve resilience.

Climate-related goals include:
• Toronto is more resilient to climate change, including the hazards of flooding and heat;
• Infrastructure and buildings are resilient to a changing climate and reduce greenhouse gas emissions; and
• Institutionalize resilience into the City's decision-making and take leadership on resilience.

Annotation: In June 2014, City Council received the 39 page report, 'Resilient City: Preparing for Climate Change' (item 2014.PE28.6). This report outlined an approach for integrating climate change resilience into decision-making and co-ordination of City operations and services. That approach was endorsed with the adoption of the Climate Change Risk Management Policy (CCRMP is on page 26 of the report), which defines responsibilities within the Toronto Public Service executive management for identifying 
and taking action to address significant climate risks. Council also directed at this time 
that there be regular implementation status reports, starting in 2016.

It should be noted that the CCRMP is not widely known at this time. The Resilience Strategy serves as a major update to this 2014 CCRMP. However, the Resilience Strategy, although widely known and issued very publicly after major stakeholder consultation efforts, was never officially adopted by City Council and thus no new resources were assigned to its implementation. The CCRMP has never been rescinded and technically does remain in effect.

Activity is currently ongoing to review current climate adaptation requirements involving an updated city-wide climate risk assessment to be coupled with an update review to physical climate risk governance update requirements.

A model was used to explore pathways to net zero GHG emissions. All pathways analysed the GHG impacts between 2020-2050. The modelling enabled us to understand the GHG impact of various activities, and the impact of taking or delaying action. In December 2021, Toronto City Council adopted (IE26.16) an ambitious strategy to reduce community-wide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in Toronto to net zero by 2040 - 10 years earlier than initially proposed.

The Net Zero Strategy triggers new and accelerated implementation actions to drive down community-wide emissions, particularly in the short term, and establishes the trajectory needed to reach net zero by 2040.

With the adoption of the Net Zero Strategy, the City's GHG reduction targets, from 1990 
levels, are:
• 30 per cent by 2020
• 45 per cent by 2025
• 65 per cent by 2030
• net zero by 2040.

Background: In July 2017, Toronto's TransformTO climate action strategy was unanimously approved by City Council. It includes a set of long-term, low-carbon goals and strategies to reduce local greenhouse gas emissions and improve our health, grow our economy, and improve social equity. The Net Zero Strategy adopted by Council in December 2021 builds on the initial TransformTO Strategy.

2030 targets set by the City of Toronto to show 'leadership by example' include: 

• City of Toronto corporate greenhouse gas emissions are reduced by 65 per cent over 2008 base year
• All City Agency, Corporation and Division-owned new developments are designed and constructed to applicable Toronto Green Standard Version 4 
standard achieving zero carbon emissions, beginning in 2022
• Greenhouse gas emissions from City-owned buildings are reduced by 60 per cent from 2008 levels; by 2040, City-owned buildings reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions
• All City-owned facilities have achieved zero waste
• Generate and utilize 1.5 Million Gigajoules of energy from biogas
• Approximately 107,700 tonnes CO2e per year are reduced through Organics Processing with Renewable Energy and Landfill Gas Utilization
• 50 per cent of the City-owned fleet is transitioned to zero-emissions vehicles
• 50 per cent of the TTC bus fleet is zero emissions
• Greenhouse gas emissions from food the City of Toronto procures are reduced by 25 per cent

Meeting the targets will require significant levels of investment (see link below), and coordination from all Divisions, Agencies and Corporations.

In March 2024, A Staff Report was adopted by City Council, ' Toronto's Climate Change Readiness: Updates on commitments and a refreshed mandate for coordinating resilience activities' This council adopted staff report constitutes a 'plan to get a refreshed plan' and is therefore relevant to this question. The staff report is available at this link: 

https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2024/ie/bgrd/backgroundfile-244181.pdf

In 2022-2023, a new team was established within the Environment, Climate, and Forestry Division at the City to specifically support climate resilience. 

An outcome of this work identified the benefit of establishing centralized, refreshed guidance on climate resilience that builds on past work, incorporates up-to-date information, aligns us with peer cities, and protects vulnerable people. Four priority areas for action surfaced:

(i) clear direction to address climate resilience as a priority
(ii) an approach that will prioritize Indigenous worldviews, relational views of land protection and Indigenous community leadership to enhance climate resilience
(iii) more access to evidence, information, expertise, and advice to guide the City's priorities and actions
(iv) development of a clear framework, mandate and objectives for addressing climate impacts at a City-wide level. 

Key outcomes of the staff report directives will be the Executive Director, Environment & Climate Division in collaboration with all City Divisions, Agencies, Boards, and Corporations to report
back to the Infrastructure and Environment Committee in Q4 2025 with the following:

(a) an update on Division, Agencies and Corporations' current activities and future plans where current and future climate conditions are included in their respective infrastructure, operational, policy, and program planning
(b) a refreshed governance approach that integrates climate resilience into decision-making and co-ordination across the services, assets, and communities of the City of Toronto, that builds upon the climate-specific learnings from the City's 2019 Resilience Strategy
(c) a list of climate resilience priorities and recommended next steps based on technical analysis of climate risk that incorporate insights from engagement with internal and external partners
(d) a discussion of how Indigenous worldviews and relationships with Indigenous communities have been prioritized in climate resilience planning to date.

Toronto's Corporate Asset Management Policy establishes the framework and a whole-of-government approach to asset management for assets owned that are managed by City Divisions, Agencies and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation (TCHC) and reported as part of the City's consolidated financial statements. Section 8.1.6. of the Corporate Asset Management Policy requires climate to be considered in the 
development of asset management plans:

The City will consider, as part of its asset management planning, risks and vulnerabilities and the impact of climate change on its municipal infrastructure assets and relevant adaptation and mitigation actions including:

i) The actions that may be required to address risks and vulnerabilities in respect of such matters as: 
• Operations, such as increased maintenance schedules; 
• Levels of service; and 
• Lifecycle management 

ii) The anticipated costs that could arise from these risks and vulnerabilities; 

iii) Adaptation opportunities that may be undertaken to manage these risks and vulnerabilities; 

iv) Mitigation approaches to climate change, such as greenhouse gas emission reduction goals and targets; and 

v) Disaster planning and contingency funding.

Through this Climate City Contract (CCC), the Municipality of Athens aims to work with all relevant stakeholders and citizens of Athens to achieve the transformation of the city to climate neutrality by 2030. The contract aims to achieve a reduction of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from the city's activities by 80% and at the same time make Athens green, beautiful, clean, with strong social cohesion, and a sustainable economy. The Climate City Contract consists of 3 parts: 1) The Climate Neutrality Commitments, which is signed not only by the Municipality but also by institutions and citizens in order to constitute a political commitment for policies, practices, and actions that will support
change towards the climate neutrality of the city.
2) The Climate Action Plan, that describes a detailed action plan for achieving these goals,
complementing the strategic priorities that are presented in the CCC Commitments document. 3) The CCC Investment Plan is then assessing the investment needs for achieving these strategies and actions and explores different options for securing these investments.

column23: According to the requirements of the Berlin Climate and Energy Act, the climate action plan must be regularly updated and submitted to the parliament one year after the constitution of the parliament. Against this background, the former climate action plan (BEK 2030) was updated in 2022 for the implementation period 2022 to 2026, taking into account new climate targets, scientific findings and recommendations for action. As part of the further development, the strategies and measures were therefore aligned with Berlin's new climate protection targets and reduction paths for the interim target 2040 (minus 90 percent compared to 1990) and climate neutrality target 2045 (minus 95 percent compared to 1990) were identified. A scientific project consortium was commissioned with the preparation and further development of the BEK 2030, and another consortium was in charge of the public participation process. In addition to expert forums, workshops and public events, there were two phases of online participation for citizens in the approximately one-year development process, in which suggestions and tips for further development as well as concrete measures could be submitted and evaluated.

column30: With the continuation of the BEK 2030 for the implementation period 2022 to 2026, far-reaching measures were adopted in the areas of climate protection and climate adaptation, which the governemt is to implement in the coming years. In the area of climate protection, the switch to fossil-free energy sources in the electricity and heat supply plays a central role in the field of energy. All available renewable energy potentials in the areas of solar, wind, waste heat, geothermal and bioenergy must be tapped in the best possible way and appropriate infrastructures for storage solutions must be developed. In the buildings sector, the increase of the energetic refurbishment rate in existing buildings, the climate-neutral construction of new buildings and the phase-out of fossil fuels for the supply of buildings are named as central key factors. Important measures here are the development of spatial heat planning and the expansion of advisory services and state funding programmes for building owners. The City of Berlin will also advocate the socially acceptable implementation of renovation obligations in existing buildings at the federal level. In the transport sector, a transofrmation of mobility within the city is key. In the field of passenger mobility, this means the expansion of cycling and walking infrastructures or the qualitative improvement and quantitative expansion of public transport services. The conversion of the municipal vehicle fleet to climate-friendly drive systems is to be exemplary. Climate adaptation was strengthened in this Climate Action Plan's update. Fields of action such as biodiversity and tourism, sport and culture have been newly included in the BEK 2030.

El objetivo de la ciudad, en materia de mitigación, es que Bogotá sea carbono neutral a 2050. El criterio para fijar ese objetivo está basado en la ciencia climática, particularmente los informes de evaluación de IPCC, que indican que para evitar un aumento de la temperatura media del planeta por encima de 1.5°C es necesario alcanzar la carbono neutralidad hacia mitad de siglo y la neutralidad de los otros gases en las siguientes pocas décadas. El objetivo de la ciudad busca contribuir con la meta global de evitar un calentamiento global superior 1.5°C con respecto a los niveles preindustriales, estableciendo metas de mitigación a corto plazo y mediano plazo (reducción del 15% de las emisiones GEI respecto al escenario BAU 2024 y reducción del 50% de las emisiones GEI respecto al escenario BAU a 2030), que permitan alcanzar la carbono-neutralidad de la ciudad en función de su potencial de mitigación.

En cuanto a adaptación, se integraron escenarios de cambio climático a escala nacional y regional que especifican que para el año 2040, se proyecta un aumento en la temperatura promedio de Bogotá de 0,25 °C en la zona rural y 0,65 °C en el área urbana. Asimismo, mientras que hacia el occidente de Bogotá se pronostica que aumentará el porcentaje de lluvias hasta en un 35 % para 2040, en los Cerros Orientales. Esta información sirve como base para el desarrollo de la evaluación de riesgos climáticos, con la cual se identificaron las principales amenazas climáticas, determinando así el índice de riesgos climáticos y se conoció la vulnerabilidad de la ciudad.

En el proceso de diagnóstico de la política pública de acción climática se realizaron talleres de participación ciudadana con enfoques (incluyendo participación de pueblos indígenas, afros, comunidad LGBT, mujeres, jóvenes, niños, adultos mayores). El instrumento de política pública se monitorea anualmente por la Secretaría Distrital de Planeación y la política pública puede ser revisada, cada 4 años o antes si es necesario (por ejemplo para ajustarse a los presupuestos nacionales de carbono en caso de que estos sean más estrictos que las metas de la ciudad). Hay productos con metas específicas en esta política para la actualización anual o bienal del inventario de emisiones, de los escenarios proyectados de emisiones y para la actualización periódica de la evaluación de riesgos climáticos en todo el horizonte hasta 2050.

column23: En el marco del Plan de Acción Climática 2050, se analizaron variaciones en el clima para diferentes escenarios y horizontes, evaluando los cambios que podrían ocurrir en el clima de la ciudad de Buenos Aires en términos de temperatura y precipitación bajo los umbrales determinados como objetivos de estabilización de la temperatura media global respecto del período preindustrial (1850-1900) en el Acuerdo de París. A estos umbrales de calentamiento (1,5°C y 2°C) se incorporó en el análisis las posibles consecuencias de un incremento de la temperatura global de 3°C ya que representa el calentamiento que se alcanzaría a fin del presente siglo como resultado de las políticas implementadas a la fecha . Asimismo, al estudio realizado sobre los cambios previstos en función de diferentes umbrales de calentamiento global se le agrega la evaluación de los cambios para tres horizontes temporales durante el presente siglo: 2021-2040 (corto plazo), 2041-2060 (mediano plazo) y 2081-2100 (largo plazo). En todos los casos, las proyecciones de clima futuro son realizadas a partir de la información provista por modelos climáticos globales utilizados por el Panel Intergubernamental de Cambio Climático en diferentes reportes recientes y considerando dos escenarios de trayectorias representativas de concentraciones. En cuanto a escenarios futuros de emisiones de GEI fueron elaborados con apoyo de la red C40, y se encuentran en línea con lo establecido en el Acuerdo de Paris, obtenidos a través de la herramienta Pathways desarrollada por C40 para el programa CAP (Climate Action Planning) Latinoamérica.

column23: Em 2020, como parte do Programa de Assistência Técnica do Grupo C40, a Avaliação de Risco Climático da Cidade de Curitiba foi elaborada pela iCare & Consult. O objetivo deste estudo foi ampliar o conhecimento sobre os riscos presentes e futuros das mudanças climáticas na cidade de Curitiba, relatando elementos suficientes para subsidiar o desenvolvimento de ações para aumentar a resiliência da cidade por meio do PlanClima.A primeira fase do estudo incluiu a avaliação histórica das tendências climáticas da cidade, abrangendo o horizonte temporal da base disponível (1960-2019) e a projeção de variáveis climáticas até 2100. Análises climáticas futuras consideraram um cenário de aumento crítico das emissões de GEE estimado pelo Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) no quinto relatório de avaliação do IPCC, AR5, divulgado em 2014 (RCP 8.5).Na segunda fase, o estudo buscou identificar as principais ameaças climáticas registradas na cidade, com base em dados sobre a ocorrência de eventos extremos entre 2012 e 2020. A partir de uma análise probabilística desses dados - incluindo avaliações históricas e futuras de variáveis climáticas, além da disponibilidade de dados que pudessem ser espacialmente explícitos - foram priorizadas as principais ameaças climáticas: inundações, inundações, deslizamentos e suscetibilidade a ondas de calor.A terceira fase da avaliação consistiu em uma análise de risco, compreendendo uma análise de exposição, vulnerabilidade e ameaças climáticas. Na análise da exposição, foi realizada modelagem do uso do solo (pinçando as infraestruturas críticas da cidade) como forma de simular a expansão urbana para o horizonte temporal de 2100. População da cidade, carga rodoviária e estabelecimentos ativos por setor de atividade econômica. A avaliação da vulnerabilidade foi realizada por meio de indicadores de sensibilidade, que explicam as iniquidades socioeconômicas existentes no município, e indicadores relacionados à sua capacidade adaptativa. A quarta e última fase avaliou o nível de resiliência da cidade em geral, como forma de identificar as lacunas que impactam a adaptação da cidade às mudanças climáticas.

Since İstanbul is a city that is acutely aware of the vulnerability created by climate change and being a signatory of Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM), IMM is committed to reduce GHG emissions 40% by 2030 from 2019 levels and prepare and implement Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) in this respect. SECAP defines the activities and measures set up to achieve this target. For Climate Change mitigation, the main target sectors are buildings, equipment/facilities, urban transport, and waste.

Through SECAP, energy efficiency measures are targeted at the sectors with the greatest potential for energy savings, such as the building, industry, transport, and waste sectors. IMM is responsible for public transportation, waste management, water supply, sewerage system and treatment, recreational areas, road paving, urban and zone planning. IMM is not involved in the production, transmission, distribution of electricity, or public street lighting for the city. However, it does operate several energy production plants, such as solar and waste-to-energy plants, to generate electricity for its own use.

The municipality's buildings will begin their energy efficiency journey by modernizing the largest and most energy-intensive buildings. 19 buildings have been identified and have undergone energy audits and are ready to start their modernization projects. The remaining buildings of the municipality will be grouped according to their energy consumption in order to prioritize their modernization, starting with the most energy-intensive buildings. A program, consisting of installing solar PV plants and using alternative energy sources to generate around 50% of the municipality's current electricity demand by 2030, is also planned.

The 'Koru Istanbul' initiative, prepared by the IMM, is a comprehensive strategy and planning initiative aimed at protecting Istanbul's natural and rural areas. The Istanbul Natural and Rural Areas Strategy Document was prepared as part of this roadmap. The main objectives of the strategic document are as follows:
- To protect and preserve the resources and biodiversity in natural areas
- To achieve rural development,
- rehabilitating degraded areas and restoring the integrity of forests and rural areas
- To establish a sustainable natural and rural area management model based on the principles of good and democratic governance.

Istanbul's total surface area is 534,000 hectares, with a total agricultural area of 86,884 hectares and a total forest area of 240,000 hectares. This study determined that the percentage of agricultural land is 16.25%, while the percentage of forest area is 45.02%.

The Koru Istanbul Action Plan covers a total of 66 actions, 6 project packages, and 50 projects.

6 priority actions were identified:

1- The Sazlıdere Basin and Water Resources, which are under threat and destruction from Canal Istanbul, have been identified as the priority action area for projects such as developing spatial plans focused on conservation and rural development, establishing a platform to monitor Canal Istanbul's implementation and outcomes. 

2- The Terkos Basin, which is under pressure from construction by the Third Bridge, the Third Airport, and the Northern Marmara Highway, and the agricultural areas within its impact area have been identified as priority action areas for projects focused on expanding forests under protection status and species conservation.

3- The Ömerli Basin, which is under mining activity, has been identified as priority action areas for projects focused on raising awareness, prevention, control, and restoration against mining activities.

4- The Belgrade Forest and its severed parts have been identified as priority action areas for projects focused on habitat consolidation, ecological network creation, and corridor creation.

5- The Northern Forests and Rural Areas, which underlie Istanbul's urban areas, have been identified as priority action areas for projects focused on establishing green buffer zones.

6- Forest Parts within Densely Urbanized Areas have been identified as priority action areas for projects such as forest clearing and ecosystem-based management plans.

According to the 2024 ISTON (Concrete company of IMM) Sustainability Report, significant environmental steps have been taken. These include: Acting with awareness of its responsibility to protect natural ecosystems, İSTON develops projects to minimize its impacts on biodiversity and support the sustainability of ecosystems.

1) Artifical Reef Production by Concrete

By creating artificial concrete reefs, it supports the revitalization of marine ecosystems and improves marine habitats. This product helps prevent seabed habitat loss and encourages the enrichment of underwater ecosystems.

2) Ensuring Shelters to Vulnerable Groups

Meeting the urgent and cost-effective shelter needs of vulnerable groups such as refugees and earthquake victims is crucial. This need is typically met through quick and inexpensive tents and prefabricated structures. However, these solutions, due to ongoing wars and economic fluctuations, have forced people into almost permanent temporary housing, forcing them into poor living conditions that can lead to undesirable consequences such as thermal discomfort, disease, fire hazards, and security vulnerabilities. Within the scope of the TÜBİTAK 2551 Bilateral Cooperation Program, the project titled 'Climate Resilient 3D-Printable Building Components Incorporating Sustainable and Low-Cost Materials (3D-PC): Providing Low-Cost and High-Speed Housing for Vulnerable Populations' was carried out and completed in partnership with METU.

3) SPP Installation

İSTON has taken a significant step in sustainability and renewable energy, commencing work on the installation of a 1,000 kWp solar power plant (SPP) on the roof of its Hadımköy factory. Following project approval, the agreement was signed in August 2024. Completion is planned for 2027.

column30: District heating (Fernwärme)\nThe environmental office of the city of Heidelberg has been working on a municipal heating plan since spring 2022. This envisages a completely climate-neutral heat supply for the city by 2040 and for municipal properties by 2030. The municipal heating plan is being carried out in cooperation with the Heidelberg municipal utility company. It is being prepared by the engineering firms Enerko and ebök and the ifeu research institute. For the heat turnaround, two central strategies must be pursued, in addition to the reduction of heat demand through energy refurbishment and increased efficiency. On the one hand, a strong expansion of district heating and the establishment of heating networks in the city districts in connection with CO2-free heat generation are necessary. Second, outside the future district heating areas, the fossil heat generators natural gas and oil must be replaced by heat pumps. Municipal heat planning takes place in four steps: With the inventory analysis now completed, the current and future heat demand has been determined. Now the possibilities for energy saving, district heating expansion and new green heat sources from renewable energies and waste heat are being evaluated. This step is currently underway and will also be a focus of the public information event. Subsequently, a scenario will be developed of what a climate-neutral heat supply in Heidelberg could look like. In addition, an energy and greenhouse gas balance by sector and energy source for 2030 and 2040 will be presented. The local utility continuously expands its district heating system. To date, 80% of the heat is supplied by a coal-fired CHP plant in Mannheim (neighboring city). This amount will decrease continuously by integration renewable heat sources to the grid. At the moment this is 20% from the wood chip fired CHP plant. The municipal utility Stadtwerke Heidelberg aims to further increase the share of renewables by constructing further CHP plants, a heat storage tower, coupling waste incineration plant to the grid and using solar thermal power. https://www.heidelberg.de/2167309

column23: Rencana Pembangunan Rendah Karbon Daerah yang Berketahanan Iklim (RPRKD) ini merupakan bentuk komitmen Provinsi DKI Jakarta dalam memberikan kontribusi aktif bagi pencapaian kontribusi yang ditetapkan secara nasional (NDC) serta komitmen global yang telah disepakati dalam Perjanjian Paris dengan mengakselerasi aksi mitigasi dan adaptasi peru bahan iklim dalam tenggat waktu yang tersisa menuju tahun 2030 sebagai batu loncatan menuju netralitas emisi (net zero emission) pada tahun 2050. Skenario penurunan Emisi GRK 30% pada tahun 2030 Berdasarkan Lampiran Peraturan Gubemur Nomor 131 tahun 2012 tentang RAD-GRK dinyatakan bahwa upaya penurunan Emisi GRK yang direncanakan periode implementasi tahun 2010 sampai dengan 2030 dengan target penurunan Emisi GRK sebesar 35 juta ton CO2e. Target tersebut diharapkan dapat menurunkan tingkat Emisi GRK di DKI Jakarta sebesar 30% di bawah tingkat Emisi GRK baseline di tahun 2030. Tingkat Emisi GRK baseline diproyeksikan mencapai 114 juta ton CO2e di tahun 2030 dengan tahun dasar (base year} 2005. Tingkat Emisi GRK pada base year (2005) adalah 37 juta ton C02e sedangkan tingkat Emisi GRK pada tahun 2010 adalah 40 juta ton C02e. Skenario ambisius penurunan Emisi GRK langsung sampai dengan 50% pada tahun 2030 Skenario ambisius penurunan Emisi GRK langsung ini disusun berdasarkan fakta bahwa Provinsi DKI Jakarta telah berhasil menurunkan Emisi GRK pada tahun 2018, 2019, dan 2020 secara berturut-turut, serta apabila mempertimbangkan kemajuan dan perkembangan yang telah dilakukan DKI Jakarta pada lima tahun terakhir, khususnya pada sektor transportasi, penurunan Emisi GRK langsung dapat diproyeksikan secara optimis sampai dengan 50% pada tahun 2030 apabila komitmen dan upaya-upaya yang telah dilakukan dapat di akselerasi.

column23: El punto de inicio de estas proyecciones es el inventario de GEI de la ciudad de Lima del 2015. A partir de estos resultados, se inició con el cálculo de una línea base tendencial (BAU por sus siglas en inglés) que proyecta el crecimiento de las emisiones de GEI a futuro, en base a estimaciones del crecimiento de la población y el PBI de la ciudad. Esta línea base tendencial asume que no se implementará a futuro ninguna acción para reducir las emisiones de GEI.Para analizar la reducción de emisiones de GEI se construyeron tres escenarios, los cuales emiten resultados frente al escenario tendencial identificado en la línea base. Los escenarios incluyen todas las emisiones de la ciudad, se encuentren o no dentro de la competencia de la Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima. A continuación, se describen los tres tipos de escenarios (ver Figura 37): Escenario de acciones existentes y planificadas: Este escenario incluye todas las acciones(políticas, proyectos, programas) existentes o planificadas en los próximos años dentro de la ciudad de Lima. Escenario de acciones ambiciosas: Este escenario incluye estrategias y acciones que, si bien son más ambiciosas que el escenario anterior, se consideran aún realizables. Este es el escenario más importante para entender la real ambición que puede tener la ciudad frente a la reducción de emisiones de GEI. Escenario extendido: Este escenario sirve para identificar las estrategias que se necesitan para reducir aún más las emisiones de GEI con el objetivo de acercarse a la carbono neutralidad. Sin embargo, la implementación de estas estrategias no se considera posible en la actualidad debido a una o más barreras económicas, técnicas, políticas o sociales. Finalmente, se calculó las emisiones residuales, las cuales se refieren a las emisiones que la ciudad determina como muy complicadas de mitigar, aun cuando las limitaciones y barreras definidas en el escenario extendido se lograran superar.

column30: El PLCC tiene por objetivo describir cómo la ciudad se adaptará a las amenazas climáticas y reducirá sus emisiones de GEI, teniendo como eje central a las poblaciones más vulnerables bajo un enfoque de inclusión y equidad. Ha sido elaborado por la Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima, con apoyo valioso del Grupo de Liderazgo Climático C40 Cities a través del Programa de Asistencia Técnica de Planificación Climática ejecutado entre 2019 y 2020. El alcance del plan comprende a nivel geográfico los 43 distritos de Lima Metropolitana, incluyendo sus áreas naturales y sus áreas rurales, lo cual permitirá tener una gestión climática integral de la ciudad, contando con ejes transversales en sectores vitales. El alcance temporal comprende el periodo de tiempo 2021-2030 con una visión al 2050. Para su diseño se ha identificado el estado actual de la ciudad y se han elaborado proyecciones de escenarios de cambio climático al 2030, y dos proyecciones de emisiones de GEI para dos periodos de tiempo adicional, 2040 y 2050. Para su formulación, se realizó un intercambio de conocimientos con expertos de entidades públicas y un proceso participativo con actores sociales claves de la ciudad como niñas y niños, las juventudes, municipalidades distritales, organizaciones sociales y la academia; lo cual enriqueció el proceso de definición de objetivos y acciones. Se ha identificado a las autoridades y actores sociales relevantes que deben de comprometerse para alcanzar las metas de mitigación y los objetivos de resiliencia de la ciudad, de forma sostenible. \n\nSe debe de considerar que el desarrollo de las acciones planteadas en el PLCC de la provincia de Lima, es de competencia de diferentes unidades orgánicas de la Municipalidad Metropolitana de Lima; así como de otras entidades o instituciones gubernamentales, por lo cual no se tiene un presupuesto estimado. Así mismo se recalca que estas acciones se encuentran enmarcadas dentro de sus competencias y compromisos.

En cumplimiento con la Ley de Mitigación y Adaptación al Cambio Climático y Desarrollo Sustentable para la Ciudad de México (Ley de Cambio Climático), se diseñaron los dos instrumentos que dirigen la política climática en la Ciudad de México, la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática 2021-2050 (ELAC) y el Programa de Acción Climática 2021-2030 (PACCM), en ambos se busca integrar, coordinar e impulsar políticas públicas para disminuir los riesgos ambientales, sociales y económicos derivados del cambio climático, y así encaminar a la ciudad hacia un desarrollo bajo en carbono y resiliente, enmarcado en los enfoques y principios de la economía circular, la inclusión social, los derechos humanos y la equidad de género. 
La Estrategia, con horizonte temporal 2021 - 2050 tiene como objetivo específico , presentar la visión, objetivos, los ejes y las líneas de acción de la Ciudad de México en materia de cambio climático durante el periodo 2021-2050. Visualiza el futuro de la ciudad en 8 ejes estratégicos y 23 líneas de acción, que se articulan para responder a la emergencia climática actual y construir un futuro cero emisiones y resiliente a los impactos del cambio climático a mediados del siglo .
El cumplimiento de los objetivos planteados a largo plazo dependerá de las medidas transformadoras implementadas en el corto plazo mediante el Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México, así como de condiciones habilitadoras de tipo jurídico, institucional, técnico y financiero que faciliten la progresividad y viabilidad de las metas a 2050 en cada uno de los ejes que integran la Estrategia.
La revisión y actualización de los escenarios, objetivos y líneas de acción de la Estrategia se sustentarán en los resultados de los reportes de seguimiento de las medidas de acción climática que permitan conocer el avance del cumplimiento de las metas, y se llevarán a cabo en los términos y periodicidad señalados en la Ley del Sistema de Planeación del Desarrollo de la Ciudad de México, la Ley de Cambio Climático y su Reglamento.

La Ciudad de México, a través de la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática, considera escenarios generados para la ciudad obtenidos del ensamble de los modelos del Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 5 (CMIP5). Los escenarios se realizaron para temperaturas medias, mínimas y máximas anuales y cambios en la precipitación para las cuatro trayectorias de concentración representativas (RCP) del Panel Intergubernamental de Cambio Climático. Estos escenarios se consideraron para el diseño de medidas de adaptación y resiliencia en el corto, mediano y largo plazo. 
Con base en el Análisis elaborado en el apartado “Peligros, riesgos y vulnerabilidad ante el cambio climático' de la Estrategia, consideró la identificación de peligros asociados al cambio climático; los desastres ocurridos vinculados a dichos peligros; los escenarios de cambio climático; un análisis de eventos extremos e isla de calor urbana; el cambio de uso de suelo; los peligros por Alcaldía; la vulnerabilidad de las Alcaldías al cambio climático, con base en cruce con indicadores socioeconómicos; amenazas a la biodiversidad, a las actividades económicas y a la salud. 

Expuesto lo anterior, dichos escenarios ha permitido el desarrollo e implementación de acciones de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático, en el marco tanto de los Programas de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México 2021-2030 (PACCM) y Ambiental y de Cambio Climático 2021-2024(PACC).

El Programa Ambiental y de Cambio Climático 2019-2024(PACC), busca mejorar las condiciones ambientales en todas sus dimensiones,crear resiliencia y mitigar las emisiones de compuestos y gases de efecto invernadero. Las acciones en materia ambiental se basan en la innovación, la ciencia la tecnología y la participación de la ciudadanía.

Como parte de dicho Programa, la Ciudad de México se comprometió a reducir en 10% las emisiones actuales de CGEI para el 2024
con respecto a los niveles del 2016. Esta reducción refleja las acciones y condiciones necesarias para que las emisiones totales no sobrepasen las 24.8 MtCO2e en 2024, como una meta intermedia hacia la descarbonización para el 2050. Este escenario incluye las políticas emblemáticas actuales y planificadas, como el Programa Integral de Movilidad, el Programa Basura Cero y el proyecto Ciudad Solar, entre otros.

En enero de 2024, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente de la Ciudad de México informó que gracias a las acciones implementadas a través del Programa Ambiental y de Cambio Climático (PACC) 2019-2024, ya se logró superar la meta establecida para el año 2024, que consistía en reducir el 10% de las emisiones de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2e) con base en las emisiones del año 2016. 

Las acciones desarrolladas a través de los siete ejes del PACC ya permiten evitar 2.26 millones de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente al año. Esto representa una mitigación comparable a reforestar y cuidar 5.7 millones de árboles de pino durante 50 años y representa el 102.7% de la meta a la que el Gobierno de la Ciudad de México se comprometió en 2019, que consistía en reducir para 2024 el 10% de las emisiones de gases causantes del cambio climático que se generaban

El Programa de Gobierno de la Ciudad de México 2019-2024 a través del eje “Ciudad Sustentable” busca conseguir un desarrollo económico sustentable que fortalezca la capacidad para generar empleos en las diversas actividades productivas de la Ciudad, sin detrimento del medio ambiente y promoviendo la generación de nuevas fuentes de energía renovable y empresas ambientales. Además reconoce que frente a los problemas ambientales locales y globales, es indispensable generar un desarrollo económico sustentable e incluyente así como sectores productivos que disminuyan la contaminación y promuevan nuevas tecnologías como las energías renovables y el uso eficiente de los recursos naturales. Asimismo, en dicho eje se establecen acciones que apoyen a la industria innovadora, sustentable y la economía circular, generar incentivos para promover el uso de fuentes renovables de energía en las industrias de la ciudad e incentivar su permanencia en diversas zonas de la ciudad, así como fomentar el uso de energías renovables, en particular la energía solar en calentadores solares y paneles fotovoltaicos. Con la puesta en marcha de este programa, se espera lograr la generación de 10,700 empleos y la mitigación de 2 millones 26 mil 600 toneladas de CO2 durante el período 2019 - 2024. 
Sin embargo; a pesar de ser una estrategia energética, forma parte de los 7 ejes estratégicos del Programa Ambiental 2019-2024 y que a su vez, dichas emisiones contribuyen a la meta global de reducción de emisiones del Programa de Acción Climática de la Ciudad de México 2021-2030.
