The City of Paris is taking significant steps to combat climate change by reducing its carbon footprint and preparing for adaptation Its strategy comprises two approaches: mitigation involving actions to cut greenhouse gas emissions and atmospheric pollutants and adaptation encompassing measures to enhance resilience to climate hazards and protect residents. The City is committed to fostering an ecologically just transition with a focus on social inclusion at the core of its Climate Plan and Resilience Strategy. 

The last Climate Action Plan (2018-2024) resulted from extensive public consultation between November 2016 and April 2017 and it underwent a climate referendum engaging over 73,000 Parisians with more than 15,000 becoming climate volunteers. As with this third edition, the fourth edition adopted by the Parisian council in November 2024 aligns with the Paris Agreements core objective aiming for carbon neutrality by 2050 with intermediate goals set for 2030 Significant reductions in energy needs 35% by 2030 and 50 by 2050 are crucial for transitioning to a 100% renewable and recovery-based energy supply. The plan also targets increasing the share of renewable energy consumed in Paris from 17% in 2014 to 25% in 2020, 45% in 2030 and 100% in 2050 while phasing out fossil fuels by 2030, 2040 and 2050 following different perimeters. 

The 2024-2030 plan inscribes new adaptation targets, in order to better articulate the long term of the future Parisian climate with the short term of municipal mandate planning (6 years). Consequentially, the fourth Parisian Climate Action Plan sets the objective of reaching 40% of the territory permeable by 2050 (estimated to be 26% in 2018), to reach the recommended 10m² of green space per inhabitant by 2040 (7m² in 2022, requires an additional 300 ha of green space), reduce water withdrawal by 15% by 2030 (compared to 2019) and reach 100% of Parisians at less than 7 minutes walking from a cool island 24/7 during a heatwave by 2030 (99% by day and 68% by night in 2023).

Paris considers this plan a societal transition that will generate jobs drive innovation and facilitate professional conversions. The Climate Plan has been supported by the Bleu Climat an annual activity report tracking progress since 2007. The 2018-2024 Climate Plan has achieved almost all major objectives for 2020, and the steering of the 2024-2030 climate plan will be heightened in order to more finely monitor all objectives, major and minor.

column23: Pathways scenario exercise was conducted to establish an evidence base that could be used to set emissions reduction targets for Mumbai's energy, transport and waste sectors in line with the fair-share 1.5 degree scenario and identify the strategies to achieve these. column23: The City's comprehensive All Hazard Mitigation Plan is an aspirational plan to mitigate, or reduce risk to both natural and human-caused hazards with the goal of improving the safety and resiliency of our City. Therefore, while \'mitigation\' is in the title, it is not a plan to mitigate emissions, rather, it is a plan to mitigate risk from various hazards. In the 2022 update to Philadelphia's hazard mitigation plan, climate change was identified as one of three main priorities and since climate change is cross-cutting, it is addressed in many sections throughout the plan. Regarding climate related hazards, the plan developed risk profiles and strategies to mitigate risk for extreme temperature, flooding (precipitation increases, sea level rise, extreme storms), hurricanes, tornados, winter storms and drought. Of all the hazards examined, floods, extreme storms (tropical cyclones), extreme heat, winter storms and tornados, all of which are exacerbated by climate change, were identified in the highest risk factor rating category. The plan specifically looks at the ways climate change will impact the intensity and frequency of future disasters and used RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 emissions scenarios for temperature and precipitation projections. Precipitation projections as well as 4 ft. sea level rise scenarios were used to examine current and future flood risk, beyond FEMA's floodplains. The plan includes maps and Hazus loss estimates for a 1% annual chance flood, 0.2% annual chance flood and future scenarios using storm surge and sea level rise.

The 2018 update to the State Guidance integrates the latest findings from national and regional studies, uses a probabilistic projection method which differs from the NRC report, and includes an extreme, but unlikely, scenario referred to as H. The HCR report relies on the CPC Guidance values derived from the NRC 2012 report. 3) Precipitation:: Considering RCP4.5 mean projections, most regions of the state can expect to see at least modest increases in mean wet-season precipitation compared to historical amounts. However, the San Francisco Bay area is projected to see potential average late-century increases of up to 10.5 percent, the highest in the state, making the region most likely to see changes in future storm events.30 This trend is also evident in the RCP8.5 projections that point to average wet-season mid-century changes as much as 10.3% and as much as 18.7% by late-century.

column23: In 2016, the IPCC estimated that to remain under a 1.5C increase in average global temperature, CO2 emissions would need to fall by 45-75% from 2010 levels and cumulative global emissions after the end of 2017 must be less than 420 GtCO2. In 2018, scientists prepared a subsequent report to document progress towards long-term goals of the Paris Agreement and inform preparation of nationally determined contributions. The report found that limiting global temperature increase to 1.5 C would require rapid transitions in energy, transportation and land use, industry, and buildings. It notes that global net human-caused emissions must reach net-zero around 2050, which means remaining emissions will need to be balanced though carbon sequestration. Global organizations such as C40 and One Planet City Challenge (OPCC) provided specific guidance for cities based on these IPCC reports and recommended a 57%-68% reduction from baseline emissions inventories to meet a global 2030 target. To estimate emission reductions for San Francisco's 2021 CAP, a business-as-usual (BAU) baseline scenario was created to project the effect of emissions reduction strategies. The BAU assumptions, in which demographic and economic changes—namely population and job growth—serve as the primary drivers of changes in emissions, resulted in a scenario that showed emissions steadily increasing over time, rising 21% above 2017 levels. From this baseline, a variety of emissions-reducing strategies and actions are applied to San Francisco's emissions forecast, which are described in Section 5 of the CAP; details about the methods used for the Transportation and Land Use and Building Operations sectors are in Appendix C. From this analysis, it was determined that if San Francisco successfully implemented all CAP strategies and actions, the City would achieve a 61% reduction in emissions by 2030 and an 87% reduction by 2045. Based on this data, analysis, and consideration of external factors, San Francisco has proposed the bold and aggressive goal of equitably reaching net-zero sector emissions by 2040, with a 61% reduction by 2030.

column30: Since its first Climate Action Plan in 2004, San Francisco has been leading the way on local climate action, environmental justice, and launching innovative community programs and outreach campaigns for residents and businesses. Tackling the interwoven climate, equity, and racial justice challenges we face has been the driving force for the development of the 2021 Climate Action Plan (CAP). It provides a summary of progress through existing programs, and a detailed list of priority actions that San Francisco can take that will have the greatest potential to reduce emissions, while also having the greatest potential to provide an equitable distribution of benefits. The process of creating the CAP brought City departments, residents, community-based organizations, and businesses together to craft a plan focused on science and equity and grounded in compassion and lived experience. This data-driven, community-based plan outlines a detailed list of strategies and actions to achieve net-zero emissions by 2040, while creating solutions that serve intersectional challenges of racial and social equity, public health, economic recovery, and resilient communities. To advance climate justice, the 2021 CAP makes four core commitments:1) Build greater racial and social equity; 2) Protect public health; 3) Increase community resilience; and 4) Foster a more just economy. In addition to integrating these four climate justice commitments, the 2021 CAP proposes two ambitious and achievable climate emission reduction targets: 1) An interim target of cutting sector-based emissions 61% below 1990 levels by 2030; and 2) Net-zero sector-based emissions by 2040, a 90% reduction from 1990 levels. San Francisco is currently in the process of updating its Climate Action Plan. The updated plan is slated for publishing at the end of 2025.

Essa distribuição foi realizada de acordo com o caráter de cada estratégia. A primeira estratégia tem como principal objetivo zerar as emissões de GEE e apresenta um total de 18 ações, que envolvem os setores de maior contribuição de emissão, identificados no Inventário local, sendo eles transportem, energia estacionária e resíduos. A segunda estratégia apresenta o foco em adaptar a cidade para os principais riscos climáticos identificados a partir de um 11 ações, envolvendo os setores de construção civil, serviços de suporte e administração, serviços de habitação e informação e comunicação. Já a terceira estratégia, busca fortalecer as iniciativas com objetivo conjunto de mitigação e adaptação a partir da conservação do bioma local e apresenta um total de 3 ações. Pensando nas vulnerabilidades sociais, atividades de proteção e saúde, educação ambiental e desenvolvimento de capacidades foram consideradas de maneira transversal no detalhamento das ações e são evidenciadas nas estratégias “3. Proteger pessoas e bens” e na “4. Gerar trabalho e riqueza sustentáveis.” É importante destacar que as estratégias e ações foram elaboradas em conformidade com a divisão de competências da gestão municipal. Cada ação foi designada aos órgãos municipais responsáveis pela sua implementação e já executavam iniciativas correspondentes antes da criação do Plano, ficando sob sua responsabilidade gerenciar o orçamento para assegurar a execução adequada. No entanto, esse sistema não garante o financiamento efetivo das ações por parte dos órgãos e dificulta a estimativa do custo total para a implementação do plano até o momento. Para os próximos anos, é esperado que as ações do PlanClima SP sejam incorporadas aos planos de gestão e orçamentos anuais, garantindo que as secretarias aloquem recursos específicos para sua execução.

1. 참조한 시나리오
- IPCC 제6차 평가보고서(AR6) SSP2-4.5 및 RCP 4.5: 온실가스 배출이 중간 수준에서 관리되는 시나리오를 바탕으로 2030~2050년 창원의 기후 리스크(폭염, 집중호우, 해수면 상승 등)를 전망.
- 국가기후위기 적응대책(2021~2025): 환경부 및 국무조정실 주관 국가 시나리오를 반영하여 지역 적응계획과 연계.
- IEA World Energy Outlook(2022): 에너지 수급 및 전환 부문의 글로벌 추세를 참고하여 신재생에너지 확대 및 수소에너지 보급 로드맵 설계에 활용.

2. 온실가스 감축 계획에 미친 영향
- 2030년까지 2018년 대비 40% 감축이라는 창원시 목표는, RCP 4.5 시나리오 기준 지구 평균온도 상승 억제 필요성과 일치.
- 건물, 수송, 산업, 폐기물 등 부문별 감축목표 설정 근거로 활용됨.
- 수소경제(수소차·수소충전소·연료전지 발전)와 신재생에너지 자립률 확대 정책은 IEA와 IPCC 시나리오에서 제시한 에너지 전환 필요성을 반영.

3. 기후위기 적응계획에 미친 영향
- 폭염, 폭우, 해안범람 등 지역 기후재해 발생빈도 증가 전망을 근거로 “3℃ 낮은 Cool 창원 만들기”, “도시침수 예방사업”, “해안범람 대응 인프라” 등 적응과제 수립.
- 농업부문에서는 가뭄 및 물 수요 증가 위험에 대응하여 농업용수 확보 및 스마트농업 기술 도입 근거로 반영.

4. 정책 및 실행전략 조정
- 기후 시나리오 분석 결과, 단기(2030), 중기(2040), 장기(2050)로 구분된 로드맵을 마련.

column30:
Our city, following the National Climate Change Adaptation Framework, has adopted a two-stage, six-dimension approach based on national adaptation scenarios to develop and revise its implementation plan. The two stages are 'Identifying Climate Risks and Adaptation Gaps' and 'Adaptation Planning and Action,' while the six dimensions include 'Defining the Scope,' 'Reviewing Current Conditions,' 'Assessing Risks,' 'Integrating Decisions,' 'Promoting Implementation,' and 'Review and Adjustment.'
The plan takes into account the city's natural environment and socio-economic development characteristics, conducting climate change impact analysis and assessments to identify key issues that require early attention, such as 'heavy rainfall,' 'high temperatures,' and 'drought.' During the first stage, 'Identifying Climate Risks and Adaptation Gaps,' the scope of adaptation is defined, current conditions are reviewed, and risks are assessed. Existing adaptation measures are evaluated against future climate risk scenarios to identify adaptation gaps.
In the second stage, 'Adaptation Planning and Action,' the city integrates decision-making, promotes implementation, and conducts reviews and adjustments. This process includes reviewing and integrating existing policies and related plans. Based on the city's current conditions and climate change impact analysis, the plan is tailored to the local context and focuses on six major areas: 'vital infrastructure,' 'water resources,' 'land use,' 'energy supply and industry,' 'agricultural production and biodiversity,' and 'health,' along with 'capacity building.' The plan serves as the framework for driving the city's adaptation implementation plan, setting climate change adaptation goals, strategies, and actions across different sectors and agencies.

column30: In order to promote the City's net zero transformation, the City proposed the \'Taipei City Net Zero Emission Management Autonomy Act\' , which was revised after public hearings and consultation with various sectors. Incorporating the 2050 net zero emissions target into this Act, specifying the authorities and responsibilities of various city government agencies, introducing a \'carbon budget\' system, and setting up a climate transformation fund. In response to the United Nations IPCC AR6 ,the Act will be strengthened with a special chapter on adaptation. The Act is divided into 7 chapters and 55 articles.1. In order to increase the carbon reduction to 40% by 2030, with a net zero emissions target by 2050. Also, promote a \'carbon budget\', set carbon emission caps for various sectors.2. In order to promote industrial transformation, City will set up a climate transformation fund, which will be dedicated to climate change adaptation, greenhouse gas reduction, and taking care of the underprivileged in climate transformation to ensure fair transformation.3. It specifies that public buildings and buildings of a certain size in Taipei City should publicly label information on building energy consumption and strengthen controls from 2030 onward to improve building energy efficiency.4. From the public sector to private sector, the City government has set 2023 as the target year for electrification of public motorcycles and 2030 as the target date for electrification of urban buses and public cars as the key policy priority. Low-carbon transportation zones will be promoted gradually toreduce the amount of carbon emissions from transportation.5. The Act stipulates the reduction and banning of the use of disposable items, that the use of tableware should be paid for and completely banned, and requires public and private venues to set up environmentally friendly container recycling systems. In addition, it stipulates that existing old incinerators should be upgraded to high-efficiency green energy power plants and environmentally friendly green energy recycling parks, and carbon capture and utilization equipment should be introduced.6. The Act stipulates that the City Government should conduct studies and surveys on the City's land use,vulnerability and regularly review urban plans. https://www.taiwannews.com.tw/en/news/4579962

column30: Taipei City has been actively implementing reduction measures, resulting in a decrease in emissions of11.388 million metric tons of CO2e in 2020, representing a 12.9% reduction compared to the baseline year of 2005. The residential, commercial, and transportation sectors are the main sources of emissions, accounting for 74.6% and 20.6% of the city's total emissions, respectively. Emissions from the residential and commercial sectors decreased by 13.1% in 2020 compared to the baseline year, while emissions from the transportation sector decreased by 8.2%.The residential, commercial, and transportation sectors constitute the city's major carbon sources, accounting for 74.60%, 20.58%, and 2.69% of the total emissions, respectively. Together, these three sectors contribute to nearly 98% of the city's carbon emissions.Based on projections of future population and economic changes, it is estimated that without any relevant reduction measures, emissions in 2050 would reach 12.496 million metric tons of CO2e.The promotion of net-zero emissions in Taipei City is pursued through the implementation of smart zero-carbon buildings, green and low-carbon transportation, a circular economy with zero waste, and the enhancement of carbon sinks. A collaboration between the central government and public-private sectors is crucial to achieve the net-zero emissions goal. The main strategies for the three major sectors include energy efficiency inspections, disclosure, and regulations in the residential and commercial sectors, along with the integration of renewable energy and hydrogen use to achieve zero-carbon buildings. The transportation sector focuses on promoting green transportation and the adoption of electric (hydrogen) vehicles. The waste sector aims for a circular economy with zero waste and ultimately zero emissions from waste treatment facilities. The agriculture and forestry sector emphasizes afforestation to increase carbon sinks and strengthens wetland conservation to maintain carbon sequestration.By implementing these strategies, Taipei City aims to achieve its net-zero emissions goal and actively contribute to mitigating climate change.

column30: Taipei City has conducted an independent greenhouse gas inventory operation at the city level, showing a gradual decrease in emissions from 13.074 million metric tons of CO2e in 2005, in 2021, greenhouse gas emissions were 11.1426 million metric tons of CO2e, representing a reduction of approximately 1.9311 million metric tons compared to 2005, a decrease of 14.77%.The main sources of greenhouse gas emissions in the city are the residential, commercial, and transportation sectors, accounting for approximately 95% of the total emissions. To achieve energy-saving and carbon reduction goals, the city initially focused on the public sector and formulated an energy-saving plan for the Taipei City Government and affiliated agencies. The city government implemented measures to promote energy-saving and carbon reduction in the industrial and commercial sectors. These measures include energy-saving counseling, law enforcement and advocacy, incentive subsidies, and the promotion of energy-saving products. On-site inspections of energy-consuming equipment are conducted, and compliance with regulations is ensured. The promotion of energy-saving products is carried out through cooperation with various stores. In 2021, the service sector's electricity consumption decreased by 349 million kWh compared to 2020, resulting in an electricity saving rate of 3.77%.Solar photovoltaic systems have been installed on government agencies and schools, resulting in significant power generation and carbon reduction. Citizen power plants managed by civic groups have been established on city-owned buildings. Landfill sites are being transformed into energy parks, and small hydropower generation systems are being introduced. The city is also actively promoting the electrification of vehicles. An electric vehicle subsidy program has been announced, and charging stations are being constructed. The proportion of electric scooters in the city has significantly increased, and efforts are being made to establish a public bicycle system.To achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, the city government has revised environmental impact assessment regulations and promotes green building certifications. It has allocated funds for circular economy buildings and is actively promoting the concepts of an \'agricultural city\' and a \'sponge city.\'

column23: O Plano de Redução de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa de Belo Horizonte (PREGEE) estrutura-se a partir de cenários climáticos que reforçam sua consistência ao integrar aspectos do desenvolvimento urbano, econômico e social da cidade. A estrutura da cidade, sua expansão urbana, o avanço da economia e das relações sociais são resultados inerentes ao processo de desenvolvimento, diretamente relacionados às emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GEE), seja pela escolha de fontes energéticas, pela geração e tratamento de resíduos, pelo uso dos recursos naturais ou ainda pelos hábitos da população. Estima-se que metade da população mundial já viva em cidades e que, até 2050, este valor alcance 70%, concentrando cerca de 80% do consumo global de energia e, consequentemente, proporção equivalente de emissões de GEE. Diante dessa realidade, Belo Horizonte se insere como exemplo desse desafio, pois, ao mesmo tempo em que é responsável por parcela significativa das emissões, também é altamente vulnerável às consequências da mudança do clima. Os eventos extremos recorrentes, como chuvas intensas e ondas de calor, evidenciam essa vulnerabilidade e conferem solidez ao PREGEE, justificando sua elaboração como instrumento estratégico para orientar ações de mitigação, alinhadas às especificidades do território urbano e às demandas de sustentabilidade da cidade.

column30: The Climate Action and Energy Strategy 2030 of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB) provides a comprehensive framework to address mitigation, adaptation, and energy transition in line with international and national commitments. The plan builds upon the objectives of the Paris Agreement, the EU Green Deal, and Turkey's National Climate Change Action Plan, and integrates them into a jurisdiction-wide approach covering all sectors of urban life. One of the plan's strengths is its inclusive process, with more than 50 stakeholder workshops organized to engage citizens, academia, NGOs, and vulnerable groups. This ensured that equity, gender sensitivity, and protection of disadvantaged communities were central in identifying priorities. The plan includes detailed actions across renewable energy expansion, sustainable transport, building energy efficiency, waste reduction, water resilience, and forestry enhancement. To ensure transparency, ABB committed to annual monitoring reports and periodic evaluations every three years, with updates feeding into adaptive management of targets. Scenario modeling, based on IPCC AR6 pathways, informed the prioritization of investments and highlighted risks from both physical hazards (heatwaves, floods, drought) and socio-economic challenges (energy poverty, affordability). The plan also emphasizes co-benefits: cleaner air quality, public health gains, and green jobs are quantified as part of the rationale for accelerating low-carbon transitions. Trade-offs, such as the upfront costs of renewable energy infrastructure or potential affordability challenges in low-income neighborhoods, are acknowledged, and mitigated through social support and subsidies. By covering a wide range of sectors, from agriculture and forestry to transport, energy, education, and health, the plan ensures integration across municipal departments and alignment with Sustainable Development Goals (SDG7, SDG11, SDG13). The plan is designed as a living document: it was approved in 2021, updated in 2023, and will next be reviewed in 2026. Its end horizon is 2030, but it includes a long-term vision to 2050 for net-zero emissions.

column30: The adaptation plan of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB) establishes a comprehensive roadmap to address increasing climate risks such as urban heat island effects, droughts, flooding events, and loss of biodiversity. It prioritizes resilience building across urban infrastructure, ecosystems, and communities. Key interventions include expanding green infrastructure, integrating nature-based solutions for flood and erosion control, enhancing early warning systems, and redesigning critical infrastructure to withstand extreme weather. The plan integrates community engagement, particularly targeting vulnerable populations, to ensure inclusive resilience. Financial mechanisms combine local funds with national and EU resources, allowing cross-sectoral implementation. The strategy is monitored with annual reporting to align with SDG11 and SDG13, and evaluation occurs on a 3-year cycle to ensure iterative learning. Co-benefits include reduced health risks, economic savings from avoided damages, and enhanced urban livability. Trade-offs such as initial investment burdens are mitigated through phased financing. Synergies with mitigation targets are embedded by promoting energy-efficient adaptation measures. Overall, the adaptation plan strengthens the city's preparedness for projected climate impacts in 2030 and beyond, fostering resilience and sustainable urban development in line with GCoM and EU Mission on Adaptation. |

column30: The ABB Greenhouse Gas Mitigation and Net Zero Strategy was formally adopted in 2021 with the primary aim of reducing the city's emissions by 60% by 2035 and achieving net zero by 2050. This plan builds on Turkey's National Climate Change Action Plan and aligns with EU Green Deal and GCoM Mitigation Pillar requirements. The plan is comprehensive, covering energy, transport, waste, buildings, and industry sectors. Quantitative modeling tools, such as the Long-range Energy Alternatives Planning (LEAP) model and IPCC AR6 Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), were used to develop emissions reduction scenarios consistent with 1.5°C and 2°C temperature stabilization goals. These scenarios informed strategic priorities, including the large-scale deployment of renewable energy, energy efficiency retrofits in public and residential buildings, electrification of public transport, expansion of cycling and pedestrian infrastructure, and development of a circular waste management system. The plan identifies multiple co-benefits: reducing local air pollution, improving energy security by lowering fossil fuel dependency, creating green jobs, and stimulating sustainable economic growth. Trade-offs are acknowledged, particularly high upfront costs of clean energy infrastructure and the need for industrial transitions, which may temporarily affect employment in certain sectors. Financial mechanisms include national climate funds, EU programs, international climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund), and revenues from carbon credits under voluntary markets. Private sector engagement is emphasized, especially for renewable energy investments and sustainable mobility solutions. Communities and citizens were engaged through workshops, surveys, and participatory forums to ensure local ownership of mitigation measures. Vulnerable groups, including low-income households, were considered to minimize distributional impacts, with targeted subsidies and social support mechanisms planned. Monitoring is conducted annually, while evaluations and updates occur every 1-3 years, ensuring that the plan remains adaptive to evolving technologies and socio-economic conditions.

Adaptation Scenarios: 
•The City's Climate Change Hazard, Vulnerability and Risk Assessment study (2019) was based on projections under RCP 8.5, for a mid-future period of 2021 - 2050 and a far future period of 2070 - 2099. This study informed the development of the City's Climate Change Action Plan (CCAP) as it relates to heat, fire, flooding, and drought. The study is being updated (2025-2026) and will inform the next update of the CCAP. 
•Sea-level rise projections (2008/9) were based on two main scenarios for coastal inundation (temporary) and erosion as a result of storm surge - the present day “worst case scenario” and the scenario at the end of the next decade. This study also looked at a long-term scenario for polar ice-sheet melting resulting in permanent inundation. This study informed the development of the CCAP as it relates to coastal erosion and sea-level rise. 
•The City's CCAP was also informed by a 2016 Climate Change Projections report which identified 3 narratives of future climate - “hotter and drier”, “warmer and no rainfall change”, and “hotter and mixed rainfall change”. 

Mitigation scenarios: 
•The City's GHG emission reduction targets was developed based on the C40 Deadline 2020 (D2020) methodology. The methodology, developed for C40 cities under the D2020 programme, is aligned with 1.5 degrees and qualifies as a 'Science Based Targets' methodology. D2020 provides an emissions reduction trajectory, based on four city typologies and indicates 2030 and 2050 targets. Cape Town falls under the developing south typology and has an early peaking developing city envelope. 
•The tool employed for the City's carbon neutral scenario modelling is the Pathways Tool developed by C40. Pathways is a forward-looking simulation model that builds on the City's GHG inventory and previous Energy2040 modelling. It makes projections for future emissions according to a set of context-specific growth assumptions and intervention possibilities for each of the emissions-producing sectors in the city.
 •A scenario development approach was adopted: 1) A BAU scenario and two pathways of ambitious action under optimistic (green economy) and pessimistic (ambition under limited mandate and opportunity) conditions were modelled. These scenarios informed the City's GHG emission reduction targets reported in CDP: 1) Emissions reduction of 9.4% to 18.6 Megatons CO2e for Cape Town's BASIC inventory by 2030 and 2) Emission reduction of 81% to 4 Megatons CO2e by 2050.

The City has a long history of progressively and technically responding to climate change and aligned its response to global ambition through participation in the C40 Deadline 2020 programme from 2017. This commitment required the development of a climate action plan by mid-2021, aligned with the Paris Agreement. 

The City's Climate Change Strategy was subsequently approved by Council in May 2021 and shortly thereafter the Climate Change Action Plan - a detailed programme-level implementation plan of the Strategy. The strategy went through a formal public participation process, and various key stakeholders were engaged as part of the Action Plan development process. 

The Plan includes 101 actions across 10 Strategic Focus Areas: Urban cooling and heat responsiveness, Water security and drought readiness; Water sensitivity, flood readiness and storm management; Coastal management and resilience; Managing fire risk and responsiveness; Spatial and resource inclusivity; Carbon-neutral energy for work creation and economic development; Zero-emissions buildings and precincts; Mobility for quality of life and livelihoods; Circular Waste Economy and 5 Cross-cutting Work Areas: Mainstreaming, governance, research and knowledge management; Economic impacts and green economy opportunities; Business models, and financing climate change response; Communication, collaboration and skills development and Human and ecosystem health. 

A monitoring and evaluation (M&E) framework was developed in 2022, with the aim of tracking both progress against the actions contained in the Action Plan, as well as monitoring trends in indicators that have been developed to assess whether medium-term outcomes related to the goals of the Strategy are being achieved. This includes annual action status level updates, and detailed/in-depth assessments every 3 years which will inform the full update of the plan every 5 years. Three implementation review reports have been developed and are available here: https://www.capetown.gov.za/Family%20and%20home/greener-living/why-go-green/lets-act-against-climate-change 

Cost estimates are allocated to the actions according to range categories, but a detailed quantitative assessment of the entire plan has taken place, although high level work on this was done in partnership with the World Bank/IFC group to use a GHG emissions modelling and an investment analysis tool to analyse key actions and better understand funding required/ financing options.

column23: Climate-related scenarios underscored the need for this plan, and influenced several of the actions included in the plan. In 2015, most of Texas was in extreme drought, with the four water supply reservoirs in north Texas at about 25% of yield. This condition continued until May, 2015, when this area experienced an unprecedented month of rainfall, with the area receiving the annual rainfall amount during this month. All four reservoirs went from 25% yield to an uncontrolled overflow condition simultaneously; this exceeded design probabilities for this system, and led to months of flooding, exacerbated by two additional 100-year frequency events occurring later in the year. The following year, there were two severe wind events that knocked power out in affected areas for several weeks; Hurricane Harvey occurred in the year after that. The post-Harvey report included data for the entire state showing a 40-percent increase in flooding in areas located outside of the regulated floodplain. As a local government needing to address these events when they occur, it was time. So the City committed to meeting the international emission reduction targets set by the Paris Agreement in 2016 and the goal to keep warming temperatures at or below 1.5 degrees Celsius. In 2017, Mayor Rawlings signed the Mayors National Climate Agreement in support of the Paris Agreement. Upon election in June 2019, Mayor Johnson reaffirmed the City of Dallas' commitment to this agreement. The City of Dallas is fully committed to protecting the community from the impacts of climate change and taking measures to reduce its GHG emissions. Ante la necesidad de limitar el aumento de la temperatura global a 1.5°C, el AMG ha establecido un compromiso de ser carbono neutral, resiliente e inclusiva al año 2050. 

Así en materia de adaptación, se integró al PACmetro los resultados del Análisis de Riesgos Climáticos del AMG, en el cual se presentan los escenarios de cambio climático en el AMG a través del análisis regionalizado de los Modelos de Circulación General (GCM por sus siglas en inglés), ya que permiten simular la respuesta del sistema climático global a los aumentos en los gases de efecto invernadero. 

Se seleccionaron los modelos MPI-ESM-LR, GFDL-CM3, HADGEM-ES y CNRM, ya que poseen una mejor resolución (30'' x 30'', aproximadamente 926 m x 926 m) y se elaboró el ensamble de los mismos para la caracterización de los escenarios, trabajando así con resultados promediados de los cuatro modelos. Los forzamientos radiactivos o Trayectorias Representativas de Concentraciones (RCP's por sus siglas en inglés) seleccionados corresponden con el RCP 4.5 (emisiones bajas) y RCP 8.5 (emisiones altas) y los horizontes temporales considerados son el futuro de corto plazo (2015-2039) y de medio plazo (2045-2069). Se analiza la distribución espacial de las proyecciones en AMG para porcentaje de cambio de la precipitación y el delta o anomalías en la temperatura En materia de mitigación el PACmetro tiene como base la estimación y modelación de escenarios de reducción de emisiones de GEI considerando los sectores que más contribuyen: energía (generación y consumo final), transporte (parque vehicular público y privado) y residuos (tratamiento de residuos generados dentro de los límites de la ciudad), en un marco temporal que comprende los periodos 2030, 2040 y 2050. Lo anterior se ve reflejado dentro del PACmetro en sus objetivos 1 Y 2 (mitigación y adaptación) en los diagnósticos correspondientes como en la estructura de acción climática (estrategias, metas, medidas y acciones). 

El PACmetro se encuentra en ruta de actualización.

El IMEPLAN constituye una pieza clave en la implementación del proceso de planeación descentralizado y de largo plazo, con autonomía técnica, desde una perspectiva integral; con énfasis en la planeación para el desarrollo y el ordenamiento territorial, el manejo de riesgos y la sistematización de la información metropolitana. Su constitución como instancia técnica autónoma tiene por objeto reforzar en la gestión de proyectos estratégicos y recursos económicos para mejorar la provisión de los servicios públicos a escala metropolitana. A finales de 2018, el Municipio de Guadalajara se incorporó al Grupo de Liderazgo de Ciudades C40 (C40), adquiriendo el compromiso de contar con un Plan de Acción Climática en 2020. Dicho plan demostrará cómo la ciudad será carbono neutral, resiliente e inclusiva, para 2050. Asimismo, considerando el modelo de gobernanza existente en el AMG, el municipio, en coordinación con el Instituto de Planeación y Gestión del Desarrollo del AMG (IMEPLAN) decide desarrollar un Plan a escala metropolitana, con el objetivo de contar con un instrumento metropolitano rector de la política pública en materia de cambio climático, que establezca estrategias, directrices, objetivos, acciones, metas e indicadores a implementarse con una visión de corto, mediano y largo plazo.
Con fecha 14 de diciembre de 2020 en sesión ordinaria de la Junta de Coordinación Metropolitana del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara, se aprobó por unanimidad el proyecto denominado “Plan de Acción Climática del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara” el cual se alinea con los compromisos del Acuerdo de París para mantener el aumento promedio de la temperatura global por debajo de los 2ºC, promover esfuerzos adicionales para que la temperatura global no supere los 1.5°C y aumentar la resiliencia a los impactos del cambio climático, y se ratifica el compromiso de los municipios que conforman el AMG y el Gobierno del Estado de Jalisco para su implementación.

El plan, además de incluir la mitigación y adaptación, incluye un tercer objetivo que habilita la búsqueda de financiamiento, el mecanismo de monitoreo, así como demás acciones habilitadora para e cumplimiento del Plan.

Al ser un plan vivo que integra a los diferentes órdenes de gobierno, es difícil conocer el monto exacto requerido para su implementación; sin embargo, desde nuestro Sistema Informático de Monitoreo, Evaluación y Reporte, integra un módulo de financiamiento, que permitirá monitorear lo asignado y ejercido.

In 2024, two days in May reached record breaking heat indices of 112°F.Projections suggest that by mid-century, Miami could face 88 days annually with a heat index of 105°F or greater, equivalent to roughly three months of extreme heat. Research from the University of Miami indicates that the annual average heat index in Miami has increased by 0.59°F per decade since the 1950s, emphasizing the need for a local extreme heat plan. In response to the growing number of high heat days, Miami-Dade County has officially recognized a “Heat Season” spanning from May 1 to October 31 every year. In addition, r the National Weather Service Miami - South began an experimental pilot program for Miami-Dade County to reduce the Heat Index threshold for Heat Advisories and Heat Warnings, so community members receive alerts before heat indices reach highly dangerous levels. column30: In response to extreme heat Miami has been experiencing in the summer, the City of Miami has developed an Extreme Heat Plan that outlines actions related to shading, cooling, and initial design that can address ambient heat, especially during Heat Season (May 1 - October 31). The plan is organized into three main cooling solutions - Shade, Water, and Design - along with a Heat Response Protocol. The Shade solutions focus on increasing tree canopy, greenery, and shaded structures in public spaces. The Water solutions aim to improve access to water bodies, drinking fountains, and cooling amenities like pools and splash pads. The Design solutions involve policies and programs to help residents cool their homes and workplaces, as well as protect outdoor workers. The Heat Response Protocol outlines the actions different City departments will take during heat events, including notifying the public, providing assistance to vulnerable populations, and coordinating emergency response. The City collected feedback from the public through the end of July 2024 and released the plan to the public in December 2024. The intended benefits of the Extreme Heat Season Plan are expected to be realized in phases, with short-term (2-3 years) improvements in shading and cooling infrastructure, and long-term (5 years) enhancements in urban design and environmental sustainability. The plan aims to provide immediate relief during heat events while building a robust system for future challenges. To inform implementation of this plan, the City will be using heat mapping data from the City's CAPA Strategies Heatwatch study, FIU iButton sensor deployments, and Google Environmental Insights Explorer tree canopy data. The CAPA Heatwatch study was completed in June and July 2020. The implementation of the Extreme Heat Season Plan will be overseen by the City of Miami's Office of Resilience and Sustainability, alongside various other internal departments.

Se realizaron proyecciones a futuro de cuatro escenarios de cambio climático en el corto, mediano y largo plazo, en comparación con las condiciones históricas entre 1981 - 2010. 

Cada uno de ellos muestra una representación de las condiciones que podrían presentarse a futuro bajo ciertas consideraciones, además de representar el escenario más pesimista a largo plazo (2081-2100). 

Las proyecciones de la precipitación muestran en el escenario más favorable, un ligero incremento en los diferentes periodos, mientras que en el escenario más pesimista tiene un ligero incremento en el corto plazo, y una disminución gradual de la precipitación en el mediano y largo plazo, hasta llegar a 6.7% por debajo del nivel presentado de 1981 a 2010. 

Las proyecciones de temperatura muestran un incremento gradual en todos los escenarios de cambio climático, que va de 1.2 a 1.6°C en el escenario más favorable, y de 1.4 a 5.1°C en el escenario más pesimista.

Phoenix completed a study in partnership with RTI International (formerly Research Triangle Institute) and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to create a Phoenix-specific assessment regarding indicator-based community vulnerability from site and waste management facilities following extreme events. The assessment included identifying sources of vulnerability to extreme events, like droughts, wildfires, extreme heat, and flooding. This included identifying waste sites and facilities, along with vulnerable communities in the surrounding areas. The assessment looked at the sensitivity of different populations to these events, including socioeconomic attributes, demographic attributes, and existing medical conditions. In addition, analysis was performed to assess the vulnerability depending on different carbon emission pathways, Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 4.5 vs. 8.5. https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/climate/cdp/UrbanVulnerability_R9_July2020_Clean_v2.pdf The climate-related scenarios also included data from the USA Fourth National Climate Assessment, the IPCC Assessment Report 5, and the 2021 Maricopa County Multi-Jurisdictional Hazard Mitigation Plan. 

Extreme heat in Phoenix has been studied by many including: 

The Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco has looked at Extreme heat in Phoenix https://www.frbsf.org/research-and-insights/blog/community-development/2024/03/26/extreme-heats-impact-on-a-local-economy-phoenix-arizona/ 

In early 2025, Harvard produced a study of a Phoenix Heat emergency. https://salatainstitute.harvard.edu/harvard-professors-simulate-and-study-phoenix-heat-emergency/ 

The Nature Conservancy has also looked at Heat in Phoenix. Economic Assessment of heat in the Phoenix Metro Area https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/TNC_EcoHeatAssement_AZ_Report.pdf 

 

The Arizona Department of Water Resources regularly examines groundwater supplies in the state. Here is their 2024 update to the Phoenix Active Management Area Groundwater Model. https://www.azwater.gov/phoenix-ama-groundwater-supply-updates 

Another investigation from May of 2025, looks at groundwater impacted by declining Colorado river basin sources: https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2025GL115593 

another study on water from the Communications of earth and environment, looked at a multidecadal impact of drought. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43247-025-0214

column30: o\tPhoenix was the first in the nation to create a publicly funded office focused on heat response in 2021. The Office of Heat Response and Mitigation creates a Heat Response Plan every year that is presented to Phoenix City Council for approval. Phoenix City Council approved the 2025 Heat Response Plan in March of 2025. (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/heat/heat-response-programs/heat-response-plan.html). The plan provides an overview of heat response programs and services, currently 30 in total, that are being implemented in the summer of 2025. The Plan draws content and direction from a network of related plans, including Phoenix's 2021 Climate Action Plan, the 2021 Maricopa County Hazard Mitigation Plan, the Maricopa County Department of Public Health Strategic Plan for Climate and Health, the Heat Action Planning Guide for Greater Phoenix, and the Arizona Department of Health Services Climate and Health Adaptation Plan. Examples of the programs and services within the heat response plan include first responder services, public engagement like the We're Cool Volunteer Program and Public Health Heat Relief and Opioid Education Program, support of the regional Heat Relief Network led by Maricopa Association of Governments, weatherization and emergency utility assistance, and reduction of workplace safety heat concerns. The City added extended hours, overnight capacity, and professional navigation services at five Heat Relief Network locations in the summer of 2024, operating May 1 through September 30. During 2025, a dedicated heat respite and navigation space is available at a large warehouse and is open 24-hours daily. Other respite centers have extended hours. In 2024, Phoenix implemented a pilot program to increase access to chilled drinking water in public spaces. As of May 2025, five fountains have been installed for this initiative and have delivered the equivalent of more than 130,000 average-size plastic bottles of water to residents from July 2024 to April 2025. Three additional fountains are expected to be installed in 2025.

column23: Pensando na dinâmica de Porto Alegre, observa-se que, para além das características físicas como solo, relevo e formação geológica, alguns fatores de vulnerabilidade contribuem para a ampliação do risco. Construções próximas a encostas e planícies, esgotos a céu aberto e descarte inadequado de resíduos, somados a chuvas torrenciais, favorecem a ocorrência de pontos de alagamentos, proliferação de vetores de doenças e deslizamentos. Há também a possibilidade de contração de doenças em locais distantes das residências, como no caso dos coletores de material reciclável que se deslocam pelo território, ampliando as chances de contágio por vetores de arboviroses, bem como enfermidades decorrentes da exposição ao calor intenso. A ocorrência de ondas de calor também vem se tornando cada vez mais frequente, e fatores como a pavimentação e a densidade de edifícios e superfícies que absorvem calor contribuem com a formação de ilhas de calor e a concentração de gases poluentes. Ainda há registros recentes de eventos de secas em partes do estado do Rio Grande do Sul e em Porto Alegre, o que, somado às situações de contaminação e poluição dos corpos hídricos, poderão resultar em escassez hídrica e impactos no abastecimento de água. Em face aos impactos provenientes das mudanças do clima, a Prefeitura de Porto Alegre tem concentrado esforços para qualificar seu território e aumentar a qualidade de vida da população, ao mesmo tempo em que busca identificar e estabelecer ações prioritárias de redução de emissões de GEE, de mitigação e de adaptação social, econômica, ambiental e territorial. O Plano de Ação Climática traz um conjunto de estratégias que o município irá adotar para enfrentar as alterações do clima, reduzindo impactos negativos sobre a população, a economia e o meio ambiente.

column30: O Plano de Ação Climática de Porto Alegre (PLAC) é o instrumento base para a cidade firmar seus compromissos de atingir a neutralidade em 2050 e adaptar a cidade para os impactos dos eventos climáticos. A partir do PLAC, Porto Alegre irá implementar ações de redução das emissões e de adaptação e resiliência, vinculando-as à redução da vulnerabilidade da população e da incidência de doenças e à melhoria da qualidade de vida. As medidas de mitigação contemplam as principais fontes de emissão identificadas no inventário de emissões de GEE, como o uso de combustíveis fósseis no transporte terrestre, o consumo de energia em fontes estacionárias e o tratamento de efluentes. As de adaptação consistem em medidas que amplificam a resiliência da cidade, garantindo maior preparo no enfrentamento das ameaças climáticas, considerando as vulnerabilidades sociais, econômicas e ambiental. Estas ações vieram tanto de projetos, programas e planos já existentes na cidade, quanto de propostas geradas a partir dos diagnósticos desenvolvidos para o PLAC, considerando-se os aspectos climáticos e visando gerar cobenefícios para população, como saúde, bem estar, acesso à biodiversidade, justiça social, emprego e renda. Fundamental salientar que, resguardadas suas especificidades, todas as medidas contempladas fazem parte de um único conjunto balizado de ações climáticas, que buscam equilibrar a mitigação e adaptação, já que ambas tratam de um mesmo problema, a despeito de focos distintos. Por fim, é possível realizar o acompanhamento do progresso das ações do PLAC através da seguinte Plataforma: https://prefeitura.poa.br/plano-de-acao-climatica-plataforma/

Page 27-33: The federal government's recently completed Fourth National Climate Assessment outlines the most current understanding of climate change and its potential impacts for regions across the United States. 61% of major Southeast cities are exhibiting worsening heat waves, higher than any other region, with more than 100 additional warm nights per year expected by the end of the century. This heat affects our waters, our energy demands, vegetation, and habitats, with many more unknowns. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) suggests that sea levels will rise by 14 to 18 inches in the Gulf from 2020 to 2050, with flooding to occur more than 10 times as often as is experienced today. The Tampa Bay Climate Science Advisory Panel has concluded that Gulf waters will be anywhere between 1.5 to 5.5 feet above 2020 levels by the year 2100. Many coastal communities are built to the edges without much room to spare. Drainage systems, which rely on ponds and soil for water storage, will be affected by increased groundwater levels. These and other issues associated with climate change are described in the following pages.
- Tampa currently experiences approximately 73 days each year with 'feels like' temperatures of 100° F and above. By 2053, that number is expected to reach 103 days.
- Hotter temperatures, especially at night, will require air conditioners to work harder and longer. Air conditioning accounts for approximately 27% of home energy use in the
Tampa region and it is predicted that in 30 years, Floridians will pay $300 million more in cooling costs than they do today.
- Increased sea levels will cause flooding at the coast, but will also put pressure on stormwater systems inland. Combined with an expectation of more intense storms, urban areas could see more flooding, especially in low-lying zones.
- The National Oceanic Atmospheric Administration has recently said that, based on historic trajectories, we can expect 4-8 inches of sea level rise in the next 30 years, with high levels of confidence. This change at the coast will not
only affect water entering stormwater systems and overtopping sea walls, but habitats will change, stormwater ponds will become brackish and will not serve their purpose, aquifers will also be affected by salinity, and infrastructure will
become impaired, such as roadways and utilities.
- Warmer coastal waters can create more intense storms for the Gulf region, with heavier and longer-lasting rain.

column30: Tampa's environment, climate, and natural resources are among its greatest assets. We live in a city surrounded by water, on one of the country's most productive urban estuaries, with a river running through it. Tampa also has an incredible tree canopy, recently ranked number one in the world.1 While these attributes make Tampa a beautiful and comfortable place to live, and help to shape the economy and local culture, its geography presents many challenges in a world of environmental change. With consistently higher temperatures, elevated water levels, and the potential for increased storms, Tampa, as other cities across the globe, will have to adapt and respond. We will have to make changes to our infrastructure, our policies, and our priorities, especially considering the disproportionate impacts that climate change will have on vulnerable communities. The effects of climate change are real, and will have broad impacts, as described in this Plan. Going forward, we will have to work together - across city departments, neighborhoods, and sectors - to ensure success, and to make progress towards meeting this challenge.\nThis Climate Action and Equity Plan has been created to set forth principles, initiatives, and actionable projects. By following its guidance in the years to come, we will reduce greenhouse gas emissions, adapt our infrastructures, and make sure to do this with all Tampanians in mind - listening to their input and responding to their needs. These are the three primary goals, fundamental to an overall approach established by this Plan. It will take time to align the trajectory of our city with these new community needs. We are fortunate, however, to have leadership that is looking ahead and making our first steps toward progress.\nTo guide our next steps, the following 10 Climate Action Categories have been established. These categories organize initiatives as well as acting as a checklist for future work. The ultimate goal is for climate action and equity to be integrated into all departmental projects, from master plans to capital improvements, so that it becomes fundamental to City operations.

Tel Aviv-Yafo's Adaptation Plan is a comprehensive framework designed to guide the city's response to the challenges posed by climate change. The plan recognizes the need for a sectoral approach, addressing the specific vulnerabilities and adaptation needs of different sectors within the city. The Adaptation Plan is centered around two key pathways: cooling the city and managing water resources. These pathways address the interconnected challenges of heat stress, flooding and overflows and water scarcity, which are exacerbated by climate change.
Within each pathway, the plan focuses on the following key sectors:
Cooling the City:
•	Urban Planning: Implementing strategies to mitigate the urban heat island effect, such as increasing green spaces, promoting sustainable building practices, and improving urban ventilation.
•	Energy Efficiency: Promoting energy-efficient buildings and appliances to reduce energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions.
•	Public Health: Developing public health initiatives to raise awareness about heat-related risks, provide cooling centers, and ensure access to healthcare services.
Managing Water Resources:
•	Runoff Management: Implementing measures to reduce stormwater runoff and prevent flooding, such as green infrastructure, permeable pavements, and rainwater harvesting.
•	Water Conservation: Promoting water conservation practices in households, businesses, and public spaces to reduce water consumption and ensure adequate supply during dry periods.
•	Wastewater Treatment: Improving wastewater treatment and reuse to enhance water security and reduce reliance on freshwater sources.
By addressing these key sectors within the two pathways, Tel Aviv-Yafo can effectively adapt to the challenges of climate change and build a more resilient city.

The Mitigation and Green Growth plan based on 
a cpredictive emissions model was developed to estimate the expected emissions in the city by 2050 compared to the base year. This model examined three scenarios:

Business As Usual (BAU) Scenario: This scenario accounts for the growth in greenhouse gas emissions based on population projections until 2050 without taking significant actions to reduce emissions. According to this scenario, greenhouse gas emissions are expected to reach 3,900,318 CO2e, an increase of about 30% compared to the base year.

National Reduction Scenario: This scenario includes the total emissions forecasted by 2050 based on population growth projections and assumes full implementation of reduction actions to meet national targets. The conservative approach considers the existing and planned national initiatives to reduce emissions and projects a reduction of approximately 70% compared to the base year.

Ambitious Municipal Scenario: This scenario combines municipal actions to meet reduction targets and the expected growth trends. It considers goals set in energy, waste, and transportation to achieve total carbon neutrality by 2050 compared to the base year.

The predictive model is a working tool to calculate the carbon footprint of different action channels and their relative impact on the city's carbon footprint. Municipal consumption data were input into the model, and in cases where data reliability was low, assumptions were made, which are detailed later for each sector. The dynamic model must be updated based on the quality and availability of data, as outlined in the monitoring and evaluation chapter.

column23: Na escala de Campinas, no âmbito do Plano Local de Ação Climática, o WRI (World Resources Institute - Instituto de Recursos Mundiais) aplicou para a realidade local um método desenvolvido pelo próprio instituto em parceria com a Universidade de Stanford para as projeções climáticas na cidade. Os resultados obtidos são indicadores sobre perigos climáticos que poderão afetar o município no futuro, visando prover insumos para o planejamento urbano e rural. Buscou-se responder a seguinte pergunta: “Como as mudanças climáticas e ameaças relacionadas ao clima irão evoluir em um futuro tendencial (Business as usual) com uso intensivo de combustíveis fósseis até 2050, considerando as principais preocupações da gestão pública?” A metodologia se baseia em simulações climáticas globais desenvolvidas por instituições de pesquisa em todo o mundo e escalonadas pela NASA, dados históricos baseados em satélite fornecidos pelo ECMWF e um método de modelagem probabilística desenvolvido pelo WRI. Campinas participou da construção do método como cidade-piloto, e este está exposto a futuras revisões. O objetivo foi prever o número de ocorrências de um evento climático específico durante um período de tempo futuro determinado em Campinas. Foram selecionados para projeção climática 13 (treze) indicadores vinculados aos seguintes perigos climáticos futuros: calor, Frio, Precipitação e Estiagem. Foram adotados 3 períodos de tempo, que são os horizontes de planejamento definidos no Plano Local de Ação Climática de Campinas: Curto Prazo (2025 a 2032), Médio Prazo (2032 a 2040) e Longo Prazo (2040 a 2050). Após o processamento das metodologias de cálculo escolhidas, os resultados da projeção climática para Campinas puderam ser realizados, de forma quantitativa. Relatório disponível em: https://portal-api.campinas.sp.gov.br/sites/default/files/secretarias/arquivos-avulsos/142/2024/06/27-084218/PLAC_Campinas_Padr%C3%A3o.pdf. A realização destes cenários trouxe maior clareza sobre as tendências futuras e orientou a definição das ações.

O primeiro workshop do GT identificou e orientou o grupo na construção de ações, elaborando uma lista preliminar de objetivos e ações climáticas integradas. No segundo workshop foi revisitado e calibrado o quadro da lista de ações, pensando nos desafios de adaptação, mitigação, seu alinhamento com as prioridades da cidade e co-benefícios para as pessoas e natureza. A priorização das ações foi realizada com base em análise multicritério:o potencial de mitigação; o aumento da resiliência; a promoção de co-benefícios sociais, ambientais e econômicos; e viabilidade das ações (financeiras e institucionais). No terceiro workshop as ações e subações foram validadas, e finalizada a identificação de barreiras, ações habilitantes e marcos de implementação. Ainda, a análise das discussões e opiniões da sociedade durante o processo participativo (conferência, workshops, reuniões e consulta pública on-line) indicou tendências, preocupações comuns e ações prioritárias. Tais informações foram sobrepostas às ações e subações previamente indicadas pelo GT e então foram reformuladas ou tiveram importância reforçada, de modo a incorporar a contribuição comunitária na definição das metas específicas, no delineamento de programas de educação climática e na alocação de recursos para projetos prioritários.

In 2018, to support our initial Five-Year Environment Plan, GMCA commissioned 
research SCATTER 26 to understand potential carbon reduction pathways for Greater 
Manchester. This work identified that the original plan would deliver considerable 
carbon reduction, but that further work would be required at local and national level to 
meet our 2038 target and our ambition to keep within the envelope of carbon needed 
to keep the UK on track to meet the Paris Agreement goals of limiting global warming 
to 'well below 2C with efforts to limit to 1.5C' - our Tyndall budget.
Five years on, we have commissioned further work to understand emissions 
projections given our progress to date, and so we can clearly understand the 
challenges we face over the next five years to inform this action plan. The work helps 
understand what Greater Manchester's emissions reductions are likely to be over the 
duration of this plan, accounting for both national action and local action (Figure 17, pg119).
Figure 17 shows two main pathways. First, the 'No further action' pathway which 
assumes emission reductions in Greater Manchester occur only as a result of 
currently committed UK Government policy and action (as at July 2024), and no 
additional activity is undertaken within Greater Manchester. 
'The 'No Further Action Pathway' does consider anticipated growth in future energy 
demand and some decarbonisation of the wider energy system, but does not take into 
account recent government proposals to bring forward the full decarbonisation of the 
electricity grid to 2030, to ban installation of gas boilers in new buildings from 2027 
and bringing forward the Internal Combustion Engine Vehicles (ICEV) ban for new 
sales from 2030. Nor does it currently account for government's recent 
announcement to set a new target for 81% net zero emissions by 2035. These 
changes can be incorporated into future iterations of the model.
The second pathway, the 'Five-Year Plan' pathway, takes this national position, and 
applies the impact of additional activities within Greater Manchester that are included 
within this plan. This modelling demonstrates that, through the actions identified in this plan, there will be a significant reduction with emissions reducing to 7.3MtCO2 by 2029, and 
3.9MtCO2 by 2038, a 79% reduction from 2005. This identifies that whilst we are 
making considerable progress, there is still work to do at local and national level.

Estrés por calor y calor extremo → aumento de la temperatura urbana y efectos de isla de calor.
Sequías y estrés hídrico → reducción de disponibilidad de agua que impacta la sobrevivencia de la cobertura vegetal.
Aumento de la demanda de agua → presión sobre los recursos hídricos urbanos.
Clima propicio para incendios forestales → incremento del riesgo de pérdida de cobertura arbórea.
Inundaciones urbanas y fluviales, precipitaciones intensas → afectaciones al suelo y al arbolado existente.
Pérdida de espacios verdes y degradación/erosión del suelo → disminución de biodiversidad urbana.

column30: Looking at 2050, every city, large, medium-sized or small, can make a difference and every single person can contribute to achieving a future that leaves no one behind. Finally, to measure effectiveness of the actions reported in the plan, a particular attention was paid to the monitoring and evaluation aspects of the interventions. Thanks to a research project, it has been developed an innovative and flexible framework capable of expressing a quantitative assessment of infrastructures, environment and governance. column30: Despite several obstacles (UNESCO site, wide cultural heritage, >14 million tourists per year, many commuters, large administrative structure, competence on services shared with other municipalities...), Florence has tackled seriously its commitment to sustainability in a sort of never-ending pathway (from the Aalborg Charter to the new Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy to Green City Accord...).Based on human-centric soul, in 2010 Florence adopted an interdisciplinary, co-productive and integrated approach to strategic planning, convinced that only exploiting synergies among sectors, empowering stakeholders and involving citizens, the city could have been able to face challenges.The first two examples of participated and integrated plans have been the SEAP and the Structural plan “Zero Volume” when the city set up a specific “task force” involving all departments and implemented a wide participatory process in “100 squares”.The team has been supported (definition and monitoring) by external consultants in the framework of the European Energy Award process and several H2020 projects (Come2CoM, STEEP, Replicate, CoME Easy).The SEAP, following the CoM requirement, targeted mitigation actions in each sector of municipal competence: public, tertiary and residential buildings and facilities, municipal fleet and public transport, private mobility... Several adaptation issues have already been included like green spaces and water management. The monitoring of the plan shown higher impacts than expected, thanks to the strong administration commitment in daily operations and to citizens' engagement.

column30: Following the SEAP and urban plan experience and thanks to an FP7 project, the city developed an innovative and comprehensive \'Smart City Plan\' exploiting system thinking methodologies and co-production approaches.The plan, adopted in 2015, was meant as a \'master plan\' for any future urban development, setting the guiding strategy and principles for the evolution of the local regulatory framework. The targets set at 2030 and 2050, very ambitious, were already in line with the recent EU indications (carbon neutrality at 2050) and adaptation and energy poverty issues already addressed.This one-of-a-kind master plan has become the reference for the following policies and governance tools of the city; the Smart City Plan, as the SEAP/SECAP, is meant to be a cross-cutting tool integrating different sectors: it shows the ambition to influence every sector of competence, exploiting technology and innovation only with the aim of “prosperity” and well-being (reported also as best practice in the Smart Cities Guidance Package).Florence's target vision is not merely related to IT, perceived as “tools”, but to a wider scope, in line with UN SDGs, for sustainability and wellbeing; this have been reflected in the \'Smart prioritization\' concept developed in H2020-SCC1 REPLICATE project based on the assessment of all different direct impacts and indirect externalities (health, inclusion, poverty, justice...).The city has decided to focus on vulnerable people, energy poverty and social inclusion also in its innovation testbeds with intervention in low-income districts and social housing, advanced mobility services for vulnerable people, affordable public transport, dedicated trainings on digital competences for elderly people, .... Florence is also aware of its weaknesses and boundary conditions: playing an exemplary role, the public sector began to involve more and more stakeholders in sharing data to take together the best decision. The Smart City Control Room best practice is the materialisation of this cooperation between different stakeholders for the common good.Aimed at optimising the daily management, the SCCR demonstrated during COVID periods its flexibility, supporting emergency analysis and in providing useful services/info to citizens.

Current water availability issues in the region are exacerbated by the water demand management 
issues associated with water losses and unaccounted for water, an infestation of alien invasive 
plants, loss and degradation of ecological infrastructure within the catchments which reduces the 
capacity to deliver water-related ecosystem services and deterioration of water quality due to poor 
land use management activities and lack of coordinated efforts to manage water resources within 
the catchment.
The land-use activities in this region include increased pollution from the formal and informal 
settlements; lack of maintenance of the aging sewer infrastructure; poor waste management; poor 
effluent discharge and poor sanitation systems. Other land uses include water use from industrial 
production and streamflow reduction activities from invasive alien vegetation. All of these factors 
have direct impacts on water quality and water availability in the region. The major cause for 
concern is that the water quality and quantity issues resulting from poor land-use management 
have serious implications for water supply. They result in increased costs of water supply through 
increased water treatment costs and increased cost of sourcing raw water from distant 
catchments to augment supply where there is high demand.
As a result, the Msunduzi Municipality intends to undertake and develop a Detailed Integrated 
Catchment Management and Implementation Plan that will highlight and seek to work towards 
addressing issues that are contributing to the deterioration of the water resources within the 
Msunduzi Catchment area. A need for the development of an integrated catchment management 
and implementation plan has been identified to ensure sustainable water resource management 
and improve water security in the Msunduzi Catchment area. Integrated Catchment Management 
Plans are strategic plans for ensuring coordinated management of water resources by various 
water users to ensure improved health, productivity, and resilience of ecological infrastructure 
and water resources. They are used to identify and prioritise interventions that need to be 
implemented to ensure the long-term sustainable management of water resources within 
catchments

column23: Invasive alien species are plants, animals, pathogens and other organisms that are non-native to an ecosystem, and which may cause economic or environmental harm or adversely affect human health. IAS have the ability to spread natural into natural or semi natural habitat because they lack competition on their new environment. Invasive alien species, introduced and/or spread outside their natural habitats, have affected native biodiversity in almost every ecosystem type on earth and are one of the greatest threats to biodiversity. Since the 17th century, invasive alien species have contributed to nearly 40% of all animal extinctions for which the cause is known (CBD, 2006).Some impacts of IAS Cause species extirpation and even extinction.Cause soil degradation and erosion.Reduce land and water recreation opportunities.Cause human and animal suffering in the case of invasive microbes and pathogens.Reduce production in forests, agriculture and fishing sector which harm the economy.They damage infrastructure e.g. gum tree root destroy roads and houses.The impact of invasive alien species on native ecosystems, habitats and species is severe and often irreversible, and can cost millions of Rand's each year

Os cenários climáticos foram fundamentais para conferir consistência técnica e robustez ao Plano Municipal de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças do Clima de Salvador (PMAMC). Eles permitiram compreender os riscos presentes e projetar os impactos futuros das mudanças climáticas na cidade, servindo de base para a definição das metas e ações estratégicas do plano.
A elaboração do PMAMC utilizou projeções climáticas alinhadas ao Painel Intergovernamental sobre Mudanças do Clima (IPCC), considerando diferentes trajetórias de aquecimento global e suas consequências para Salvador. Com base nessas projeções, foi possível estimar aumentos nas temperaturas médias, alterações no regime de chuvas, elevação do nível do mar e a intensificação de eventos extremos, como enchentes, secas prolongadas e deslizamentos de terra.
Esses cenários serviram de base para a aplicação da metodologia de Avaliação de Riscos e Vulnerabilidades Climáticas (CRVA), que envolveu o cruzamento entre a exposição aos eventos climáticos futuros, a sensibilidade socioeconômica da população e a capacidade adaptativa dos territórios. Essa análise permitiu identificar áreas prioritárias para adaptação climática, como o Subúrbio Ferroviário, Cajazeiras e outras regiões periféricas vulneráveis à degradação ambiental e à falta de infraestrutura urbana.
Com isso, as ações previstas no plano, como investimentos em infraestrutura verde, sistemas de drenagem, mobilidade sustentável e habitação resiliente, foram direcionadas com base na identificação de riscos reais e esperados. Além disso, a meta de alcançar a neutralidade climática até 2049 foi definida com base nas projeções de emissões e na capacidade da cidade de transitar para uma economia de baixo carbono.

O Plano de Mitigação e Adaptação às Mudanças Climáticas de Salvador (PMAMC) representa um avanço significativo na promoção da justiça climática e da igualdade social. Ao reconhecer que os impactos das mudanças do clima recaem de forma desproporcional sobre os grupos mais vulneráveis, justamente aqueles que menos contribuem para a crise climática, o plano busca garantir que as soluções propostas sejam justas e inclusivas.
A justiça climática consiste em abordar os desafios do clima de forma integrada com os princípios de equidade e a proteção dos direitos humanos. Isso significa criar alternativas que reduzam os riscos climáticos de maneira equitativa e assegurem que os custos e benefícios das ações sejam distribuídos de forma justa entre toda a população e os ecossistemas da cidade, com atenção especial às comunidades mais expostas e desassistidas.
Dentro do eixo estratégico Salvador Inclusiva, o PMAMC coloca a justiça climática no centro de seus objetivos. Além disso, o plano reforça diretrizes de outros instrumentos e políticas públicas municipais voltadas à participação ativa da população, especialmente dos grupos historicamente marginalizados, em todas as etapas da ação climática: formulação, implementação e monitoramento.
Ciente de que o acesso à informação, à educação e à capacitação é essencial para qualificar a participação social e o controle social das ações públicas, o plano também propõe a formação de cidadãos conscientes dos efeitos das mudanças climáticas em suas vidas e no planeta. Com isso, as ações climáticas passam a ser entendidas como uma oportunidade de ampliar direitos, reduzir desigualdades e promover a inclusão social.

In 2021, the City of San Antonio became the first city in Texas to fight heat with the cool pavement treatment, testing it on a small stretch of asphalt at the east end of the Hays Street Bridge.

Now, the City is expanding its initiative, applying cool pavement treatments -- GuardTop, PaveTech, GAF, and SealMaster -- to sections of roadway in all 10 Council Districts.

The application of the pavement treatment began on Monday, April 24, 2023. After the cool pavement is applied, the City will study the locations for six months and work with the University of Texas at San Antonio to evaluate its potential to cool the city down.

BENEFITS TO THE CITY

While more costly than typical seal coating materials, Cool Pavement can last longer than traditional asphalt seal coats. It also has the potential to make our streets cooler and more sustainable. That's in line with the City's SA Climate Ready, Climate Action & Adaptation Plan adopted by City Council on October 17, 2019.

COST AND FUNDS

In total, the program will cost about $1 million. That includes the cost of installing the cool pavement at all ten (10) sites as well as evaluating the materials for both temperature and product performance. The City's Resiliency, Energy Efficiency, and Sustainability Program Fund will fund the project. Its goal is to reduce temperatures in the hottest parts of the city in partnership with local institutions such as UTSA.
