column23: To reduce the nation's mounting natural disaster losses, the U.S. Congress passed the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (DMA 2000) to invoke new and revitalized approaches to mitigation planning. Section 322 of DMA 2000 emphasizes the need for state and local government entities to closely coordinate on mitigation planning activities and makes the development of a hazard mitigation plan a specific eligibility requirement for any local government applying for federal mitigation grant funds. These funds include the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP), the Pre-Disaster Mitigation (PDM) program, and the Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) Program, all of which are administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) under the Department of Homeland Security. Communities with an adopted and federally approved hazard mitigation plan thereby become pre-positioned and more apt to receive available mitigation funds before and after the next disaster strikes. This plan was prepared in coordination with FEMA Region IV and the North Carolina Division of Emergency Management (NCEM) to ensure that it meets all applicable federal and state planning requirements. A Local Mitigation Plan Review Tool, found in Appendix A, provides a summary of FEMA's current minimum standards of acceptability and notes the location within this plan where each planning requirement is met. One significant resource in this effort was the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI), which has been tracking various types of severe weather since 1950. Their Storm Events Database contains an archive by county of destructive storm or weather data and information which includes local, intense and damaging events. NCEI receives storm data from the National Weather Service (NWS). The NWS receives their information from a variety of sources, which include but are not limited to county, state and federal emergency management officials, local law enforcement officials, SkyWarn spotters, NWS damage surveys, newspaper clipping services, the insurance industry and the general public, among others. The NCEI database contains 641 records of storm/weather events that occurred in Mecklenburg County in the 20-year period from 1999 through 2018.

column23: A science-based target requires an awareness of how much carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases are being pumped into the atmosphere because of human activity (both within Charlotte and beyond). To meet the goal of the Paris Climate Accord - to stay below a temperature increase of 2°C globally - the global community must reach peak global GHG emissions by 2030 and reduce them by at least half by 2050. It is important to understand that these targets for 2050 represent mid-points, as the reductions of GHG emissions must continue beyond this point. Climate change is caused by global warming and global warming is caused by a buildup of greenhouse gas emissions in the atmosphere. This concentration of gases in the atmosphere is built up over time for differing periods - for example, carbon dioxide lasts for 100 years, while methane9, which is 28 times more potent than CO2, lasts for 10 years in the atmosphere. It is therefore the total amount of greenhouse gases released, between now and 2050, that will determine the level of global warming that cities around the world will experience. A per capita target helps to address many of these concerns. The concept of a per capita target is displayed in Figure 2, alongside the targets for the Paris Climate Accord. The use of a per capita target allows for a forward-looking approach, as well as setting the pathway for a carbon budget (should one be set in the future by Charlotte). The concept of using a per capita target was discussed and presented to the community at one of the Stakeholder Meetings and was widely endorsed. Bilateral meetings also took place with a range of advocacy groups, government departments, and businesses within Charlotte to further discuss the approach and assess support. The per capita target of 2tCO2e was subsequently unanimously supported by City Council on June 25, 2018. To achieve the 2tCO2e per capita target, Charlotte's City government needs to 'show the way'. The City, therefore, adopted higher targets for its own buildings and fleet. These commitments extend far beyond that of the original resolution. The City ultimately committed to 'striving to source 100% of its energy use in [City of Charlotte] buildings and fleet from zero carbon sources by 2030' via a unanimous vote by City Council.

column30: This is the City of Charlotte's first Strategic Energy Action Plan (SEAP), as required by its commitment to the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM). The SEAP provides a framework for delivering the 'Sustainable and Resilient Charlotte by 2050' Resolution. The Resolution was championed by City Council's Environment Committee as an example of their leadership and commitment to Charlotte's low carbon future and was unanimously passed in June of 2018.The SEAP provides a roadmap for the City's transition to a low carbon future, delivering the City Council's resolution to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to less than 2 tons of CO2e per person across the City by 2050.To be a competitive city in a globally engaged era, Charlotte recognizes that the City needs to become more sustainable and resilient. This needs to be achieved by employing an integrated, inclusive, and systematic approach to urban development. The SEAP will form one part of the City's broader resiliency strategy and will be used to build stronger and more inclusive neighborhoods that can make informed decisions around the use of energy. The SEAP provides the City with the framework it needs to deliver the transition to a low carbon economy that attracts and retains talent, and grows local jobs and a green economy. Recommendations provided by the SEAP will encourage innovative administration, organization, and mechanisms that ensure strategic alignment and efficiencies within implementation efforts. These recommendations enable the SEAP to align with other current and future City strategies, so that they are better integrated and mutually reinforcing. This includes key issues such as funding models, total costs of ownership, and policy revisions. The City of Charlotte acknowledges that the SEAP is ambitious in documenting what the City wants to achieve, as the City seeks innovative approaches to the challenges and opportunities an energy regulated state provides. However, a key part of the SEAP is looking at recommendations and projects that are not only about energy generation, but how the City and its residents can change how they use and think of energy. The effort to successfully implement the SEAP and achieve a low carbon future lies within a citywide collaborative effort. Thus, the total cost of implementation has not yet been estimated. Finally, the city is currently undertaking an update of the SEAP which is anticipated to be finalized in early 2025.

The prioritization of actions within the plan was informed by several factors, including urgency for emissions reduction, availability of funding, societal needs, and the potential for synergistic benefits. For instance, actions targeting energy efficiency in buildings and the transition to sustainable mobility were prioritized based on their substantial emissions reduction potential and positive co-benefits, such as improved air quality and public health. 

The CCC Action Plan outlines clear responsibilities, timelines, and indicators for each action, and progress is continuously monitored and evaluated.

The SECAP of the City of Ljubljana is composed of four interrelated parts: (1) Climate City Contract (CCC), which, besides adaptation measures, includes the aspect of organisational and public participation methodological approach, the same for both areas (mitigation and adaptation). (2)Preparation of the framework for climate change adaptation, ensuring a support system and political backing for the planning and implementation of adaptation measures. (3) Climate vulnerability and risk analysis for the City of Ljubljana, carried out in accordance with the IPCC AR5 methodology, aligned with the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change and with methodologies applied at the national and regional level in Slovenia and (4) Adaptation action plan - Climate Change Adaptation Strategy. The analysis uses quantitative and qualitative methods to consider the impacts of different climate scenarios on the city, focusing on the period up to 2030 and 2050.

The SECAP uses historical climate data as well as projections based on scenarios provided by the Slovenian Environment Agency (ARSO) under the RCP 8.5 framework, which explores pathways for temperature increases up to 1.5 and 2 C. These scenarios include evaluations of temperature, precipitation, and extreme weather events. By understanding these trends, the plan identifies the key risks and opportunities for energy efficiency, local renewable energy production, and community resilience.

The scenario analysis primarily helps in shaping the long-term goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving energy security, and adapting infrastructure to future climate conditions. column23: The Bursa Sustainable Energy and Climate Adaptation Action Plan (BUSECAP) sets out a roadmap for mitigation of emissions from energy consumption in different sectors identified with the participation of urban stakeholders. The point of this origin of this plan is the city-scale greenhouse gas inventory, the bases of which are prepared by various institutions according to the future visions of the urban stakeholders and the future of the city, as well as the Metropolitan Municipality.BUSECAP has set out Bursa's BAU (Business as Usual) scenario using predictions from different institutions on population, sectoral growth and calculated 2030 emissions as approximately 10.9 million tons of CO2e. Unlike the reference year, the largest component of 2030 emissions is transportation (44%). It is expected that the category of residential and nonresidential buildings will be 36% and 16%, respectively.Turkey's urban growth rate, is similar to developing countries rather than industrialized countries in terms of quality and quantity. Since it is not possible to make reference to absolute emission reductions at these growth rates, it would be appropriate to express emission reduction targets as per-person emissions. According to the BAU scenario, per capita emissions increase from 2.48 tCO2e to 3.24 (31% increase).With the reduction measures put forward in every sector, Bursa can achieve its development by 2030 with 22% less greenhouse gas emissions, while per capita emissions can achieve a reduction of about 40% by 2030 compared to 2014. In this case, per capita emissions will be reduced by 40% to 1.56 tonnes of CO2/day, compared to 2014.Due to high population growth and high growth rates in the transport sector, absolute emissions may be reduced by only 28% compared to the base year of 2014, despite the proposed measures. Energy efficiency measures in various sectors and investments in renewable energies are estimated to reduce the possible emissions of 2030 to 5.9 million tonnes of CO2e.The per capita GHG emissions can be significantly reduced by the same reduction scenario, with a reduction of 54% according to the BAU scenario and a 40% reduction over the reference year 2014. On the contrary, the reduction scenario shows that despite high growth rates, Bursa can achieve growth by reducing its emissions, which should be regarded as a significant achievement.

In alignment with national policies and to prepare for the new climate system, it is essential to establish greenhouse gas emission management and reduction strategies tailored to the characteristics of Daegu Metropolitan City. This is to contribute to achieving carbon neutrality and the goals of greenhouse gas reduction.

Daegu Metropolitan City needs to build a systematic greenhouse gas management system, including detailed greenhouse gas reduction implementation plans and performance evaluations for sectors such as energy, industrial processes, waste, agriculture and livestock, and carbon sinks. To meet the national greenhouse gas reduction targets for 2030, the role of local governments, which are key actors in climate change response, is crucial. Therefore, Daegu Metropolitan City has developed a greenhouse gas reduction roadmap that reflects the 'National 2050 Carbon Neutral Scenario' and 'National 2030 NDC (Nationally Determined Contributions)' and is tailored to the local context while encouraging citizen participation.

This plan aims to establish a comprehensive greenhouse gas reduction and management system across eight key sectors: climate and environment, citizen life, circular economy, forestry and agriculture, economy and industry, energy transition, green transportation, and buildings and urban areas. The goal is to derive policy measures and set reduction targets that align with regional characteristics and needs.

In line with the global trend towards carbon neutrality by 2050, both the central and local governments in South Korea have announced carbon neutrality declarations and plans. On October 28, 2020, President Moon Jae-in first announced the goal of '2050 Carbon Neutrality' during the budget address at the National Assembly. Subsequently, on December 10, 2020, the '2025 Carbon Neutral Vision' was declared.

The carbon neutrality declaration is part of the preparation for the Long-term Low Greenhouse Gas Emission Development Strategies (LEDS) that all parties to the Paris Agreement are required to submit to the UN by the end of 2020. To prepare for this, a social vision forum was established in early 2019 and operated for about a year, during which discussions led to the development of five basic scenarios and an additional scenario for carbon neutrality.

In addition to carbon neutrality, there is a need to address changes in economic and social structures due to low growth and COVID-19. Consequently, both central and local governments have formulated Green New Deal plans. To facilitate a major societal transition, it is crucial to improve public awareness and secure the momentum for transition. The role of local governments is essential in this process, and efforts are underway to jointly explore strategies and cooperative models between central and local governments.

● The 1.5℃ Special Report was approved at the 48th IPCC General Assembly held in Incheon on September 11, 2018. The Paris Agreement stipulated that 'We will strive to keep the global average temperature rise significantly lower than 2℃ and limit it to 1.5℃ compared to the pre-industrial level.' The 5th IPCC Report (2014) only suggested a scenario of a rise of 2℃, so the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change formally requested the IPCC to prepare a 1.5℃ special report by 2018. The 1.5℃ Special Report is an important scientific input data for the follow-up negotiations of the Paris Agreement, which first evaluated the path to achieving the 1.5℃ target. If global warming continues at the current rate, the global average temperature increase is expected to exceed 1.5°C between 2030 and 2052. In order to achieve the 1.5℃ target, it is necessary to reduce CO2 by 45% compared to 2010 by 2030, and to achieve NET-ZERO emission, where CO2 emission and absorption are completely offset by 2050. By 2050, the use of coal must be completely stopped, the proportion of renewable energy must be increased to 85% of the total energy supply, and forest protection and restoration are also important means of reducing greenhouse gas emissions. 
● In the Goyang Basic Plan for 2030, the basic directions of the energy sector are to create an environment that can reduce energy consumption, expand the use of clean fuels for environmental conservation, and establish a stable and efficient energy supply and demand system, and promote energy conservation and rational use by sector.
● For this purpose, an action strategy was prepared to establish a comprehensive energy management plan. The vision of the energy management (climate change) sector of the Goyang City Environmental Conservation Plan was set as an energy self-reliant city where citizens act, and the establishment of an efficient energy self-reliance foundation and promotion of climate change adaptation activities were presented as a strategy. To achieve the vision, 2 strategies and 7 projects were presented. The ratio of renewable energy to electricity was set to increase from the current 6.9% to 12.0% by 2022, which is the target year, and to 17.0% by 2027. The goal was to increase the number of energy independent villages from the current 4 to 12 by 2022, the target year, and to 32 by 2027.

column30: AMC used the 'Net Zero ClimateResilientCITIES' methodology to develop its climate action plan to achieve net zero emissions by 2070. This methodology includes a multi-stakeholder approach that involves assessing climate vulnerabilities, estimating GHG emissions, proposing climate resilient interventions that address adaptation and mitigation, and developing frameworks for financing, implementing, monitoring and reporting climate actions. By incorporating expertise and experience from initiatives led by ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability, the plan benefits from a wealth of knowledge and best practices in climate planning and action. This methodology provided a step-wise approach to address climate change adaptation and mitigation. Its nine steps are organised into three phases: Analyse, Act, and Accelerate. Ahmedabad embarked on a climate-resilient journey through this ninestep process. AMC committed to climate action by forming a City Climate Core Team to lead the charge. A Stakeholder Committee was constituted to seek inputs from and involve the community, including the private sector, in the implementation of the action plan. The city's socio-environmental landscape and key challenges were identified, climate risks and vulnerability assessed, and emissions baselines established. Goals, strategies, and actions that address identified climate vulnerabilities and thematic actions to reduce GHG emissions across sectors, were defined. To guide emissions reduction strategies across three different planning horizons, i.e., 2030, 2050 and 2070, the CRCAP scales the defined goals, strategies, and actions across two emissions reduction scenarios.

column30: La Estrategia de Cambio Climático, Calidad del Aire y Salud de Zaragoza, ECAZ 3.0 horizonte 2030, es la herramienta estratégica de la ciudad de Zaragoza para la acción frente a la crisis climática, la mejora de la calidad del aire y la protección y promoción de la salud de las personas y las comunidades ante estos retos. Además, la ECAZ 3.0 incorpora el papel que los recursos pueden tener para garantizar la sostenibilidad urbana. Por este motivo considera 4 recursos clave: •\tlas energías renovables •\tla alimentación sostenible •\tla gestión sostenible del agua •\tel aprovechamiento y minimización de los residuos para convertirlos en recursos

column23: Climate-related scenarios have significantly shaped Porto's Climate City Contract, ensuring that the city's strategies align with international commitments and the municipality's vision for sustainability. The development of this contract was influenced not just by prospective climate scenarios, but also by concrete outcomes from existing climate initiatives. These scenarios provided a forward-looking perspective on climate risks, challenges, and opportunities, enabling Porto to adopt a proactive stance in its climate action plans. Porto's approach was guided by the commitments made through international frameworks such as the Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy, the Green City Accord, and the EU Mission for 100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities by 2030. These frameworks established ambitious targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, enhancing energy efficiency, and fostering climate resilience, which the city of Porto incorporated into its strategic planning. The climate scenarios helped identify priority areas, setting the stage for interventions that are both impactful and aligned with the global goal of climate neutrality. For instance, they informed the adoption of renewable energy projects, the expansion of green infrastructure, the promotion of sustainable mobility, and the enhancement of energy-efficient buildings. By integrating these insights, the Climate City Contract emphasizes a systemic and multi-sectoral approach to urban transformation, addressing climate challenges in a holistic manner. Furthermore, the contract reflects Porto's understanding that climate action is an evolving journey. It builds on lessons learned from ongoing initiatives, creating a dynamic strategy that remains flexible and responsive to emerging climate data and trends. This adaptability ensures that Porto not only meets but exceeds its climate targets, demonstrating leadership in the transition to a sustainable, climate-resilient future.

In 2020, the Office of Sustainability launched a multi-faceted outreach and engagement effort to identify priorities of community members on the frontlines of climate change and obtain feedback on those priorities from the broader community. This effort included virtual listening sessions, an Ambassador program, and tapping into previous surveys from community organizations and planning processes to gain insight on community needs without over-surveying. A community-wide survey also obtained feedback on the vision for equitable climate action and resilience.

Beginning in the fall of 2020, the next step in the RVAgreen 2050 process convened community organizations serving frontline communities, institutional partners, government content experts, and other stakeholders for the RVAgreen 2050 Roundtable (as the central advisory group) and topical working groups in order to uplift the community priorities identified through the listening process: community wealth; housing & buildings; neighborhoods; and, health & well-being.

Starting in 2021, during the Plan Development Phase, the Office began working with residents, frontline community organizations, stakeholders, and technical experts to translate the community priorities into strategies that achieve the following goals and ensure that the plan addresses the community priorities in an equitable way:
1) Increase equity, particularly racial equity
2) Reduce greenhouse gases and pollution
3) Enhance resilience to climate impacts

During this phase of the process, metrics and implementation frameworks were also developed to create accountability. The draft plan was then shared for community-wide input. 

Informed by this community-driven process, the final plan centers around five climate-related pathways: 1) Buildings & Energy; 2) Community; 3) Environment; 4) Transportation & Mobility; 5) Waste Reduction & Recovery. The plan is a roadmap to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 45% by 2030, achieve net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and help the community adapt to Richmond's climate impacts of extreme heat, precipitation, and flooding. The plan was adopted by City Council in February of 2023.

column23: As per the climate scenarios applied in the Freetown climate action planning process, climate hazards are driven by rising precipitation and temperature. The climate profile of the city is characterized by tropical conditions characterized by warm temperatures and significant rainfall between May and November (recently extending into December). Outside of the rainy season, the climate is humid, with the hottest, driest months are between December and March. Regarding precipitation, the average rainfall in Freetown is 3000mm per annum. The city experiences seasonal rainfall variability with a rainy season between May and November, with the maximum precipitation in August. Historical rainfall averages for August in Freetown indicate that 530mm can fall within August. Precipitation projections are less consistent, with slight increases projected at 34. According to the IPCC AR6 Atlas, up to a 10% increase in rainfall can be expected under RCP 2.6, and up to a 20% increase under RCP 8.5 by 2060. The IPCC also indicates a high confidence in increasing seasonal rainfall variability and an increase in heavy precipitation events by 2060 (from a 1960 baseline). Regarding temperature, the average temperature in Freetown is 26°C. The yearly average minimum temperature is around 23.8˚C, while the average maximum temperature is 29.9˚C [although a recent NOAA-supported heat mapping exercise in 2023 suggests that the maximum temperature has already exceeded this number]. December is the warmest month with an average of 26.6°C, while August has the lowest average temperature of the year, at 24.4°C. The data over the past 40 years suggests that temperature is getting warmer in Freetown due to climate change. According to the IPCC AR6 Atlas, there is high confidence that the average temperature in Freetown and surrounding areas will increase. The mean temperature is projected to increase by up to 2˚C by 2100 under RCP 2.6, while under RCP 8.5 projections indicate over 2˚C increase by 2060 and over 4˚C by 2100 under RCP 8.5 (from a 1960 baseline). The number of days with maximum temperatures over 35˚C and is expected to increase by 2060 under RCP 2.6, while under RCP 8.5 an increase in days over 40 ˚C can be expected to increase.

column30:
Freetown completed and published its first integrated Climate Action Strategy in 2022 addressing both climate mitigation and adaptation targets through 2030. This included a baseline GHG inventory with 2018 data (recently updated with 2021 data) and a participatory Community Climate Risk Assessment. To address the adaption challenge, Freetown committed to building the institutional capacity and enabling environment required to adapt to climate-related hazards and natural disasters by 2030 and create climate resilient people, infrastructure and city systems by 2030. To address the mitigation challenge, Freetown committed to reduce GHG emissions by at least 44% by 2050 compared to the base year (2018) level and an interim target of 13% below base year levels by 2030.
Based on both climate modeling and the community risk assessment, the following core elements of the Freetown Integrated Climate Action Strategy were identified jointly by local government and community stakeholders:
1 / Resilience - Disaster Risk Management & 
Climate Resilient Infrastructure
Vision:
Developing climate resilient communities in Freetown by promoting the safety of communities in the face of climate change and extreme climate events.
2 / Resilience - Heat
Vision:
Increasing Freetown's climate resilience to heat impacts and becoming a more livable, cool and sustainable city for its people.
3 / Resilience - Environmental Management
Vision:
Developing climate resilient communities in Freetown by enhancing nature in our urban environments and the natural ability of ecosystems to buffer climate change impacts.
4 / Healthy City - Water
Vision:
Creating water security for all users and uses in Freetown.
5 / Healthy City - Sanitation
Vision: 
Freeing Freetown from waste and developing a smart and sustainable waste management system that enables and fosters quality of life and livelihoods for communities.
6 / Urban Mobility 
Vision:
Building a cleaner, safer and more equally accessible transport system.
 7 / Urban Energy
Vision:
Transitioning to a clean, accessible and equitable city energy system.
The Integrated Climate Action Strategy is linked to the city's development plan (Transform Freetown Agenda), through with we express our Ecosystem-based Adaptation and biodiversity strategies. Also the Climate Action Strategy is aligned with the Sierra Leone Climate Change policy, Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and the National Adaptation Plan (NAP).

Waste Management: Strengthening waste systems to reduce methane emissions and improve management in extreme weather events.

This sectoral coverage ensures a multi-dimensional approach to resilience and aligns with national adaptation goals and global frameworks.

The Climate Contract is a document outlining the approach to bridging the gap between projects that have already been implemented or planned and the actions necessary to achieve climate neutrality. The contract consists of three parts. The first part, called Commitments, describes the city's climate ambitions, sets the target, and includes a declaration to take the necessary actions to achieve it. The second part, the Action Plan, identifies the intervention areas, lists the measures, and describes how they will be implemented. The third part, the Investment Plan, presents cost scenarios, funding sources, as well as barriers and risks associated with implementation.

The target adopted in Krakow's Climate Contract is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 80% by 2030 compared to 2018 levels. A large part of the emissions reduction (4,473 thousand tCO2e) will result from actions implemented after 2018 or planned in the city's and the Polish government's strategic documents. The contract contains a detailed description of an additional 58 measures that should be undertaken to achieve a further reduction of 1,614 thousand tCO2e (carbon dioxide equivalent). The cost of these measures is estimated at PLN 28,769 million.

Calculations from the Economic Model indicate, however, that the overall financial benefits, both direct and indirect (lower energy expenditures, reduced health costs, additional jobs, etc.) outweigh the costs of the transformation. The majority of emissions reductions will result from implementing national strategies carried out by private entities: energy companies, businesses, and building owners and managers. Eight key actions on the path to climate neutrality are:
1. Decarbonization of the district heating system
2. Development of citizen energy communities
3. Renovation of municipal public utility buildings
4. Modernization of street and square lighting
5. Construction of the metro and development of rail transport
6. Renovation of residential buildings and built-up areas
7. Increasing resilience to the impacts of climate change
8. Engagement of residents and entrepreneurs in city governance.

The commitment is of a moral and reputational nature. Despite being signed by the Mayor, the contract is not a legally binding agreement.

La acción climática no concluye con la aprobación de un Plan de Acción Climática: su impacto real depende de la implementación efectiva, respaldada por instrumentos normativos, sistemas de monitoreo y mecanismos de comunicación. La etapa de ejecución requiere poner en práctica las medidas, informar a la ciudadanía sobre avances y fortalecer a las instituciones responsables mediante un sistema de mejora continua.
El monitoreo, basado en la recolección sistemática de datos con indicadores específicos, permite evaluar el progreso y orientar la toma de decisiones. Estos indicadores deben ser medibles, concretos, objetivos, específicos, económicos, aceptados, monitoreables y consistentes en el tiempo.
En mitigación, los indicadores suelen medir tanto avances de proceso (obras, implementación) como resultados (reducción de emisiones), cumpliendo con relativa facilidad las condiciones requeridas. En cambio, los de adaptación presentan mayores desafíos: falta de metodologías estandarizadas, dificultad para establecer líneas de base en escenarios cambiantes, uso de indicadores proxy poco precisos, necesidad de evaluar “no eventos” y complejidad para atribuir impactos a medidas concretas.
La evaluación continua retroalimenta al plan, optimizando su diseño y garantizando eficiencia en el uso de recursos. Para ello es clave definir qué, por qué, cómo, cuándo y quién monitorea, además de establecer cómo se comunicarán los resultados a gobiernos y sociedad civil.
Cada medida climática cuenta con una hoja de ruta que incluye: título, descripción, metas específicas, alcance geográfico (municipal), clasificación como adaptación, mitigación o pérdidas y daños, riesgos abordados, autoridad responsable, estado de implementación, periodo de ejecución (con horizonte 2030 en línea con el Acuerdo de París), instrumentos normativos, necesidades y barreras, indicadores de monitoreo, análisis de impacto en salud y vinculación con la Ley N.º 27.520 de presupuestos mínimos.
Este enfoque asegura que el plan no sea un documento estático, sino un proceso dinámico de acción, control, aprendizaje y ajuste permanente que fortalezca la resiliencia y la reducción de emisiones frente al cambio climático.

En conformidad con los instrumentos diagnósticos y en atención a las principales amenazas que afectan a Rosario -de naturaleza hidrometeorológica-, y atravesada por una pandemia de origen zoonótico, se consideró relevante actualizar la planificación e implementación. A tales fines, se dividió el eje de agua, resiliencia y riesgo para abordar sus especificidades. Este nuevo eje incluyó objetivos estratégicos, directrices sectoriales, acciones, de acuerdo a la estructura metodológica del PLAC 2030, metas a 2025 y 2030 e indicadores de seguimiento. Al mismo tiempo que se realizó la actualización de los ejes, priorización de las acciones, metas e indicadores del PLAC 2030, y de la conformación de una agenda climática que fomente el desarrollo climáticamente resiliente y la transición ecológica justa y la sustentabilidad del proceso, se abordó un proceso de gobernanza climática. Formado por el Gabinete Local de Cambio Climático y Transición Ecológica Justa que a su vez, está compuesto por otras dos instancias: Gabinete político y Gabinete técnico; y, por el Comité Asesor frente al Cambio Climático.El Gabinete político conformado por las principales autoridades de las áreas del ejecutivo municipal, presidido por el Intendente Municipal y se presentan los insumos y recomendaciones del Gabinete Técnico de cambio climático y del Comité Asesor frente al cambio climático. El Gabinete técnico es un espacio de capacitación a los equipos municipales para mejorar el conocimiento sobre las estrategias de cambio climático. column30: El proceso de planificación estratégica, implementación y seguimiento participativo a través de la búsqueda de consensos intersectoriales y participación ciudadana han sido base para la construcción democrática de Rosario. El desarrollo del PLAC, su implementación ha sido llevado adelante por la Secretaría de Ambiente y Espacio Público bajo la responsabilidad de la Dirección General de Acción Climática y Calidad Ambiental de la Municipalidad de Rosario. Después de la actualización de los ejes (que incluye 7 ejes: Riesgo y resiliencia, Biodiversidad y uso de suelo, Salud, Agua, Energía, Residuos Sólidos y Transporte), la priorización de las medidas y la conformación de una agenda climática para la implementación de dichas acciones, se ha continuado con la consolidación de los espacios de gobernanza climática: Gabinete Local de Cambio Climático y Transición Ecológica Justa, conformado por dos espacios de trabajo, Gabinete político y Gabinete técnico; y el Comité Asesor frente al Cambio Climático. En el año 2022, dicho comité realizó 6 encuentros de trabajo, y en el año 2023 se llevaron a cabo 4 reuniones, abordando temáticas, tales como, la coordinación de la agenda del propio comité y el Gabinete Político, la priorización de las acciones de mitigación y adaptación de los ejes que conforman el PLAC, las metas identificadas de las medidas, el acompañamiento en la elaboración del sistema de monitoreo, etc. Este proceso participativo de políticas de gobernanza basadas en la reflexión y el consenso, con enfoque interdisciplinario en la planificación y en la búsqueda de soluciones (con una base técnica y científica), han sido premisas para la construcción de las políticas públicas locales. column23:
La elaboración del Plan de Acción Climática del Municipio de Chihuahua estuvo profundamente orientado por los principales retos, tendencias y riesgos asociados al cambio climático que enfrenta el territorio municipal. Estos temas funcionaron como elementos rectores tanto en el diagnóstico como en la definición de estrategias, líneas de acción y prioridades de inversión.

En primer lugar, el análisis de variables climáticas, como el incremento sostenido de la temperatura promedio, la mayor frecuencia de olas de calor, la disminución de la disponibilidad hídrica y la intensificación de eventos extremos de precipitación, nos permitió identificar sectores críticos y vulnerabilidades estructurales, especialmente en materia de recursos hídricos, infraestructura urbana, movilidad, salud pública y gestión del territorio.

A partir de este diagnóstico, los temas de cambio climático se incorporaron como criterios obligatorios de planificación, orientando la alineación del Plan con metodologías nacionales e internacionales, tales como los enfoques de mitigación basados en inventarios de emisiones y los análisis de riesgo climático. Esto facilitó establecer metas cuantificables de reducción de GEI y definir acciones prioritarias en sectores emisores como transporte, energía, residuos y eficiencia en edificaciones.

Asimismo, la identificación de impactos climáticos permitió orientar las estrategias de adaptación hacia la protección de zonas de riesgo, el fortalecimiento de la resiliencia urbana, la gestión sostenible del agua, la conservación de servicios ecosistémicos y el diseño de infraestructura verde.

El proceso también integró consideraciones de gobernanza climática, equidad social y participación comunitaria, reconociendo que el cambio climático no solo es un fenómeno ambiental, sino un factor transversal que afecta la toma de decisiones en todos los ámbitos del gobierno municipal. Por ello, los temas climáticos sirvieron como marco para articular capacidades institucionales, fortalecer mecanismos de coordinación con el estado y la federación, y definir instrumentos de financiamiento climático.

En conjunto, los temas de cambio climático permitieron que el Plan de Acción Climática del Municipio de Chihuahua se estructurara como un instrumento estratégico, basado en evidencia, con enfoque de sostenibilidad, resiliencia y competitividad urbana de largo plazo.

El Plan de Acción Climática del Municipio de Chihuahua incorpora un enfoque integral que abarca diversos sectores estratégicos con el propósito de reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero y fortalecer la resiliencia del territorio frente a los impactos del cambio climático. Para ello, el Plan estructura sus acciones en los siguientes sectores clave:

En materia de mitigación, se consideran los sectores vinculados al consumo y generación de energía, incluyendo transporte, electricidad y combustibles utilizados en los ámbitos residencial, comercial, industrial y agropecuario. El sector transporte se aborda como una de las principales fuentes emisoras, lo que requiere intervenciones orientadas a la movilidad sostenible y a la modernización de la infraestructura urbana. 

En cuanto a adaptación, el Plan contempla sectores específicos asociados a la vulnerabilidad climática del municipio. Entre ellos destacan el sector hídrico, debido a la creciente presión sobre la disponibilidad de agua; el desarrollo urbano, que requiere incorporar criterios de resiliencia en la planeación del territorio; y el sector de biodiversidad, que demanda acciones para conservar ecosistemas y servicios ambientales esenciales. También se consideran sectores relacionados con servicios básicos como agua potable, energía y saneamiento; así como el sector rural productivo, que comprende actividades agrícolas, ganaderas y forestales en zonas rurales. De igual forma, se incluye el sector económico, con énfasis en la capacidad del municipio para mantener la competitividad bajo escenarios climáticos futuros, y el sector salud, debido a los riesgos que el cambio climático representa para la población.

Además, el Plan incorpora sectores transversales que abarcan aspectos de educación ambiental, participación ciudadana, comunicación, financiamiento y gobernanza climática, con el propósito de garantizar la implementación adecuada de las acciones y su sostenibilidad en el tiempo.

Para la creación del PACMUN, se contemplan los escenarios climáticos descritos en el Estudio de Riesgos y Vulnerabilidad al Cambio Climático de Mérida evalúan el impacto de los cambios proyectados en variables como temperatura y precipitación, utilizando diferentes Trayectorias de Concentración Representativa (RCP, por sus siglas en inglés). Estos escenarios son esenciales para gestionar los riesgos futuros.
El documento analiza principalmente dos trayectorias:

RCP4.5 (estabilización media): Considera una estabilización de las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero hacia el 2100, con un forzamiento radiativo de 4.5 W/m².
RCP8.5 (altas emisiones): Representa un escenario en el que las emisiones siguen aumentando sin mitigación, con un forzamiento radiativo de 8.5 W/m²
Ambos escenarios proyectan una reducción en la precipitación y un aumento en las temperaturas para Mérida durante el periodo 2021-2040, con el escenario RCP8.5 siendo el más extremo. Se espera que la precipitación acumulada disminuya en un 17% en comparación con los registros históricos, afectando principalmente los meses de julio y agosto, con algunos incrementos aislados en los meses de octubre y noviembre.
En cuanto a la temperatura, los cuatro escenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7 y SSP5-8.5) proyectan incrementos en la temperatura media de hasta un 1.03% en el corto plazo (2021-2040), con aumentos más drásticos hacia el final del siglo.

column23: The All-Plan was conducted by the County to address climate change concerns using community engagement processes for the residents' insights and living experiences, to include in the planning process. Southern Nevada is expected to gain an additional 1 million residents in the region and must adapt to sustain the population. This region faces increased hazards including extreme heat periods and drought due to climate change. Clark County addresses the need to reduce greenhouse emissions (GHGs) and prepare for the impacts of climate change through this plan. Henderson encountered one of the hottest summers with record temperatures reaching 120 degrees F and the most consecutive days with temperatures over 112 F. Some regional projections indicate that the number of days over 115 F in Clark County could increase by 10 times by the end of the century because of GHG emissions that have been released into the atmosphere over multiple decades. The region will continue to experience warming for years to come even if no more emissions are ever released into the atmosphere. Lake Mead, which is part of the Colorado River Basin and fed by the Colorado River, provides drinking water to more than 2.3 million residents and receives much of its water from snowmelt from the Rocky Mountains of Colorado and Wyoming. Climate change is projected to continue reducing snowpack, runoff, and rainfall in this region, which could lead to more extreme, long-term droughts.

column23: Hamilton's Climate Action Strategy is Hamilton's most recent and ambitious climate plan to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and become a national leader in climate adaptation. Even if worldwide GHG emissions were reduced to zero today, temperatures and extreme weather events would increase, leading to more impacts on cities and communities locally and globally. Observed changes in Hamilton since the 1970s show that the average mean temperature has increased by 0.9°C, we are seeing warmer seasonal temperatures, and annual precipitation has increased by 26mm (a 3% increase in annual average precipitation). In recent years, we have already seen extreme weather events, flooding, increase daytime and nighttime temperatures, ice storms, and extreme temperature ranges. As these observed trends continue so does the frequency and possibility of increasingly extreme events.

column23: London's Climate Emergency Action Plan is a commitment to collectively achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. However, it is important that short-term and medium-term milestone targets be set to ensure that emission reduction activities are accelerated in the near term and progress is being tracked towards the 2050 target. The following community milestone targets for 2030, 2035, and 2040 will be used based on a 2005 baseline (same baseline as used by senior levels of government, and year when per-person emissions were near their peak) :•55 per cent reduction in total annual city-wide emissions by 2030 (about 1.75 million tonnes per year), consistent with the 1.5°C science-based target established by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change's Race to Zero campaign;•65 per cent by 2035 (about 1.35 million tonnes per year); and•75 per cent by 2040 (about 1 million tonnes per year).The City of London has partnered with the Canadian office of the International Council for Local Environmental Initiatives (ICLEI) to update the previous climate risk assessment, confirm previous climate assumptions and assessments, and expand the focus to the entire London community. ICLEI, a non-profit organization that supports local governments for sustainability, and London along with 21 other Ontario municipalities, are actively participating in the Advancing Adaptation Program. ICLEI Canada has decades of experience assisting municipalities in completing Adaptation Strategies using industry-standard adaptation processes (e.g., Building Adaptive and Resilient Communities, or BARC, tool). Preliminary targets have been prepared to suggest that:•By 2030, address 50 per cent of the areas where London is most vulnerable as identified by the Adaptation Plan and provide clear direction to address the remaining 50 per cent.•By 2050, address 90 per cent of the areas where London is most vulnerable as identified by the Adaptation Plan and provide clear direction and timetable to address the remaining 10 per cent.\nClimate scenarios were evaluated to be used in the early stages of plan development and documented in a background report titled \'Impacts of Climate Change in London\' which was released in 2021 to aid in consultation with the public on CEAP goals and actions. Three climate futures were examined (RCP 2.6, 4.6 and 8.5) to determine likely conditions that could be planned for, which were later reflected in proposed actions for the plan.

column30: The CEAP is a city-wide plan, intended to cover all sectors of society and infrastructure in London. Although new funding to implement the CEAP was not provided along with its unanimous Council approval in 2022, the most recent multi-year budget process included funding for three key elements of the plan regarding mitigation (a home energy retrofit program, a transportation demand management program targeting the reduction of commuter emissions, and the establishment and initial seed funding for a climate change reserve fund to address premiums required for infrastructure projects to align more closely with climate change objectives). City staff report to Council and the public on the progress of actions by the City and others twice per year and are accumulating a list of indicators and metrics across the 10 areas of focus to attempt to measure progress broadly. Continued engagement activities with the public, institutions and the business community are being undertaken to harness momentum achieved when climate actions are taken and to attempt to drive the CEAP further into the community. Partnerships with non-profit organizations and environmental NGOs in London are being maintained and, in some cases, advanced to further the work of the CEAP and enable and encourage action by all Londoners.

Este plano tem em consideração as mesmas premissas que o PAESC, designadamente estando alinhado com os cenário que preveem um aumento de 1,5ºC. 
As projeções climáticas para o futuro, indicam um aumento de 1.5ºC (conforme Acordo de Paris), indicam que as ameaças e oportunidades resultantes das alterações climáticas, quer a nível global quer local, terão implicações no quotidiano das populações e na atuação dos agentes públicos e privados do município de Matosinhos. Assim, tornou-se essencial, por um lado, identificar as medidas que permitem minimizar a exposição às ameaças climáticas, e por outro, aproveitar as oportunidades de introdução de novos modelos de atuação melhor adaptados ao novo contexto. A consequência destes impactos negativos e das observações dos eventos climáticos extremos, levaram à consideração de um plano de adaptação que visa ir de encontro, não só à previsão do aumento de 1.5ºC mas também ao aumento da resiliência do território de Matosinhos.
Na vertente de adaptação este plano mostra-se mais ambicioso que os objetivos definidos no quadro do Acordo de Paris, objetivando o alcance da neutralidade carbónica até 2030 (e não 2050 como identificado no Acordo). De qualquer forma o documento apresenta diferentes cenários evolutivos: 
(1) Cenário Business As Usual - BAU - Este cenário de quase estagnação na redução de emissões de GEE permite antever que o objetivo da neutralidade carbónica não é possível sem a proatividade dos atores do território e do desenho e implementação de políticas nacionais e setoriais céleres que impulsione o investimento e o desenvolvimento tecnológico e social necessários.
(2) Cenário em conformidade com a Lei de Bases do Clima (LBC) - o qual prevê redução das emissões municipais em cerca de 60% em 2030, 75% em 2040 e 88% em 2050. Neste cenário o esforço e compromisso dos atores locais teria de ser mobilizado de igual forma, embora num maior período temporal. 
(3) Cenário Matosinhos Neutralidade Carbónica 2030 - o qual objetiva a antecipação da neutralidade carbónica para 2030 através da mobilizado o esforço dos agentes do território e o seu compromisso, permitindo uma redução de 85% das emissões em 2030 face ao ano base de 2009.

column30: O Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Matosinhos surge como instrumento de política local para a mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas, combate à pobreza energética e promoção da qualidade de vida. Este plano antecipa as metas nacionais, definindo o objetivo ambicioso de alcançar a neutralidade carbónica em 2030, com uma redução de 85% das emissões de carbono face a 2009 (quando a meta nacional está prevista apenas para 2045). Integra ainda a visão do município para 2030, articulando estratégias de mitigação baseadas no PAESC, medidas de adaptação alinhadas com a ENAAC 2020 e ações específicas para uma transição justa que não deixe nenhum cidadão para trás.\nNa vertente de adaptação, o plano estrutura-se em torno de 64 medidas a implementar pelo Município e entidades parceiras, visando a operacionalização prática da EMAAC local. Já no combate à pobreza energética, aposta-se em ações que reforcem a coesão social, conheçam melhor a realidade municipal e promovam soluções equitativas. O acompanhamento da evolução rumo à neutralidade é feito através da monitorização das matrizes energéticas e de emissões, destacando-se que, entre 2009 e 2023, Matosinhos já conseguiu reduzir em 58,3% as suas emissões de CO2eq, passando de 2 867,9 para 1 197,1 ktCO2eq.

O Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e Clima (PAESC) aprovado em 2021, contempla a estratégia municipal em matéria de mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas no horizonte 2030. O PAESC-Matosinhos tinha como objetivo primordial a adoção de estratégias, por parte do município, que permitam a mitigação das alterações climáticas e a adaptação àquelas que são inevitáveis e previstas a curto prazo e longo prazo.
A elaboração do PAESC-Matosinhos, no que respeita à vertente da mitigação, considerou o diagnóstico da utilização de energia para o ano base de 2009 e um exercício de cenarização da evolução do sistema energético de Matosinhos a 2030. Deste modo, e para a obtenção do objetivo de redução de emissões assumido pelo Município de Matosinhos, foi necessária a definição de medidas nos diferentes setores de atividade, com especial foco nos setores de maior influência pelas Autoridades Locais, nomeadamente Edifícios, Transportes e Iluminação Pública. Este plano define as principais ações conducentes a uma redução de 40% das emissões de GEE em 2030, face ao ano base de 2009, apresentando um total de 22 medidas de mitigação. 
A metodologia adotada para elaboração da vertente da adaptação seguiu a base metodológica utilizada no âmbito do projeto ClimAdaPT.Local para a elaboração de Estratégias Municipais de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC), referenciada como ADAM e que foi, também, a abordagem seguida pela Câmara Municipal de Matosinhos na preparação da EMAAC-Matosinhos. 
As opções de adaptação tiveram em consideração os setores da agricultura; biodiversidade; economia; energia; florestas; saúde humana; segurança de pessoas e bens; transportes e comunicações; e, zonas costeiras e mar. Para além destas, também foram consideradas as dimensões de ordenamento do território e gestão dos recursos hídricos, dado o papel que estas políticas locais podem desempenhar na concretização das opções de adaptação.
A estratégia de adaptação do PAESC-Matosinhos consubstancia-se num conjunto de 27 opções de adaptação e 64 medidas de adaptação.

column23: As projeções climáticas apresentadas na Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas de Évora foram elaboradas com base em dois modelos regionalizados para a Europa pelo projeto CORDEX4 a partir de dois modelos globais:•Modelo 1: SMHI-RCA4 (regional), a partir do MOHC-HadGEM2 (global);•Modelo 2: KNMI-RACMO22E (regional), a partir do ICHEC-EC-EARTH (global).A elaboração de projeções climáticas pressupõe a utilização de cenários de emissões de GEE como dados de entrada (inputs) nos modelos climáticos, designados por Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) (IPCC, 2013). Estes cenários representam possíveis evoluções socioeconómicas e respetivas emissões de GEE.A partir de uma concentração atual de CO2 que ronda as 400 ppm (partes por milhão) dois RCPs foram utilizados nesta estratégia:•RCP4.5 - uma trajetória de aumento da concentração de CO2 atmosférico até 520 ppm em 2070, aumentando de forma mais lenta até ao final do século;•RCP8.5 - uma trajetória de crescimento semelhante ao RCP4.5 até meio do século, seguida de um aumento rápido e acentuado, atingindo uma concentração de CO2 de 950 ppm no final do século.Os dados simulados a partir dos modelos climáticos são geralmente representados recorrendo a grelhas com uma resolução espacial associada à capacidade de cada modelo em representar adequadamente os variados fenómenos atmosféricos e as massas terrestres e oceânicas.No caso dos modelos utilizados nesta estratégia esta representação foi de aproximadamente 11km (0.11°). Foi selecionado um ponto da grelha dentro do município de Évora para o qual foram obtidos os valores diários das seguintes variáveis climáticas:•Temperatura (máxima, média e mínima);•Precipitação (acumulada);•Velocidade do vento (máxima).De forma a apoiar o desenvolvimento da EMAAC de Évora, as projeções destas três variáveis foram analisadas, até ao final do século, para os seus valores médios anuais e anomalias (potenciais alterações), relativamente ao clima atual.De forma a identificar as potenciais alterações (anomalias) projetadas entre o clima atual e futuro, todos os cálculos foram simulados para três períodos de trinta anos (normais climáticas):•1976-2005 (clima atual);•2041-2070 (médio-prazo);•2071-2100 (longo-prazo).

column30: Elaborada no âmbito do programa ClimAdaPT.Local, a Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas de Évora foca-se na identificação de opções e ações de adaptação que visam promover a minimização dos efeitos das alterações climáticas. A partir da identificação e priorização das atuais vulnerabilidades e riscos climáticos e da sua projeção até ao final do século, o município de Évora procura promover um conjunto integrado de opções de adaptação para responder não apenas ao clima futuro e às consequências desse novo cenário, mas igualmente aos diferentes impactos climáticos já observados. https://www.cm-evora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/EMAAC_Evora_2017.pdf O município de Évora também dispõem de um Plano Intermunicipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (2017) que visa dar a conhecer melhor o fenómeno das alterações climáticas ao nível local e sub-regional e, simultaneamente, identificar as ações necessárias para a adaptação das populações, entidades e serviços públicos aos cenários climáticos. Tem igualmente como objetivo promover a integração da adaptação às alterações climáticas no planeamento municipal e intermunicipal e, dessa forma, criar uma cultura de adaptação transversal aos vários setores e atores sub-regionais, reforçando a resiliência territorial. Atualmente está em elaboração o Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas que pretende elevar a Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas a Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, nomeadamente aprofundando o conhecimento técnico e científico sobre o clima local atual e futuro, sobre a incidência espacial e setorial das vulnerabilidades climáticas específicas do concelho, desenhando um plano de ação municipal facilmente operacionalizável na próxima década, contando novamente com o envolvimento da comunidade local e incluindo a comunidade educativa. Atualmente está em elaboração o Plano de Ação Para a Sustentabilidade Urbana Évora 2030, enquadrado na iniciativa europeia Acordo Cidade Verde. Este plano pretende dar continuidade à estratégia do município ao nível da sustentabilidade ambiental, em concreto nos domínios do ar, água, natureza e biodiversidade, economia circular e resíduos, e ruído. Para tal, será estabelecido um programa de ações que integram a componente de adaptação e mitigação, incluindo eficiência energética.

O Plano Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas de Évora (PMAAC) foi foi esenvolvido no âmbito do projeto ADAPTA.local.CIMAC - Planeamento da Adaptação Climática Municipal do Alentejo Central, coordenado pela Comunidade Intermunicipal do Alentejo Central (CIMAC) e elaborado pela Câmara Municipal de Évora com o suporte técnico-científico do CEDRU - Centro de Estudos e Desenvolvimento Regional e Urbano, Lda., visa reduzir as vulnerabilidades territoriais do Município às Alterações Climáticas, criando as condições necessárias para a adaptação do território e da sua população.

Tratando-se da evolução natural do trabalho desenvolvido pelo Município aquando da elaboração da sua Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC), em 2016, o PMAAC de Évora, com um carácter fortemente operacional, permitiu consolidar o conhecimento sobre o clima local, atual e futuro, sobre a incidência espacial e setorial das vulnerabilidades climáticas específicas do concelho e desenhar um Plano de Ações de Adaptação para a próxima década. 

O PMAAC de Évora constitui o mais recente instrumento ao serviço das políticas de urbanismo, intervenção social, proteção civil, manutenção de infraestruturas e desenvolvimento socioeconómico, entre outros domínios, configurando-se como um dos contributos mais relevantes do Município de Évora para as questões globais relacionadas com as Alterações Climáticas, mas sobretudo, para garantir e melhorar a resiliência e qualidade de vida deste território e das populações.

column30: The City established Net Zero goals in 2021, and in 2023, consultants developed a net zero plan to help the City achieve its commitment of setting a science-based GHG reduction target in 2024 by 2030, followed by an additional interim 2040 target, and culminating in net zero GHG emissions by 2050. The Net Zero Plan listed 55 actions derived from 8 community-focused and 7 municipal-focused strategies. Each action was assigned an implementation priority level of 1, 2, or 3 based on a high-level qualitative analysis of factors including: timeframe, GHG impact, initial cost to the City, life-cycle cost, return on investment (ROI), level of effort (LOE), social equity impacts for the community, alignment with existing strategic priorities, co-benefits, and qualitative estimate for additional costs borne by the community (p.4 NZ plan). A principal objective of the Net Zero Plan is to ensure full engagement and input from stakeholders. “Stakeholder engagement was an invaluable component in the development of this Plan, incorporating input from nine internal City department meetings, two presentations to the Sustainability Advisory Board, two public virtual informational meetings, and two community workshops to ensure broad input and buy-in” (p.3 Net Zero Plan). The two Community Workshops served as touchpoints for deeper engagement with the community, where consultants gained an understanding of community priorities, concerns, and ideas for the Net Zero Plan. The plan's metrics will be updated in February 2027, 2 years from when it was published.

column30: The Sustainability Action Plan (SAP) outlines the City's specific “green” goals, strategies, and performance indicators, demonstrating how sustainability will be integrated into all levels of City decision-making and establishing a system of accountability. The initial SAP, published in 2010, was a collaborative effort involving the Sustainability Advisory Board, City staff, expert groups, and concerned residents. For the first time, individual programs and projects were evaluated collectively to assess their contributions to city-wide sustainability. This process involved identifying what was working, what was missing, and how each effort impacted others. The outcome was a coordinated statement introducing five priorities and 17 goals organized into eight areas: Leadership, Air Quality, Energy, Water, Built and Natural Environment, Transportation, Waste, and Progress Tracking. Each section of the SAP identifies new initiatives to encourage and assist residents, businesses, developers, and others in practicing sustainability. Certain metrics, such as the annual greenhouse gas inventory, are reported annually using the City's performance tracking tool, ClearPoint.

Adoption & Co‑Creation:

In March 2022, the Tempe City Council unanimously approved the CAP Update, marking the shift to a deeply co‑created plan with Tempe residents and local businesses. Numerous listening sessions, focus groups, and public meetings during 2021 informed four co‑created agendas: Youth, Business, Climate Justice, and Neighborhoods.

The city worked closely with organizations including Unlimited Potential, Tempe Chamber of Commerce, and Local First Arizona to ensure inclusive agenda development 

Quantifiable Impact & Progress: 

As of 2020, Tempe achieved a 2.5% reduction in municipal operations GHG emissions, and a 16% reduction in citywide community emissions compared to 2015 levels.

Key Action Areas:

1. Green Building Codes and Standards - Adoption of sustainable construction and landscape design standards to promote shade, stormwater capture, and heat island reduction in new developments 

2. Transportation Demand Management & Mobility Hubs - Development of programs, incentives, and infrastructure that facilitate low-carbon transport choices—reducing reliance on single-occupancy vehicles by boosting transit access and micro-mobility options 

3. Resilience and Energy Hubs - Deploying solar and battery storage projects at key facilities that serve as community refuges during heat emergencies and power disruptions, supporting cleaner energy access and resilience

Equity & Justice Integration: 

The Climate Justice Agenda was developed in partnership with Unlimited Potential and aimed at amplifying voices from historically marginalized neighborhoods, centering actions like transportation equity, green space access, and energy affordability. 

This agenda explicitly ties climate action planning to social justice, prioritizing frontline communities in investment and capacity-building efforts.


Tempe's CAP Update is designed to be the operational roadmap to implement sustainable systems over time, supported by dedicated staff roles, programmatic investments, and ongoing community feedback loops

Climate-related scenarios have significantly informed Fayetteville's Climate Action Plan (CAP) by incorporating both mitigation and adaptation strategies to address extreme weather and climate change impacts. Here's how specific scenarios have influenced the plan:

- **Rising Temperatures**: Fayetteville acknowledges that higher global and local temperatures will lead to increased energy demands for cooling and a higher risk of heat-related illnesses. This scenario has led the city to adopt energy efficiency measures and emphasize clean energy transitions to reduce overall energy consumption .

- **Increased Flooding and Droughts**: Fayetteville is preparing for more frequent and severe floods, along with longer drought periods. To address this, the CAP includes measures to improve stormwater management and enhance water conservation strategies, such as upgrading infrastructure and promoting water-saving behaviors 【19:18†source】.

- **Vulnerable Populations**: The CAP highlights that low-income and disadvantaged communities are disproportionately affected by climate-related events. This recognition has led to the development of climate equity goals, including targeted infrastructure upgrades, increased tree planting in heat-prone areas, and improved accessibility to cooling centers during extreme heat events 【19:18†source】.

- **Biodiversity and Ecosystem Disruption**: Changes in climate, such as extreme heat and invasive species, are predicted to harm biodiversity and forest health. Fayetteville's response includes preserving and restoring natural ecosystems that provide vital services, such as carbon sequestration and stormwater filtration 【19:18†source】. 

These scenarios have guided Fayetteville's dual approach to mitigate emissions and adapt to unavoidable climate impacts through nature-based solutions and improved resilience planning.

Building off Fayetteville's 2018 Energy Action Plan, this Climate Action Plan (CAP)
sets ambitious mitigation targets, including an overarching goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.
Setting a net-zero goal aligns Fayetteville with international targets that aim to balance greenhouse gas (GHG) production with atmospheric removals. To be on track to be net zero by 2050, the community will need to decrease our cumulative GHG emissions by 37 percent by 2030.
In addition to ambitious mitigation targets, the CAP also introduces nature-based climate adaptation
goals that recognize climate change is already having a significant impact on our daily lives. This
CAP is the city's framework and policy commitment to mitigate GHG emissions and to use naturebased solutions to enhance ecosystem services and adaptive resilience

Goals, strategies, and actions are grounded through science-based targets designed to reach net-zero
carbon emissions by 2050. Science-based targets are a way for organizations to define emissions reduction
targets by focusing on the quantity of emissions that need to be reduced to meet the targets set out in the
Paris Climate Agreement, limiting global warming to 1.5 Celsius (C). Net-zero is a key part of the Paris
Climate Agreement, defined as a condition in which human-caused residual GHG emissions are balanced
by human-led removals over a specific period and within specified boundaries.1
This five-year plan update also broadens the scope of influence beyond carbon emissions through the
addition of a Nature-Based Solutions Chapter that addresses carbon sequestration and climate change
adaptation strategies to improve resilience to extreme weather. A focus on resilient natural ecosystems as
components of the city's gray and green infrastructure is a necessary addition considering the progression
of climate change. Climate models show an increasingly shorter opportunity to keep global surface
temperatures from rising 1.5 C. Meanwhile, extreme weather events are already affecting cities and
communities. Mitigating the drivers of climate change is still critical, but we must also begin adapting to
the impacts of climate change now.
Intentionally, this CAP aligns with other city master plans and is meant to complement and reinforce the
sustainability and resilience-oriented goals, strategies, and actions identified in the City Plan 2040, theFayetteville Mobility Plan, the Parks Master Plan, the Recycling and Trash Master Plan, the Urban Forestry
Plan.

This plan updates and expands upon Spokane's 2009 Sustainability Action Plan. It identifies specific strategies and actions that will help meet our 100% renewable energy goals as adopted by the City in 2018, and to meet regulation set by the State of Washington to address greenhouse gas emissions. While climate change is a global issue, it requires action at every level, including local action. We believe that Spokane has much to gain by embracing the opportunities presented by this challenge. With this in mind, we are taking an approach to sustainability planning that balances the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions with our commitment to create good jobs, a healthy environment and an equitable community. For example, in partnership with Avista Utilities, the Spokane Regional Transportation Council, and Urbanova, we have won a $2.5 million grant to install electric vehicle charging stations throughout Spokane County as part of a regionwide transportation electrification (TE) plan. The implementation of this regional TE plan will reduce emissions, cut transportation costs, create jobs, and bring more opportunities to historically underserved areas of our city. While this Sustainability and Climate Action Plan helps our community become environmentally responsible, it will also help us become more resilient by preparing our community for impacts caused by changing weather patterns. It will help us incentivize the development of a local clean energy economy and secure the economic benefits of becoming a resilient city. With smart mitigation efforts, we'll be able to protect the economic and social benefits of our local tourism industry, beloved public events like Bloomsday, regional farming, the Spokane River, and our aquifer. Climate-related scenarios were a core input into the development of Regina's Corporate Climate Adaptation Strategy (CCAS).

The City worked with the Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative (PARC) to prepare localized climate projections for Regina and surrounding areas. These projections were based on simulations from 11 Regional Climate Models (RCMs) at a 25 km resolution, using a high-emissions scenario to model potential future climate conditions.

Three global warming time horizons were considered:

1.5 °C (short-term, ~2035)

2 °C (medium-term, ~2048)

3 °C (long-term, ~2070)

The scenarios provided detailed projections of:

Higher average annual temperatures (+2.5 °C to +4.7 °C)

A threefold increase in hot days above 30 °C and ninefold increase in very hot days above 35 °C

A longer frost-free season (+54 days)

More intense and frequent precipitation events (up to 20% increase annually)

Increased drought risk and variability in seasonal precipitation

Reduced extreme cold days, with more unpredictable freeze-thaw cycles

The Corporate Climate Adaptation Strategy (CCAS) is Regina's first formal plan to address the risks and vulnerabilities of climate change on City services, assets, and operations. The Strategy sets out a vision for building resilience by improving the City's understanding of climate change, identifying key hazards, and prioritizing actions to reduce vulnerabilities.

The plan was developed through climate modeling provided by the Prairie Adaptation Research Collaborative (PARC), extensive staff and stakeholder engagement, and the integration of Indigenous knowledge and equity considerations. It includes a Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CRVA), which identified significant hazards such as extreme heat, flooding, drought, freeze-thaw cycles, wildfires and smoke, and wind. Risks were assessed across categories including infrastructure, water and environment, recreation and outdoor spaces, City operations, and community health and safety.

The CCAS lays out adaptation goals to:

1) Increase resiliency and reduce vulnerability to climate change.

2) Optimize financial and natural resources for present and future needs.

3) Bridge gaps across existing strategies and frameworks to align climate risk management.

4) Incorporate Indigenous perspectives into City services and operations.

Implementation is guided by principles of science- and evidence-based decision making, equity and inclusion, Indigenous worldviews, and practical, collaborative action.

It should be noted that while the Strategy outlines priority actions and implementation approaches, it does not specify a total cost for implementation. Instead, the Strategy emphasizes integrating adaptation into existing planning and budgeting processes, with the expectation that costs will be determined as specific actions are developed and advanced.

2019. The cross-sector group of over 65 members included clean energy experts, conservation activists, advocates for equity, neighborhood representatives, developers,
business leaders, utility representatives, and more. Council members and working groups (transportation, buildings/energy, waste, and equity) evaluated dozens of
strategies for their impact to climate, economy, and community. Strategies were ranked not only by emission reduction but also by impact on equity and other societal

the City's 2021 Energy & Sustainability Work Plan, including:
- Expand and improve bicycle and pedestrian facilities, connectivity, convenience, and/or safety to significantly increase trips taken by walking or biking
- Make public transit investments that significantly enhance coverage, service quality, frequency, and/or speed
- Significantly accelerate community adoption of electric vehicles
- Partner with major local commercial fleet operators to transition to electric vehicles
- Create voluntary large, commercial, and multi-family energy upgrade programs (eg. incentives, technical assistance) that achieve deep energy savings (~25%+) in ~20%+
of buildings
- Amplify and opportunistically expand voluntary home energy upgrade programs that will achieve deep energy savings (~25%+) in 20% of homes
- Develop or amplify opportunities to invest in renewables at scale, including community solar and in-valley investments
- Research and develop strategies to promote opportunistic electrification (eg. replacement of fossil fuel-fired furnaces with electric heat pump technologies) in existing
buildings over time
- Pursue food waste reduction and collection programs that capture ~80%+ of organic waste from all high-volume locations (eg. restaurants)
- Increase residential recycling through community engagement and education strategies
- Promote consumption-reduction approaches such as sharing and re-use through education campaigns

column23: Sunnyvale's 2024 Climate Action Playbook (CAP) is grounded in the same science that shapes California's statewide climate targets, which are themselves tied to the UNFCCC Paris Agreement's goal of keeping global temperature rise below 2°C. California's Senate Bill 32 requires a 40% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions below 1990 levels by 2030, and Assembly Bill 1279 mandates carbon neutrality by 2045 with at least an 85% reduction. Sunnyvale's CAP reflects this 2°C-aligned framework but applies it locally through a detailed game plan of strategies and plays designed to reduce emissions across all sectors. The CAP uses scenario analysis qualitatively by contrasting a business-as-usual pathway, in which emissions remain high due to continued fossil fuel use and waste disposal, with an intervention pathway, where coordinated actions achieve deep cuts. Plays in the CAP address renewable energy adoption, electrification of vehicles and buildings, zero waste goals, sustainable water use, and urban greening, each with defined targets for 2030 and 2045. Sunnyvale's 2024 Climate Action Playbook (CAP) is the City's comprehensive roadmap to achieve carbon neutrality by 2045. The CAP is structured as a “living document,” designed to be updated regularly as new data, technologies, and community needs emerge. It organizes actions into themed “plays” across energy, transportation, waste, water, and urban greening, with each play tied to measurable milestones in 2030 and 2045. The 2030 targets serve as near-term checkpoints to ensure the City is on track for its long-term carbon neutrality goal.

Equity and community priorities are built into the CAP. Sunnyvale's position as a dense urban community in a coastal region shaped the focus on strategies that address climate risks like heat and drought while also reducing local air pollution and transportation demand. Many plays emphasize co-benefits such as lowering household energy bills, improving air quality, health and livability, community savings, partnerships, and providing more accessible, sustainable mobility choices.

Actions within the CAP were prioritized based on their emissions reduction potential, alignment with state and regional mandates, cost-effectiveness, technical feasibility, and ability to deliver community co-benefits. Plays like expanding renewable electricity (Play 1.1), increasing zero-emission vehicles (Play 3.3), and achieving zero waste (Play 4.1) were identified as core drivers of emissions reduction. Others, such as water conservation and urban greening, strengthen resilience and sustainability over the long term.

The CAP functions both as a short-term action plan and as a long-term tracking framework. Its iterative design ensures Sunnyvale can adjust course as conditions change, with regular reviews and updates tied to local emissions inventories and state-level policy updates and reporting cycles.

column30: Palo Alto established its first Climate Protection Plan in 2007. In 2020, the City launched an update to the Sustainability and Climate Action Plan (S/CAP) to develop the strategies needed to meet our sustainability goals, including our goal of reducing GHG emissions 80 percent below 1990 levels by 2030 (the “80 x 30” goal) and most recent Carbon Neutral by 2030 goal. The S/CAP is a comprehensive document laying out the City's strategy to achieve these ambitious carbon reduction goals, while improving our natural environment, adapting to climate impacts, and increasing livability for Palo Alto residents. While reducing emissions is a priority for the City, Palo Alto believes in a comprehensive view of sustainability. The S/CAP addresses eight focus areas: Climate Action, Energy, Mobility, Electric Vehicles, Water, Climate Adaptation and Sea Level Rise, Natural Environment, and Zero Waste. Each focus area sets specific goals, lays out key actions to the City will take to achieve these goals, and establishes key performance indicators that will be monitored and reported on yearly to track the City's progress towards achieving our goals.
