column30: In 2019, the city adopted a Carbon Neutrality Resolution no later than 2045. As part of the Carbon Neutrality Resolution, the City developed a Post-Carbon Framework to the updated Climate Action Plan which was adopted by the City Council on October 10, 2023. The Post-Carbon Framework establishes the following guiding values that serve as the foundation of Climate Ready Fremont: • Equity & Access: Ensure that all people have the opportunity to benefit equally from climate solutions, while not taking on an unequal burden of climate impacts.• Efficiency & Innovation: Promote the efficient use of resources and the adoption of clean and climate-smart technologies and techniques.• Health & Wellness: Safeguard and enhance the ability of the community to live, work, play, connect, and thrive in a healthy social and physical environment.• Resiliency & Capacity-Building: Provide education and training on the opportunities offered by a more resilient future and encourage sustainable behaviors across all sectors of the community. In addition, the Post-Carbon Framework identifies seven key strategies that are incorporated throughout Climate Ready Fremont. The strategies are, Electrification & Fossil fuel Phase Out, Clean & Renewable Power, Climate adaptation & resilience, Resource Conservation & Elimination of Waste, Mobility & Connectivity, Carbon Sequestration, and Restorative Ecology & Green Infrastructure.

Climate related scenarios informed the consultation, the Plan directions, and the actions. In Yarra we have mapped the most significant climate impacts we faced and built around these. We have also mapped those in our community most impacted and needing of our support and built around these.

While future projections of global
climate change are alarming, we are
already witnessing the breakdown of
essential climatic functions, the
collapse of ecosystems, and
widespread human displacement and
migration due to sudden and ongoing
environmental stress. These impacts
are being acutely felt in low and
middle-income countries, who have
contributed least to the issue.

Locally, accelerating climate impacts
are placing immense pressure on the
environment, threatening the health
and wellbeing of our community, and
interrupting the provision of essential
goods and services. These climate
impacts and emerging public health
risks are anticipated to worsen without
significant investment in climate
mitigation and adaptation

Across Yarra, there is a spectrum of
socio-economic advantage and
disadvantage. While many Yarra
residents experience relatively high
socio-economic advantage, there is a
substantial portion of our community
who experience significant
disadvantage and face elevated risk
from climate impacts. In our extensive
consultations, we heard loud and clear
that a major focus of Council should be
on supporting those in the community
facing the greatest risks. While we all
face the same climate impacts, they
affect at-risk communities more
intensely and sooner than those whose
incomes, abilities, residences, or other
factors provide greater protection

1. 应对气候变化工作成效显著:“十三五”期间，青岛市深入贯彻落实习近平生态文明思想，取得了积极的温室气体减排成效。例如，2020年单位地区生产总值能源消耗和二氧化碳排放比2015年分别下降21.5%和27%。
2. 指导思想与总体目标:规划强调以习近平生态文明思想为指导，将应对气候变化作为推动高质量发展的倒逼机制和机遇，制定了到2025年的一系列具体目标。
3. 严格控制温室气体排放:规划提出了开展二氧化碳排放达峰行动的策略，包括制定碳达峰行动方案和差异化设定区域碳排放强度目标等。
4. 适应气候变化:规划提出了适应气候变化水平提升的措施，如加强气象灾害预测、预警组织指挥系统和法规保障体系的建设。
5. 科技创新:规划强调推进应对气候变化科技创新，包括推进科技平台建设、强化科技人才队伍建设、加快关键核心低碳技术研发等。
6. 试点示范:规划中提到深化国家低碳城市试点和争取适应气候变化城市试点，打造一批具有示范效应的绿色低碳城镇、园区、社区和企业。
7. 激励约束政策机制:规划提出了强化碳市场激励调节作用、落实国家金融税收政策、完善绿色产品支持机制等措施，以推动企业和公众参与低碳发展。
8. 治理体系和治理能力现代化:规划中强调加强应对气候变化标准体系建设、建立健全应对气候变化制度体系等。
9. 保障措施:规划中提出了加强组织领导、加强调度评估、严格监督考核、推动宣传教育等一系列保障措施。

column30:
《青岛市“十四五”应对气候变化规划》（以下简称《规划》），是青岛市贯彻落实国家积极应对气候变化战略和山东省有关安排部署的重要专项规划。
一、编制过程
以习近平生态文明思想为指导，落实生态环境部、山东省生态环境厅关于做好“十四五”生态环境领域有关规划编制工作的要求，青岛市生态环境局委托中国科学院青岛生物与能源过程研究所、青岛市环境工程评估中心联合承担《规划》编制任务。
《规划》编制全程深入贯彻落实《中共中央国务院关于完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念做好碳达峰碳中和工作的意见》《中共中央国务院关于深入打好污染防治攻坚战的意见》《国务院关于印发2030年前碳达峰行动方案的通知》《山东省“十四五”应对气候变化规划》等重要文件精神，依据党中央、国务院以及山东省发布的有关“十四五”规划的纲要性、指导性文件，有机衔接《青岛市国民经济和社会发展第十四个五年规划和2035年远景目标纲要》以及能源、产业、城乡建设、交通运输、自然资源、生态环境等领域的专项规划，形成贴合青岛实际的建议文本。在征求各区（市）人民政府、市发展改革委等20余市直部门以及多位国内应对气候变化领域专家的意见建议之后，又经过数轮修改，以市生态环境委员会办公室的名义印发。
二、主要内容
《规划》共包括9章，分为三大部分。
（一）指导思想、基本原则和主要目标
指导思想：全面贯彻落实习近平生态文明思想和习近平总书记对山东、对青岛工作的重要指示要求，立足新发展阶段，完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念，主动服务和融入新发展格局，坚持系统观念，将应对气候变化作为推动实现高质量发展的倒逼机制、发展机遇和生态环境保护的治本之策，以经济社会发展全面绿色转型为引领，以能源、工业、建筑、交通等重要领域绿色低碳发展为关键，以严格控制温室气体排放、构建气候友好型社会为重点，加快形成节约资源和保护环境的产业结构、生产方式、生活方式、空间格局，支撑青岛坚定不移走生态优先、绿色低碳的高质量发展道路。
基本原则：做好七个坚持，即：坚持聚焦高质量发展、坚持全域统筹重点突破、坚持放眼未来立足当下、坚持严控排放主动适应、坚持双轮驱动两手发力、坚持风险管控安全降碳、坚持减污降碳协同增效。
主要目标：到2025年，应对气候变化工作取得积极成效，碳达峰基础进一步夯实。二氧化碳排放强度持续下降，温室气体排放总量得到有效控制，适应气候变化能力和水平进一步提升，气候变化治理能力显著增强，初步形成与经济社会发展相协调、与生态文明建设相适应、与生态环境保护相融合的应对气候变化工作新局面。《规划》确定了14项指标，其中约束性指标3项，预期性指标11项。
（二）重点任务
《规划》明确了“十四五”时期我市应对气候变化的6项重点任务。一是开展二氧化碳排放达峰行动，深入推进产业绿色低碳发展，推动能源、工业、城乡建设、交通等领域绿色低碳转型，加强非二氧化碳温室气体排放控制，着力提升自然生态系统碳汇能力。二是积极提升适应气候变化能力，提高自然生态领域和经济社会领域气候韧性，保障重要生态安全地区生态功能，加强气候变化风险及极端气候事件预测预报，做好防灾减灾工作。三是推进应对气候变化科技创新，深入开展应对气候变化基础研究，积极争创国家级、省级低碳技术创新平台，强化应对气候变化科技人才队伍建设，加强关键核心绿色低碳技术研发和集成推广应用。四是深化国家低碳城市试点，全面推动开展气候投融资试点、适应气候变化试点建设、近零碳试点示范以及绿色城市建设发展试点等试点示范建设。五是充分发挥碳市场激励调节作用，积极落实国家有关金融、税收政策，优化促进绿色低碳发展的价格政策，完善绿色低碳产品支持政策。六是加强气候治理体系和治理能力建设，健全完善应对气候变化的政策、标准和制度体系，坚持温室气体编制常态化，强化协同增效，全面提升气候治理效能。
（三）保障措施
从加强组织领导、加大调度评估、严格监督考核、推动宣传教育等4个方面明确了具体要求，按照中央和山东省有关要求，将碳排放强度控制指标纳入全市高质量发展综合绩效考核，不断完善考核机制，强化督导落实，切实保障规划顺利实施见效。
四、 创新举措
《规划》结合青岛市实际，主要提出了以下8个方面的创新性举措：包括：差异化设置了区（市）碳排放强度目标。推动重点行业碳排放与大气污染物协同控制，探索开展钢铁、化工等重点行业和轮胎制造等地方特色行业的碳排放环境影响评价试点工作；充分发挥青岛海洋领域优势，推动海洋碳汇建设先行先试；探索开展钢铁、轮胎、家电和食品等重要外贸产品碳标签制度，建立产品全生命周期碳足迹追踪体系；持续推进温室气体排放清单编制常态化，强化多源大数据应用，提高碳排放核算时效性；推进低碳城市试点、应对气候变化投融资试点和绿色城市建设发展试点等国家试点任务融合发展；依托泛能源大数据科学装置，加强碳排放与能源、环境等多维数据的关联分析和融合应用，支撑智慧控排决策；强化低碳宣传教育，加快实施碳普惠制度，构筑全民共建共治共享的气候治理新格局。

1.	能源结构调整：方案强调实施能源绿色低碳转型工程，包括发展新能源、推动可再生能源规模化发展、培育氢能产业等。这些措施旨在减少对化石燃料的依赖，降低温室气体排放，应对气候变化。
2.	节能降碳：通过实施节能降碳增效工程，提高能源使用效率，减少能源消耗和碳排放，以应对能源消耗导致的气候变化问题。
3.	工业领域碳达峰：推动工业领域绿色低碳发展，加快重点领域节能降碳步伐，提升工业园区绿色化水平，这些都是为了应对工业生产过程中的碳排放问题。
4.	城乡建设绿色低碳：推进城乡建设绿色低碳转型，提升建筑能效水平，优化建筑用能结构，这些都是为了减少建筑领域的能源消耗和碳排放，应对城市化进程中的气候变化挑战。
5.	交通运输低碳转型：加快绿色交通基础设施建设，推动运输工具装备低碳转型，构建绿色高效交通运输体系，这些都是为了减少交通领域的碳排放，应对交通发展对气候的影响。
6.	循环经济：推动园区循环化发展和废物综合利用，加强大宗固体废弃物综合利用，这些都是为了提高资源利用效率，减少废物产生和碳排放。
7.	绿色低碳科技创新：完善绿色低碳科技创新机制，加强绿色低碳技术研发应用，这些都是为了通过科技创新来应对气候变化。
8.	碳汇能力提升：巩固生态系统碳汇作用，提升生态系统碳汇能力，这些都是为了增强自然生态系统的碳吸收能力，对抗气候变化。
9.	绿色低碳全民行动：提高全民节能低碳意识，引导企业履行社会责任，这些都是为了动员全社会参与碳减排，共同应对气候变化。
10.	绿色低碳国际合作：开展国际交流合作，积极参与国际合作活动，这些都是为了在全球范围内共同应对气候变化。

一、政策背景
实现碳达峰、碳中和，是以习近平同志为核心的党中央统筹国内国际两个大局作出的重大战略决策，是立足新发展阶段，完整、准确、全面贯彻新发展理念，服务和融入新发展格局，推动高质量发展的内在要求。2021年9月22日，中共中央、国务院出台《关于完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念做好碳达峰碳中和工作的意见》，把碳达峰、碳中和纳入经济社会发展全局，要求加快形成节约资源和保护环境的产业结构、生产方式、生活方式、空间格局，坚定不移走生态优先、绿色低碳的高质量发展道路，确保如期实现碳达峰、碳中和。2021年10月22日，国务院印发《2030年前碳达峰行动方案》，进一步明确了碳达峰的时间表、路线图和施工图。
2022年12月17日，中共山东省委、山东省人民政府印发《贯彻落实〈中共中央、国务院关于完整准确全面贯彻新发展理念做好碳达峰碳中和工作的意见〉的若干措施》《关于完成准确全面贯彻新发展理念 做好碳达峰碳中和工作的意见》（鲁发〔2022〕18号），提出12方面31项重点任务。2022年12月19日，山东省人民政府印发《山东省碳达峰实施方案》（鲁政字〔2022〕242号），明确了山东省双碳工作的主要目标和重点举措。

青岛市委、市政府高度重视碳达峰、碳中和工作，成立了市委书记、市长担任双组长的领导小组，多次召开专题会议，深入学习贯彻习近平总书记关于碳达峰、碳中和的重要讲话精神，努力践行习近平生态文明思想，全面研究部署碳达峰、碳中和相关工作，大力推动经济社会发展全面绿色转型，碳达峰碳中和工作取得良好开局。“十三五”期间，青岛市能耗强度下降21.5%，处于国内同类城市先进水平，碳达峰碳中和工作基础良好。
根据党中央、国务院关于碳达峰碳中和重大战略决策部署，和山东省委、省政府工作要求，结合青岛市实际，市发展改革委在充分调研、征求意见的基础上，研究制定《青岛市碳达峰工作方案》（以下简称《工作方案》），报市委、市政府印发实施。《工作方案》是青岛市碳达峰“1+N”政策体系中的“1”，将作为青岛市高质量实现碳达峰碳中和的顶层设计，对全市系统全面推进碳达峰工作具有重要意义。
二、主要内容
《工作方案》明确了青岛市碳达峰工作主要目标、重点任务和政策措施保障。
主要目标：聚焦“十四五”和“十五五”两个经济社会全面绿色转型的关键期，提出了提高非化石能源消费比重、提升能源利用效率、降低二氧化碳排放水平等方面主要目标。
“十四五”期间，全市产业结构和能源结构优化调整取得明显进展，绿色低碳循环发展的经济体系初步形成。到2025年，非化石能源消费比重提升到15%左右，单位地区生产总值能源消耗比2020年下降12%左右，单位地区生产总值二氧化碳排放确保完成省下达任务，为全市如期实现碳达峰奠定坚实基础。
“十五五”期间，全市产业结构和能源结构调整取得重大进展，经济社会绿色低碳高质量发展取得显著成效。到2030年，非化石能源消费比重达到23%左右，单位地区生产总值二氧化碳排放比2005年下降70%以上，确保如期实现2030年前碳达峰目标。
重点任务：将碳达峰碳中和纳入经济社会发展全局，协同推进降碳、减污、扩绿、增长，推动形成绿色低碳的生产方式和生活方式，重点实施“碳达峰十大工程”。
一是实施能源绿色低碳转型工程，大力发展新能源，合理控制化石能源消费，加快建设新型电力系统，构建清洁低碳安全高效的能源体系。二是实施节能降碳增效工程，全面提升节能管理能力，推动重点领域节能降碳，推进重点用能设备节能增效，加强新型基础设施节能降碳。三是实施工业领域碳达峰工程，推动工业领域绿色低碳发展和钢铁、石化化工、建材等主要行业碳达峰，坚决遏制高耗能、高排放、低水平项目盲目发展。四是实施城乡建设绿色低碳工程，推进城乡建设绿色低碳转型，加快提升建筑能效水平，大力优化建筑用能结构，推进农村用能结构低碳转型，持续推进农村清洁取暖。五是实施交通运输低碳转型工程，加快绿色交通基础设施建设，推动运输工具装备低碳转型，大力推广新能源船舶及岸电设施，构建绿色高效交通运输体系和绿色出行体系。六是实施循环经济助力降碳工程，推动园区循环化发展，加强大宗固体废弃物综合利用，健全再生资源循环利用体系，推进生活垃圾减量化资源化。七是实施绿色低碳科技创新工程，完善绿色低碳科技创新机制，加强创新能力建设和人才培养，加强绿色低碳技术研发应用，构建海洋低碳科技创新体系。八是实施碳汇能力巩固提升工程，巩固生态系统碳汇作用，提升生态系统碳汇能力，大力发展海洋生态系统碳汇，推进农业农村减排固碳，加强生态系统碳汇基础支撑。九是实施绿色低碳全民工程，提升全民节能降碳意识，推广节能低碳生活方式，引导企业履行社会责任，强化领导干部培训。十是实施绿色低碳国际合作工程，加快发展绿色贸易，加强节能环保产品和服务进出口，开展国际交流合作。
政策措施保障：一是健全统计监测。建立覆盖重点领域的碳排放统计监测体系，加强数据监督管理。二是完善投资和价格政策措施。用好“两高”行业重点企业碳账户，鼓励社会资本设立绿色低碳产业投资基金。三是强化财税金融支持。持续加大对绿色低碳领域重点项目和基础研究的支持力度，支持金融机构运用政策工具加大绿色贷款投放。四是建立市场化机制。完善用能权交易制度，积极推行合同能源管理，探索推进生态产品价值实现和碳汇交易。

column30: The 'Rajkot Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan- Towards a Net-zero future by 2070 (Net-zero CRCAP)' has been prepared using ICLEI's Net-zero ClimateResilientCities Action Planning methodology. This methodology provides a step-by-step guidance, supported by a range of tools, for developing a Net-zero CRCAP that addresses both climate change adaptation and mitigation. This methodology follows a systematic 9-step process organized into three phases: Analyse, Act, and Accelerate Rajkot Municipal Corporation committed to climate action by forming a City Climate Core Team to lead the charge. A Stakeholder Committee was constituted to seek inputs from and involve the community, including the private sector, in the implementation of the action plan. The city's socio-environmental landscape and key challenges were identified, climate risks and vulnerability assessed, and emissions baselines established. Goals, strategies, and actions that address identified climate vulnerabilities and thematic actions to reduce GHG emissions across sectors, were defined. To guide emissions reduction strategies across three different planning horizons, i.e., 2030, 2050 and 2070, the CRCAP scales the defined goals, strategies, and actions across two emissions reduction scenarios.

1. Berdasarkan Dokumen RAD-GRK Kota Medan
Hasil analisa:
a. Proyeksi kenaikan timbulan sampah dari 632 ribu ton (2024) → 700 ribu ton (2030); keputusan dalam rencana pembangunan Waste-to-Energy TPA Terjun dan program pengurangan sampah 30% di sumber.
b. Emisi transportasi meningkat 5-8% per tahun jika tidak ada intervensi; keputusan dalam rencana pembangunan program bus listrik dan transportasi massal rendah emisi dengan target 20% angkutan umum listrik di 2025.
c. Kenaikan suhu 0,4°C - 1,6°C dalam 10 tahun terakhir; keputusan dalam rencana pembangunan target peningkatan RTH hingga 20% pada 2029 untuk mengurangi efek urban heat island.

- Skenario iklim berbasis BAU dan proyeksi IPCC menjadi pondasi utama RAD-GRK Kota Medan.
- Skenario ini menentukan:
* Baseline emisi sebagai pembanding target.
* Sektor prioritas yang perlu intervensi segera.
* Target penurunan tahunan selaras dengan NDC nasional.
* Program spesifik seperti waste-to-energy, bus listrik, dan rehabilitasi mangrove.
- Dengan skenario ini, Kota Medan memiliki peta jalan yang jelas menuju penurunan emisi 29% pada 2030.

2. Berdasarkan Dokumen KLHS RPJMD Kota Medan Tahun 2025-2029
a. Mitigasi (Penurunan Emisi GRK)
- Prioritas program diarahkan pada sektor penyumbang emisi tertinggi:
* Waste-to-Energy di TPA Terjun : mengurangi emisi metana ±392.000 ton CO₂e/tahun.
* Bus listrik dan transportasi massal rendah emisi : sektor transportasi.
b. Adaptasi dan Ketahanan
Rencana adaptasi yang dipengaruhi skenario:
- Kenaikan muka laut 10-15 cm; banjir rob lebih sering program dalam RPJMD yaitu pembangunan tanggul, polder, dan pompa di Medan Utara.
- Hilangnya hutan mangrove; abrasi meningkat program dalam RPJMD yaitu rehabilitasi 3.203 Ha mangrove dan perlindungan sempadan pantai.
- Peningkatan suhu; urban heat island program dalam RPJMD yaitu penambahan RTH 20% di 2029, pembangunan taman kota dan penghijauan jalan.
- Curah hujan ekstrem meningkat; banjir kota	program dalam RPJMD yaitu normalisasi drainase dan sistem pengelolaan air perkotaan.
c. Tata Guna Lahan & Infrastruktur
Skenario iklim: 
- Zona pesisir dengan risiko tinggi dibatasi untuk pembangunan industri baru.
- Kawasan resapan dan RTH dilindungi dalam RDTR.
- Integrasi KLHS dalam RTRW dan RDTR untuk mengendalikan alih fungsi lahan.

Sektor yang dicakup oleh rencana aksi penurunan emisi GRK terdiri dari empat sektor utama. Keempat sektor ini dipilih karena merupakan penyumbang emisi terbesar sekaligus memiliki potensi mitigasi yang paling signifikan.
1. Sektor Energi
Strategi dan Program:
a. Transisi energi bersih:
- Pemasangan PLTS atap di gedung pemerintahan dan fasilitas umum.
- Pembangunan pembangkit energi terbarukan berskala kecil.
b. Efisiensi energi di industri dan rumah tangga.
c. Modernisasi Penerangan Jalan Umum (PJU) menjadi LED hemat energi.
d. Pemanfaatan gas metana dari TPA Terjun untuk waste-to-energy.
Target 2030:
Mengurangi emisi energi sebesar 446.600 ton CO₂e, atau 29% dari proyeksi Business As Usual (BAU).
2. Sektor Transportasi
Strategi dan Program:
a. Elektrifikasi transportasi publik: 
- Pengadaan bus listrik untuk lima koridor utama transportasi massal.
- Penyediaan stasiun pengisian kendaraan listrik umum (SPKLU).
b. Transportasi hijau:
- Jalur sepeda dan pedestrian yang ramah lingkungan.
- Integrasi transportasi publik untuk mengurangi penggunaan kendaraan pribadi.
c. Insentif bagi pengguna kendaraan rendah emisi.
Target 2030:
Mengurangi emisi transportasi sebesar 179.800 ton CO₂e.
3. Sektor Persampahan
Strategi dan Program:
a. Waste-to-Energy Plant di TPA Terjun untuk mengolah sampah menjadi energi listrik.
b. Pengurangan sampah di sumber sebesar 30% melalui:
- Program bank sampah.
- TPS3R (Tempat Pengelolaan Sampah 3R).
- Edukasi pemilahan sampah rumah tangga.
c. Penanganan sampah 70% agar tidak masuk ke TPA tanpa pengolahan.
d. Sistem penangkapan dan pemanfaatan gas metana di TPA.
Target 2030:
Pengurangan emisi hingga 258.100 ton CO₂e, serta tercapainya pengelolaan 100% sampah kota.
4. Sektor Tata Guna Lahan dan Kehutanan (AFOLU)
Strategi dan Program:
a. Perlindungan dan rehabilitasi mangrove seluas 3.203 Ha.
b. Penambahan Ruang Terbuka Hijau (RTH) hingga mencapai 20% pada 2029 dan 30% pada 2045.
c. Restorasi sempadan sungai dan daerah resapan air.
d. Mendukung program nasional FOLU Net Sink 2030.
Target 2030:
Mengurangi emisi sebesar 87.000 ton CO₂e, sekaligus memperkuat daya serap karbon kota.

Climate trends and projections in Coimbatore
reveal notable shifts in temperature
and rainfall patterns over the past five
decades. Analyses of data from the Indian
Meteorological Department (IMD) and Tamil
Nadu State Action Plan on Climate Change
(TNSAPCC) indicate a consistent rise in both
average and extreme temperatures, along
with a decrease in annual rainfall intensity.
Stakeholder consultations have validated
these findings, highlighting the escalating
climate events experienced by the city. Analysis of seasonal temperature variation
in Coimbatore, based on IMD data from
1981 to 2022, reveals a steady increase
in annual average air temperature by
0.014°C per decade. Both maximum and
minimum temperatures show a rise, with
increases of 0.013°C and 0.015°C per decade, respectively. These trends suggest
a potential increase in heatwave events,
impacting public health, water resources,
and energy demand, affecting municipal
services and finances. The frequency of
hot years has also risen, from five per
decade in the 1980s to eight per decade
in recent years, totalling 20 hot years with
temperatures exceeding the average air
temperature of 25.39°C. According to the TNSAPCC (2017),
Coimbatore has experienced a significant
decrease in annual rainfall, supported by
IMD data from 1981 to 2022 and the IIT
Madras study. The onset of the south west
monsoon in Tamil Nadu has shifted earlier,
leading to fewer rainy days but more heavy
precipitation events. Coimbatore's annual
rainfall has decreased from 1,025mm
in 1981 to 1,022.49mm in 2022, with an
average of 37.5 rainy days per year. Urban
flooding is a concern during extreme
rainfall events due to compromised storm
water drain capacity and low infiltration
rates. Climate projections for Coimbatore
indicate rising temperatures by the end of
the century, with maximum temperatures
expected to increase by 1.3 to 3.1°C and
minimum temperatures by 1.2 to 3.3°C,
according to TNSAPCC. The GHG emissions inventory for
Coimbatore city has been prepared for
the period 2017-18 to 2021-22, with the
baseline year set as 2021-22. The GHG
inventory has been prepared according to
the Global Protocol for Community Scale
GHG Emissions (GPC) using ICLEI's HEAT+
tool.
Establishing the baseline status of GHG
emissions assists in identifying key
emission sources, setting reduction targets,
and devising evidence-based strategies and
actions across different sectors.

column30: In the Bogor City Disaster Management Plan 2024-2028, various sectors are involved in an integrated manner because disaster management is considered a cross-sectoral issue. The Bogor City Disaster Management Agency (BPBD) is the main coordinator, while the Planning, Development, Research and Innovation Agency (Bapperida) plays a role in planning and synchronization with regional development documents. The Public Works and Public Housing Agency (Dinas PUPR) focuses on infrastructure, drainage, and building management, while the Environment Agency (DLH) handles environmental and conservation aspects. The Housing and Settlement Agency (Dinas Perumahan dan Permukiman) plays a role in managing disaster-prone areas and providing safe housing, supported by the Investment and Integrated Licensing Service Agency (DPMPTSP) through spatial and building licensing aspects. Diskominfo is responsible for disaster information and communication systems, while the Fire and Rescue Service (DPKP) carries out fire prevention and response as well as emergency evacuation. On the other hand, the Social Service provides social protection for affected communities, and the Health Service ensures health services during emergency response and recovery periods. In addition to the government sector, this document also emphasizes collaboration with the business world through CSR programs, universities in research and innovation, civil society organizations and local communities in community empowerment, and the media as partners in disseminating disaster information. Thus, disaster management in Bogor City is designed as a joint effort involving cross-sectors and multiple parties to be more effective and sustainable.

column23: The 2019 Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP) for the City of Bogor clearly shows that climate-related scenarios have become an important part of its formulation. This document not only assesses air quality based on conventional pollutant parameters such as NOx, SO₂, CO, VOC, and PM₂.₅/PM₁₀, but also integrates greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions inventories such as CO₂, N₂O, and CH₄. With this approach, the issue of local air pollution is directly linked to the climate change mitigation agenda. The identification of pollution sources does not only consider the impact of air pollution on health, but also its contribution to GHG emissions. For example, the transportation sector dominantly produces SO₂, VOC, and PM₂.₅ as well as CO₂, while the industrial sector is the main contributor of NOx, CO, and carbon emissions. The action plans designed, such as motor vehicle emission control, industrial emission control, and management of other sources such as households and agriculture, are aimed at providing dual benefits: reducing public health risks (e.g., cases of respiratory tract infections due to air pollution) and reducing emissions that exacerbate climate change. All of these programs are also aligned with Bogor City's vision of being a green, healthy, smart, and prosperous city and are part of the 2020-2024 RPJMD. Thus, it can be concluded that the climate change scenario has directly influenced the policies, strategies, and actions outlined in the Bogor City CAAP.

column30: In the 2019 Bogor City Clean Air Action Plan (CAAP), various sectors are involved according to the sources of pollution being addressed. The transportation sector is a major concern because it is the largest contributor to air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, so it is focused on controlling motor vehicle emissions. The industrial sector plays an important role because it produces emissions from factory chimneys, coal-fired power plants, and large commercial facilities, which are controlled through emission standards and clean technology. The area sector, which includes households, agriculture, livestock, services, and commercial facilities, is also involved because it contributes to air pollution through daily activities and open burning. In addition, the local government sector, through various regional government agencies, plays a role in drafting regulations, supervision, air quality monitoring, and infrastructure provision. This document also emphasizes the need for the community to change their behavior, as well as collaboration with universities, research institutions, and the business world in improving capacity, technology, and funding. Thus, the CAAP involves the transportation, industrial, area (household and commercial), government, business, academic, and community sectors as a whole in efforts to maintain air quality while supporting climate change mitigation.

column30: The second Climate Action Plan (CAP) for the City of Amman reflects the commitment of the Greater Amman Municipality (GAM) to integrate climate change adaptation and mitigation across all its operations in order to enhance the quality of life of the citizens of Amman. It also reflects the evolving context of increasing human and institutional capacities for mainstreaming climate change, and for applying the C40 CAP Framework. As a learning organisation, GAM has endeavoured to apply the CAP Framework to the best of its capabilities, while recognising that there are improvements that will be brought about in future updates that are expected to be carried out at least every 5 years. It is also expected that completion of the Long term Strategy for Sustainable Low Carbon Development in Jordan in 2024 will provide more guidance for GAM to formulate long-term climate strategies in alignment with national priorities. In any case, the updated CAP has been formulated in alignment with the Climate Change Policy (CCP) 2022 - 2050. Based on stakeholder consultations, the CAP presents an Amman Vision 2050 as: “The City of Amman is carbon-neutral and climate-resilient by 2050 driven by a green and circular economy for the prosperity and wellbeing of all its citizens. We will demonstrate climate and sustainability leadership regionally and globally through fairness, inclusivity and respect for our cultural and natural heritage in transitioning to a sustainable city.” The identification and prioritisation of climate strategies and actions was based on the expert knowledge of GAM technical departments that were familiar with the mitigation analysis and climate risk assessments carried out in a CAP development process. Also, the identification of climate strategies and actions drew from the multi-criteria analysis that had been carried out under the Green City Action Plan (GCAP) in 2019.

column23: Amman used a scenario planning tool called CURB to identify and prioritize low carbon infrastructure and GHG reduction actions that would set the city on a path to achieving its 2050 vision. Data from the 2014 emissions inventory was used in the creation of the model to set the city's baseline emissions. CURB is an excel based model that uses city emission inventory data to project future emissions and suggest actions for reduction. The analysis presented here comes from the CURB model, and it helped Amman to shape its 2050 vision and action plan. The tool was developed in close coordination with the departments and units that manage infrastructure projects and policies in the Greater Amman Municipality, the government formed a technical working group that input data to the model. The actions that are selected to create the scenario are based on discussions with these departments and also reflect actions that the city is already taking.The baseline scenario is a “business as usual” projection that estimates what emission levels would be in the future with no emission reduction actions taken. The baseline uses Amman's 2014 emissions inventory data, as well as future population and economic growth rates to project emissions. Actions were then selected in the tool for each sector to build a scenario that would reduce emissions below the baseline emission projections.

column30: Amman Climate Action Plan was developed along with the Ministry of Environment, Partnership for Market Readiness of the World Bank Group and intensive consultation with GAM partners in 2019. The plan is a continuity of Amman Resilience Strategy and is in line with the government's commitments to international agreements. Amman Climate Action Plan is an ambitious and first step on the long journey to creating a sustainable, vibrant future. It lays out an approach to creating a carbon neutral Amman, while expanding services and meeting the needs of the rapidly growing city. This inaugural plan sets an interim target of a 40% reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. Carbon neutrality is a long-term goal, this plan sets out a shared vision for collaboration among the government, private sector, development partners and residents of Amman. This strategy is a living, evolving document that the city will continue to build on until we achieve our plan for a carbon-neutral 2050.Amman plan sector goals•THE ELECTRICITY SOURCE for the city will need to be predominately carbon free in 2050.•NEWLY CONSTRUCTED BUILDINGS will all comply with green building guidelines, and a majority of existing buildings will be renovated to improve energy efficiency.SUSTAINABLE MOBILITY:•Public transport will be clean, efficient and widespread.•A majority of private vehicles and taxis will be electric powered.•Walking will be a core mode of mobility in the city center.WATER AND WASTE WATER•Water will be efficiently used.•Rainwater will be captured and reused.•Waste water will be effectively treated, with a focus on capturing gases for energy use.WASTE•Waste will be reduced, sorted, composted and recycled.•Remaining solid waste will be processed in waste to energy sites.URBAN PLANNING AND LAND USE•New development areas will be focused on public transit-oriented corridors•Green spaces, parks and urban forestry will increase, and new building will be focused on underutilized landRENEWABLE ENERGY WILL BE EXPANDED•Building integrated solar photovoltaics (PVs) will provide residential and commercial buildings with the majority of their energy needs.•GAM will produce its own renewable energy.•CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT - a cross-cutting program that includes launching a city-wide awareness program about climate change action and GAM's ongoing efforts.

column23: The formulation process for Quezon City's Enhanced LCCAP is consistent with the National Climate Change Action Plan guidelines, Climate Change Expenditure Tagging Methodology, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan (DRRM) and Local DRRM Plan. Furthermore, the Enhanced LCCAP was developed through comprehensive, methodological, and participatory processes following the C40 Climate Action Planning (CAP) Framework. Quezon City Government is committed to pursuing an emission-neutral and climate-resilient city by 2050. This is through an enhanced climate action plan that aligns its policies and initiatives to support the implementation and ambitions of the Paris Agreement, both addressing GHG emission reduction and adapting to the impacts of climate change.\n\nQuezon City's Enhanced LCCAP has identified the following wider opportunities and benefits as defined in its outcome statements:1. Increased availability, stability, and accessibility of safe and healthy food2. Increased availability, stability, and equitability of access to water resources3. Optimized urban water systems management contributing to flooding mitigation4. Reduced waste impact or pressure on the environment and ecosystems, aiming for 50% diversion rate by 20305. Reduced effect of urban heat and drought on Quezon City6. Reduced vulnerability of men and women and other vulnerable groups (children, elderly, and persons with disability, etc.)7. Increased accessibility of key public services to men and women and other vulnerable groups8. Increase in green, energy-efficient, and resilient buildings and establishments in Quezon City, targeting 80-100% of building permits granted being compliant to the updated Green Building Code by 20259. Availability of accessible, clean, and affordable renewable energy, targeting 100% solarization coverage for all city-owned buildings and facilities by 203010. Increased climate-proofed, rehabilitated, and improved ecologically-efficient technologies11. Increased uptake of active mobility, tripling cycling rate from 2.2% in 2016 to 6.6% of total modal share in 2030 and expanding bike lanes from 55 km in 2016 to 350 km by 203012. Increased uptake of mass public transport, with bus modal share increasing from 6.6% in 2016 to 8.5% in 2030 and railway modal share increasing from 4.2% in 2016 to 6.0% in 2030.

The Quezon City Climate Investment Opportunities Diagnostic (CIOD) aims to support the implementation of Quezon City's Enhanced
LCCAP by evaluating several of its actions in terms of potential investments, indicative costing, and potential funding sources. It leverages a new platform developed by the International Finance Corporation (IFC) called APEX (Advanced Practices for Environmental Excellence in Cities), which is supported by the APEX Online App that helps quantify and prioritize city-based policy and investment solutions in the energy, transport, water, and waste sectors.

The CIOD identifies and outlines investment opportunities totaling USD 4,768 million that would be required to implement twenty-five measures across the four key sectors of built environment and energy, transport, solid waste, and water and wastewater. Around 69 percent (USD 3,295 million) of these total investments would be indirect cost measures, and 31 percent (USD 1,473 million) direct cost measures. If all of these investment opportunities are carried to fruition, they are expected to deliver a 25 percent GHG reduction to Quezon City across all four sectors under analysis.

The base year emissions calculations include land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF), and the target covers carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and economy-wide emissions intensity of GDP. Malaysia has a range of national, state and local-level policies instituted to help the country achieve these targets. Many, in fact, predate the Paris Agreement, demonstrating Malaysia's long-term commitment to climate action and sustainability. National-level formal policies include the 12th Malaysia Plan, the most recent of a series of 5-year comprehensive development plans, the Forth National Physical Plan (NPP-4) as well as strategies such as the National Policy on Climate Change, National Low Carbon Cities Masterplan (NLCCM) and Low Carbon Cities Framework (LCCF) and policy mechanisms such as the Green Technology Master Plan (refer to Figure 12). Selangor also has several state-specific development blueprints and environmental policies, and Petaling Jaya has local plans, PJ Smart Sustainable and Resilient 2030 (PJSSR 2030), Three (3) years program of Energy Management, Implementation of Malaysian Standards (MS) 1525 & Low Carbon Buildings (2020- 2023) as well as Carbon Management Plan (2015-2020) report prepared by Carbon Trust funded by the British Government under the UK- Malaysia Low Carbon Cities programme. Further this report, Carbon Trust also prepared the Low Carbon City Action Plan 2015-2030 for MBPJ. Malaysia ratified the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 1994, and committed in 2009 to voluntarily reducing the country's GHG emissions intensity of GDP by up to 40% by the year 2020 compared to 2005 levels. In 2015, at COP 21, Malaysia increased this commitment to 45%, to be achieved by 2030 using the same 2005 baseline, conditional on international financial support. Petaling Jaya is committed to a target of a 33% reduction in absolute GHG carbon emission by 2030 relative to the base year 2021 emissions level.

The Carbon Trust of UK worked together with Petaling Jaya City Council on a two-year pilot of a new Low Carbon Cities Malaysia programme, which has been officially launched this week. The programme was designed to accelerate the implementation of carbon reduction projects for states, cities and local authorities across Malaysia.The first year of the programme focused on developing a five-year plan for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from MBPJ's own estate and operations. This process will involve measuring current impacts, setting robust reduction targets, as well as identifying and implementing the most promising energy efficiency and carbon reduction opportunities.
The second year of the programme was intended to help MBPJ to use its influence to drive forward carbon reduction across Petaling Jaya, through engaging businesses, educational institutions and the local community.

The programme was designed and delivered by the Carbon Trust, working alongside Malaysian Green Technology Corporation (GreenTech Malaysia) and Malaysia's Ministry of Energy. Funding was provided by the UK government's Foreign and Commonwealth Office, with local support provided from the British Embassy in Kuala Lumpur

Based on the deliberations of the Low Carbon Committee Meetings, the Petaling Jaya City Council (MBPJ) has resolved to mandate compliance with energy efficiency requirements for all new developments within its administrative jurisdiction. This directive reflects MBPJ's strong commitment to advancing the low-carbon development agenda and to ensuring that every new project is implemented in accordance with established energy efficiency standards.

In further strengthening this commitment, MBPJ has undertaken proactive measures through the adoption of the Online Monitoring System (OMS) in its own buildings. Complementing this initiative, MBPJ also employs the Building Energy Development Online System (BEDOS), a platform developed under the Sustainable Energy Development Authority (SEDA), as a central mechanism for monitoring, reporting, and evaluating the energy performance of buildings.

Through the integration of these systems, MBPJ is able to monitor, assess, and manage energy consumption in a structured and systematic manner. This not only ensures compliance with prescribed energy efficiency standards but also aligns with MBPJ's broader objectives of carbon reduction and urban sustainability.

column23: 臺南市於2010年11月底正式合併升格為直轄市後，隨著行政區的整併及各項新政策與措施的推動與整合，環境負荷及產經活動已有明顯之改變，此外，民眾亦對周遭生活環境之品質愈趨重視。臺南市藉由蒐集相關環境背景資料，了解各項環境負荷，如人口、車輛、工廠數、能資源排放等變化趨勢，作為未來訂定溫室氣體管制策略之參考。臺南市溫室氣體管制執行方案以打造「低碳臺南．宜居好遊賞」為願景，分別擬定六大部門(能源、製造、運輸、住商、環境、農業)、六大目標(陽光電城、住商節能、能源轉型、綠色運輸、友善農業及資源循環)、30項關鍵績效指標，由 14 個局處通力合作推動 125 項推動做法。以2017年為基準年，2017至2020年為第一期，2021至2025年為第二期，2026至2030年為第三期，採每五年為一期滾動式檢討推動。透過定期召開臺南市低碳調適及永續發展委員會來檢視及審視整體政策及規劃。每半年函文臺南市府各局處取得資料定期書面進度管考，以及不定期召開跨局處或秘書長會議，動態追蹤並檢視本市溫室氣體管制執行方案推動情形。經統計第一期(2018~2020 年)執行成果，本市 30 項 KPI 中共有 23 項完全達標，達標率為 96%。第二期(2021~2025 年)執行至2023年，總計46項 KPI 中已有 21 項完全達標。

column30: 1. Taichung City's overall MRT network plan was approved for review by the Ministry of Transportation and Communications in 2021. MRT construction involves a wide range of areas, has a long-term impact, and incurs high construction costs. Therefore, it must be implemented in phases, divided into three stages based on demand: priority routes, a mid-term network, and a long-term network. The Wuri-Wenxin-Beitun Line (Green Line) is currently open to traffic in 2021. The Bureau's top priorities include completing the priority network, the Blue Line, the Airport MRT (Orange Line), the Green Line extensions to Dakeng and Changhua, and the Blue Line extension to Taiping. The mid-term network is also being actively developed simultaneously, including the Tun District MRT Circular Line (Purple Line), the Chongde-Fengyuan Line (Red Line), and the Orange Line extension to the Haikou section, which will be added later. With the simultaneous launch of seven lines, we strive to realize all of these plans as soon as possible. 2. column23:
In the concept study 'Münster Climate Neutral 2030', the challenges are presented transparently and openly on the one hand, and on the other hand, the scope for action of the City of Münster to achieve the target is elaborated. Based on the strategy and the room for maneuver, a consortium of experts has presented a target scenario for
climate neutrality.
It is important to emphasize that the concept study, in presenting the reduction paths for the individual fields of action and sectors (mobility, private households, commerce, industry), shows what must happen for the goal of climate neutrality to be achieved as early as 2030. In this approach, the thinking and calculations are deliberately based
on the target, and the framework conditions that influence the pursuit of this target are initially ignored. Thus, the illustrations and the chosen approach do not show the feasibility, rather the challenges and the necessary changes in all areas of social and economic life in Münster are illustrated within the framework of a scenario approach.
By analyzing the municipal scope for action, the special dimension of the challenge can be shown and, at the same time, the further design necessities and possibilities of the city of Münster can be clarified. The concept study is based on the Master Plan 100% Climate Protection 2050, the Action Program Climate Protection 2030 and the municipal energy and CO2 balance.

column30:
The results of the concept study make clear that it will take an enormous effort on the part of all those involved in urban society (private households, companies, administration, institutions, etc.) to come significantly closer to the goal of climate neutrality by 2030. The reduction paths presented in the individual fields of action make the challenge clear and show that fundamental social and political system changes are required in all areas, which would have to be brought about immediately.
It should be noted that the illustrations are not to be understood in the sense of a feasibility study, but rather as a scenario analysis that shows, on the basis of assumptions to be made, what must happen in order to achieve the goal of climate neutrality by 2030. The illustrations thus represent the absolute best-case scenario and assume that
the climate neutrality targets will also be brought forward to 2030 at EU and federal level and that corresponding measures will be taken within their scope of action. The concept study also makes it clear that, given the complexity of the challenge, there can be no concrete and purely municipal plan of action to ensure climate neutrality in 2030.
It is imperative that the municipal scope for action be exhausted in order to achieve the goal in the event of changes in the external political framework conditions. For this reason, it must be a matter for the City of Münster Group to supplement and expand the ambitious Climate Protection 2030 action program with the measures proposed in
the concept study as quickly as possible. These are not only motivating and encouraging measures, but also demanding or restrictive measures that must be initiated and permanently expanded and intensified. Climate change is real, the consequences are already severe, and measures to achieve climate neutrality cannot be delayed.

The Council adopts the Integrated Land Use Concept for Münster (IFM) in 2024 as an informal planning instrument and as the result of a technical assessment of the various demands on the area, which has been drawn up and qualified within the framework of a broad development and participation process involving representatives from politics and administration, experts (“stakeholders”) and interested citizens.
The city of Münster faces the task of balancing the current and future challenges of urban spatial development: pressure to grow in order to provide urgently needed new housing and workplaces, implementation of Münster's climate neutrality goals, protection and further development of nature and open spaces in the city. The space available for new developments is limited - it is therefore important to identify the competition for space between these different demands, weigh them carefully against each other, and resolve them in the best possible way.

column30: In accordance with the nation climate actionplan , in 2018 the city of Nijmegen has established a heat transitionvision to phase out the use of natural gas in domestic homes and Utility buildings towards collective distric heating and individuele heatpumps. The report can be downloaded under point 9 in the website https://ris2.ibabs.eu/Agenda/Details/Nijmegen/fa6166c4-c686-4788-a42d-3b57feb0dccd The road to a natural gas-free Nijmegen is neighbourhood by neighbourhood. For all of Nijmegen we looked at which place which alternative to natural gas is the most promising, whereby the affordability for the end user is central. On the base on the lowest transition costs per neighbourhood, planning by us and our partners and existing initiatives in the city, a choice has been made for the neighborhoods and areas where we will be working on the heat transition. These are Dukenburg, Hengstdal, Bottendaal, Hatert and Heijendaal station area. We aim to be natural gas-free in these areas by 2035 at the latest. In addition, we will have a for the entire city developing an approach to prepare private homes for transition by installing insulation, ventilation and electric cooking stimulate.An estimated of 25.000 homes will have an alternative heating devices such as district heating or individual heatpump. An CO2 reduction of 55.000 t-CO2 is estimated. In addition the isolation of resedential homes wil attribute another approximatley 15.000 t-CO2 reduction.These 25.000 residential homes en Ulitiybuildings are planed to be natural gas free by the year 2035. Most of the other 50.000 residential home are made natural gas gree ready so that these homes can be an transisition between 2035 en 2045.As continued in 2019 a strategy has been made how the the buildings of the city of Nijmegen can be connected to a city wide distric heating system. The plan can be downloaded by https://online.ibabs.eu/ibabsapi/publicdownload.aspx?site=Nijmegen&id=88b39552-1f9e-4bc1-8af9-10a7b6471510 Updating the heat strategy from 2019 will start at the end of 2022. column30: From 2021 the climate change mitigation and energy measures have been integrated directly into the yearly four-year municipal budget (\'Climate Budget\'). The Climate Budget is a dedicated climate chapter in the yearly municipal budget and action plan. The climate budget is a cross-sectoral tool for the operationalisation of the Municipal Plan for Energy and Climate that allocates responsibility for implementation and/or coordination of measures, in addition to centralized mechanisms for the allocation of municipal funds and reporting. It comprises 1) an emissions framework detailing business as usual compared to a emissions reduction pathway for the next four years, 2) a list of measures, with allocation of responsibility for implementation and/or reporting to the relevant municipal department, 3) a description of funding for climate measures. \nThe implementation of the measures within the climate budget are reported together with the twice-yearly financial reports from the city administration to the city council. The measures contained within the plan are city-wide and include measures to be carried out by external stakeholders. The financial aspect of the climate budget is restricted to the municipalities own funding streams (in combination with national grants). The costs referred to above are the total investment and running costs allocated directly to the climate budget in the administrative budget. The city council also made some additional funding available when passing the budget.

Climate-related scenarios have played an integral role in the development of Helsingborg's Climate and Energy Plan 2025-2030. The plan is aligned with international climate targets, in particular the Paris Agreement and the 1.5 °C pathway, and sets the goal of climate neutrality by 2030. Historical emission data (scopes 1 and 2) and reference trajectories have informed sector-specific targets for transport, buildings, energy, and industry.

Scenario assumptions include large-scale electrification of transport, expansion of renewable energy, energy efficiency measures, and the development of charging infrastructure and sustainable fuels. The plan also incorporates considerations of the municipality's limited control over certain indirect (scope 3) emissions and therefore emphasizes collaboration with businesses, citizens, the region, and the national government.

These scenarios have directly influenced the plan's targets and strategies, which are designed to reflect what is required to achieve the 1.5 °C pathway. For example, sectoral targets are based on modeled reductions achievable by 2030 under ambitious but feasible assumptions for technology uptake and behavioral change. The plan also addresses climate risks and adaptation needs linked to extreme weather and long-term resilience.

At the same time, the plan acknowledges uncertainties related to the speed of technological deployment, financial conditions, and indirect consumption-based emissions. Continuous monitoring and iterative updates are therefore part of the strategy to ensure that the plan remains relevant as scenarios and external conditions evolve.

The total cost of the investments that Helsingborg needs to make in order to achieve climate neutrality by 2030 is estimated in the Climate City Investment Plan (CIP) at:
Capital expenditures (CAPEX, net present value): approx. SEK 11.23 billion (≈ EUR 0.985 billion)
Operating costs (OPEX, net present value 2024-2030): approx. EUR 0.085 billion
Total expenditure: ≈ EUR 1.07 billion (just over SEK 12 billion) by 2030
Three capital-intensive projects - a CCS facility, climate transition from natural gas to renewable energy solutions, and the electrification of road transport - alone account for about three quarters of the total cost and are expected to deliver around 65% of the emissions reductions.
Total costs: approx. EUR 1.07 billion (≈ SEK 12 billion) by 2030.
The municipal group (the city and municipally owned companies): controls approx. 44% of the costs. Of these, around 30% are already included in the city's seven-year plan, meaning they are budgeted and financed. The actual financing gap for the municipality is therefore estimated at 14% of the total costs.
Private actors, transport operators and households: are responsible for the remaining 56% of the costs, outside the city's direct control.
The three capital-intensive projects (CCS, climate transition from natural gas to renewable energy solutions, electrification of road transport) together represent about 75% of the total costs and about 65% of the estimated emissions reductions.
In summary, the city and its companies are responsible for just under half of the total investments (44%), while the majority of costs (56%) fall on external actors such as businesses and citizens. Of the municipal costs, a significant portion (30%) is already budgeted, which reduces the city's financing gap to 14% of the total needs.
It should also be noted that additional costs for personnel, other projects, and supporting resources will arise alongside the investments listed above.

An initial science-based Climate Change Risk Assessment for Sunderland has been developed, aligned with the UK Climate Risk Independent Assessment (CCRA3) Technical Report (2022). The Risk Assessment has been considered by the Council's Chief Officer Group with agreement that it will form the basis of our Adaptation Plan. 

The risk assessment follows the same methodology for magnitude and urgency
The magnitude of the impact specified is assessed, for specific time periods in specific climate futures - the 2050s and 2080s on pathways to approximately 2°C and 4°C of global warming in the late 21st Century. These are considered to broadly represent lower and upper rates of climate change consistent with either current policies relating to greenhouse gas emissions or the successful achievement of international climate policy ambitions.
Existing levels of deprivation and inequalities including health inequalities, and the associated implications are factored into the risk assessment in addition to consideration being given to the potential for these to increase as a result of climate change.

The risk assessment identifies 44 climate risks across 4 categories: infrastructure; health, communities and the built environment; business and industry; natural environment and assets. These include risks to health and wellbeing, the delivery of health and social care and education, biodiversity, the landscape including soils and natural carbon stores, businesses both physically and through productivity decline, and risks to infrastructure including water supply, transport networks and energy demand. 
These risks have been assessed on an individual basis, to determine which current policies are working towards reducing the risks. Gaps have then been identified to understand where future risk reduction must be undertaken to ensure resilience to climate change. Priority actions to reduce the risks identified and their impact will be taken forward as part of a strategic and co-ordinated approach to adaptation, working both locally and regionally as appropriate. 
The Risk Assessment will form the basis of an Adaptation Plan which will demonstrate actions to reduce these risks.

Flooding, extreme heat and biodiversity loss are all likely to increase in frequency and intensity in the future. These increasing risks have increased the need for the provision of Green Infrastructure across Sunderland - in relation to climate change mitigation (offsetting) and climate change adaptation.

The Green Infrastructure Strategy aims to:
• Protect, Enhance and Repair the Strategic GI Corridors: Ensure that the integrity of the network is safeguarded and enhanced, unblock existing barriers to repair connectivity.
• Address GI investments - applying the evidence base, maximizing multifunctionality and greatest returns, application to funding/resources opportunities.
• Future proofing / ensuring new growth is sustainable
• Identify key stakeholders and promote partnership working: establish a Sunderland GI stakeholder network, cross boundary working
• Identify delivery mechanisms and secure funding streams: planning applications, growth and development, grants, a triage approach.
• Increase awareness of Sunderland's GI value and benefits: actively marketing Sunderland's GI assets, educating and advocating GI
• Policy aims and aspirations: regeneration across the city, such as improving health, access, quality of life, biodiversity, climate change mitigation (offsetting) and climate change adaptation.

To translate SGIS into a series of projects for delivery and action over the next 15 years, from 2018-2033, Sunderland has a Green Infrastructure Delivery and Action Plan. This sets out a range of actions, some of which include the development of a 'Green Infrastructure Offsetting Matrix', creating filter strips and natural swales, permeable paving, wetlands and woodlands wherever feasible to help cope with flash flooding, repairing broken corridors, creating reed beds at stream sources to slow down flash flooding, increasing woodland cover, and creating buffer zones to protected wildlife sites.
SGIS and Sunderland's Green Infrastructure Delivery and Action Plan help Sunderland mitigate and adapt to climate risk through nature-based solutions by: storing carbon; improving drainage and managing flooding; improving water quality; supporting adaptive management in coastal infrastructure; reducing air pollution; and increasing shading cover.
Green Infrastructure improvements proposed also seek to improve the cycle network across the city and access to local facilities on foot, thereby promoting and encouraging a modal shift to active transport.

A report from the Tyndall Centre, available at https://carbonbudget.manchester.ac.uk/reports/E08000024/print/, presents climate mitigation targets for Sunderland that are derived from the commitments of the Paris Agreement, informed by science-based climate change evidence. The report provides Sunderland with budgets for carbon dioxide emissions and from the energy system for 2020 to 2100. For Sunderland to make its fair contribution towards the Paris Agreement, the Tyndall Centre made the following science-based recommendations Sunderland to:
• Stay within a maximum cumulative CO2 emissions budget of 8.2 million tonnes (MtCO2) for the period of 2020 to 2100. At 2017 CO2 emission levels, Sunderland would use this entire budget within 6 years from 2020.
• Initiate an immediate programme of CO2 mitigation to deliver cuts in emissions averaging a minimum of -14.4% per year to deliver a Paris aligned carbon budget. These annual reductions in emissions require national and local action and could be part of a wider collaboration with other local authorities.
• Reach zero or near zero carbon no later than 2040. The report provides an indicative CO2 reduction pathway that stays within the recommended maximum carbon budget of 8.2 MtCO2. In 2040 5% of the budget remains, representing very low levels of residual CO2 emissions by this time. Earlier years for reaching zero CO2 emissions are also within the recommended budget, provided that interim budgets with lower cumulative CO2 emissions are also adopted.

Recent local extreme weather events also inform climate action in Sunderland. For example, Storm Arwen brought high winds, heavy rain and snow to Sunderland in November 2021. Homes, businesses and green infrastructure were damaged and public transport networks were suspended. There were 600 reports of storm damage and more than 85 fallen trees.
• Houses were damaged
• A tree blocked the A690 Durham Road at Bede Bank and another blocked Chester Road near the cemetery.
• Structural damage to 28 properties
• 240,000 were left without electricity.
• Tyne and Wear Fire and Rescue Service took more than 500 weather related calls in 24 hours.
• Gentoo housing group faced costs of storm damages up to £2 million.
With extreme weather events likely to become more frequent and intense in the future, this increases the importance of climate action.
The Council's annual Carbon Report (see URL) evaluates the progress made towards achieving the citywide decarbonisation goals.

The Low Carbon Framework sets out the vision, purpose and directions of actions necessary to enable the city to deliver on Sunderland's carbon neutrality goals.
The Low Carbon Framework was adopted in December 2020 by the City Partnership Board, on the recommendation of the 2030 Shadow Board, and subsequently endorsed by Sunderland City Council's Cabinet in January 2021 that at the same time adopted its Low Carbon Action Plan (LCAP) which included a target for the Council to become carbon neutral by 2030. The Council also developed a more robust version of its own LCAP, which was approved by Cabinet in July 2022 and is available at https://www.sunderland.gov.uk/media/25109/Low-Carbon-Action-Plan-2022/pdf/oce22135_Sunderland_Low_Carbon_Action_Plan_A4_2022_154cod7kbye7t.pdf?m=1722437677503. Progress in relation to the Council's LCAP is regularly reviewed as well as being reported annually to Cabinet. Details regarding the Council's LCAP are covered in the next question.

Shadow Board partners are working collectively to drive Sunderland's commitment to tackling climate change. The partnership meets quarterly to ensure that best practice is shared, that duplication is avoided, and that resource efficiency, joint working and impact are maximised. Each partner is also developing their own Low Carbon Action Plan and carrying out initiatives to enable the city to reach its low carbon goals. The Low Carbon Framework is underpinned by these individual partner Action Plans. https://www.mysunderland.co.uk/lowcarbon/workingtogether

Flooding is the most significant climate hazard in Sunderland with coastal, river and surface water flooding all being hazards to residents and the economy as identified in the climate risk and vulnerability module. Furthermore, it is expected that the frequency and intensity of flooding events in the jurisdiction will increase in the event of 1.5°C global warming being exceeded.

Sunderland prepares a Local Flood Risk Management Strategy. The purpose of the LFRMS is to act as a robust guidance tool for Risk Management Authorities operating in Sunderland to deliver a coordinated, improved approach in all flood risk management activities. In addition, the overriding vision for the LFRMS is for Sunderland City Council to take a lead role in better understanding local flood risk. Providing this information in the form of the LFRMS will enable communities to also improve their own knowledge and understanding of the risk of flooding across Sunderland.

More information can be found at https://www.sunderland.gov.uk/media/23162/Local-flood-risk-management-strategy/pdf/Sunderland_LFRMS_-_Final_Version_-_Complete.pdf?m=637502096317830000

En cumplimiento del Plan de desarrollo se pretende poner a Montería en el radar internacional incorporando medidas de acción
por el clima y el cambio climático, fortalecer la capacidad de resiliencia climática y la adaptación
a los riesgos, la conservación de la biodiversidad, educación ambiental y capacidad institucional
para ello. Dichas medidas están dispuestas en las bases del plan de desarrollo. Así mismo, la Alcaldía fomentará la economía rural mediante una política pública que contiene asistencia técnica agropecuaria, formulación y estructuración de proyectos, emprendimiento
rural, alianzas productivas, comercialización y banco de maquinaria verde, y el desarrollo de
agroecosistemas.
Por último, en el debate mundial y nacional de transición energética, la Alcaldía impulsará una
estrategia de diversificación y abastecimiento energético y el uso eficiente de la energía, lo que
implica realizar acciones demostrativas de unidades de generación fotovoltaica. Se vincula varios sectores como agricultura y desarrollo rural, medio ambiente y desarrollo sostenible, minas y energía. Más allá de las disposiciones legales, la administración de Montería reconoce y promueve los diálogos con la comunidad. Las voces ciudadanas en la co-construcción del plan de desarrollo son determinantes no solo para conocer sus problemáticas, perspectivas y sueños, sino también construir confianza y legitimidad. No solo se trata de un diseño técnico y político, sino también de un proceso de acuerdos colectivos que ponga a Montería primero.
La gobernanza busca establecer alianzas, articulaciones, diálogos y mediaciones con diversos actores sociales, políticos, económicos e institucionales. Su objetivo es formular e implementar actividades de mitigación, adaptación al cambio climático y políticas públicas que garanticen derechos individuales y colectivos, aseguren la estabilidad social, política y económica, y faciliten la participación ciudadana en los asuntos públicos relacionados con el clima y el medio ambiente.

La orientación de las acciones contenidas en el Plan propende por la mitigación, la adaptación, la compensación y la sensibilización. Lo anterior, alrededor de los temas críticos de movilidad urbana, eficiencia energética y energías renovables, gestión de residuos, saneamiento básico y agua potable, construcción sostenible, responsabilidad ambiental, desarrollo agropecuario, vulnerabilidad, adaptación y resiliencia, cultura ciudadana, conservación de ecosistemas y reforestación y zonas verdes.
Los resultados sirvieron de base para Propiciar que Montería sea una ciudad más resiliente, no sólo en lo ambiental sino también en la atención a su población. Con esta medida, se busca extender la cobertura de saneamiento básico al 100% del área urbana, contar con suficiente capacidad de absorber y responder frente a condiciones de estrés ocasionadas por fenómenos naturales o antrópicos y generar condiciones para la mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático. Para esto, se ha diseñado un eje estratégico denominado Montería resiliente, el camino al bienestar.
Promover una administración pública y para el público, un gobierno fuerte, con recursos, transparente y proactivo que logre una gestión fiscal eficiente, a partir de una mejora en los ingresos propios, en la calidad del gasto y en la implementación de un sistema de administración de contingentes. Para esto, se ha diseñado el eje estratégico Monterianos por Montería, hacia una hacienda moderna y transparente.

Integración en la planificación estratégica: Los escenarios de cambio climático se han incorporado en instrumentos de planificación como la Estrategia Municipal de Adaptación a la Variabilidad y al Cambio Climático (EMAVCC) y el Plan Municipal de Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (PMGRD). Estos documentos reconocen que los pronósticos de precipitación y temperatura son insumos clave para identificar y evaluar riesgos climáticos en el territorio.   

Priorización de riesgos: El análisis de los escenarios ayuda a priorizar los riesgos más críticos para la ciudad, como las inundaciones y los movimientos de remoción en masa (deslizamientos), que se espera que aumenten con el incremento de las precipitaciones. Por ejemplo, el escenario RCP 4.5 para 2100 proyecta un aumento del riesgo crítico en la biodiversidad de entre 0-15% en la mayoría del territorio y hasta un 45% en la zona oriental, lo que resalta la necesidad de proteger las cuencas hídricas de esa área.   

Definición de programas y proyectos: Las proyecciones influyen en la creación de proyectos específicos. Por ejemplo, se han propuesto programas para:

Monitoreo y alertas tempranas: Fortalecer las redes de estaciones hidrometeorológicas y geotécnicas para dar seguimiento a las condiciones que podrían detonar inundaciones y deslizamientos.   

Protección de la infraestructura y el hábitat: Evaluar la vulnerabilidad de la infraestructura vial, de acueducto y de alcantarillado ante eventos extremos, y planificar la reubicación de viviendas en zonas de alto riesgo.   

Uso del suelo: Recomendar la conservación de suelos y la restauración de ecosistemas en las zonas con mayor incremento de precipitación, así como el cambio en las prácticas agropecuarias en laderas de alta pendiente.   

Salud pública: Analizar cómo los escenarios climáticos futuros podrían afectar la distribución de vectores y la aparición de enfermedades.

Estatus del Plan: 
El Plan de Acción Climática de Cuenca se encuentra a la espera de su aprobación mediante ordenanza municipal, requisito indispensable para su plena vigencia, institucionalización y gobernanza. A pesar de ello, ya se ha realizado su presentación pública (lanzamiento) y se han establecido los lineamientos iniciales para su implementación.
El propósito del plan es impulsar una transformación climática e integral en Cuenca, acelerando la transición hacia un territorio bajo en emisiones y altamente resiliente. O estudo de adaptação foca em preparar a cidade para os impactos inevitáveis das mudanças climáticas. 
Os cenários indicaram um aumento na frequência de chuvas torrenciais, elevando o risco de alagamentos e enchentes em áreas específicas da cidade. As ações propostas para dar consistência a esta frente incluem:
- Melhoria e expansão da infraestrutura de drenagem urbana, como a construção e manutenção de bueiros, galerias e canais para suportar um volume maior de água.
- Mapeamento e monitoramento detalhado das áreas de risco, com a criação de sistemas de alerta precoce para a população vulnerável.
- Proteção de áreas de recarga e margens de córregos para aumentar a permeabilidade do solo e ajudar a conter o escoamento superficial.
As projeções indicaram um aumento no número de dias com temperaturas muito elevadas, representando um risco significativo para a saúde pública. 
Criação de 'refúgios climáticos', locais públicos climatizados ou com grande conforto térmico (como parques e centros comunitários) para uso da população durante picos de calor.
Revisão de normas construtivas para incentivar edificações que melhorem o conforto térmico e reduzam a necessidade de ar-condicionado.

O estudo de mitigação concentra-se em reduzir as fontes de emissão de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) do município. O inventário de Palmas, alinhado ao de outras cidades brasileiras, identificou três setores prioritários.
Principalmente pelo uso de combustíveis fósseis na frota de veículos particulares e no transporte público. As ações propostas para mitigação são: modernização e eletrificação da frota de transporte coletivo, substituindo ônibus a diesel por modelos elétricos ou movidos a biocombustíveis; criação de infraestrutura para mobilidade ativa, como a expansão de ciclovias seguras e a melhoria de calçadas para incentivar o transporte a pé e de bicicleta; implementação de um plano de logística urbana de baixo carbono para otimizar a circulação de veículos de carga.

O setor de energia estacionária refere-se ao consumo de eletricidade em residências, comércios, serviços e indústrias. As estratégias de mitigação incluem o incentivo massivo à geração de energia renovável distribuída, especialmente a solar, por meio de programas de incentivos fiscais e desburocratização (como o Palmas Solar).
Programas de eficiência energética em prédios públicos, com a troca de lâmpadas, equipamentos de ar-condicionado e a melhoria do isolamento térmico.
O Setor de Resíduos é focado nas emissões de gás metano (CH₄) provenientes da decomposição de lixo orgânico no aterro sanitário. As ações de mitigação recomendadas são, ampliação dos programas de coleta seletiva e compostagem, para desviar a maior quantidade possível de resíduos orgânicos do aterro e studo e implementação de sistemas de captura e aproveitamento energético do biogás gerado no aterro sanitário, transformando um poluente em um recurso.

column23: O Plano Municipal de Redução de Riscos (PMRR) de Santo André fundamenta-se em uma abordagem estratégica que integra cenários climáticos projetados e dados históricos para construir consistência e robustez em suas ações. A elaboração do plano partiu da premissa de que as mudanças climáticas são um agente catalisador de riscos, intensificando eventos como estiagens prolongadas, chuvas extremas e temperaturas anômalas. Para isso, incorporou projeções regionais que apontam para o aumento da irregularidade pluviométrica, com períodos de seca mais severos intercalados por episódios de precipitação intensa e concentrada, padrão já observado na região do Grande ABC.Esses cenários orientaram a priorização de áreas e a definição de medidas estruturais e não estruturais. Ao utilizar modelos climáticos regionais e dados de instituições como o IPT e o Cemaden, o PMRR transcendeu uma resposta reativa a desastres pontuais e passou a incorporar uma visão adaptativa de longo prazo. Isso permitiu que o município antecipasse vulnerabilidades futuras, como a pressão sobre recursos hídricos e a maior exposição de comunidades em áreas de risco, e desenvolvesse estratégias para mitigá-las, incluindo sistemas de alerta precoce e capacitação comunitária.Dessa forma, os cenários climáticos não apenas deram suporte técnico ao plano, mas também conferiram-lhe um caráter dinâmico, capaz de evoluir conforme novas projeções e dados monitorados surjam.

O Plano Municipal de Ação Climática de Contagem/MG foi elaborado com base em cenários climáticos e de emissões de gases de efeito estufa que conferiram consistência técnica às metas e ações propostas.

Cenários de emissões: O Inventário Municipal de GEE forneceu uma linha de base das emissões atuais, permitindo projetar cenários futuros “tendenciais” (business as usual) e “mitigados” (com políticas de redução). Isso embasou a definição de metas de mitigação até 2030 e 2050, alinhadas às metas do Estado (PLAC-MG) e do Brasil (NDC).

Cenários climáticos: Foram utilizados dados de projeções de temperatura e precipitação do IPCC, além dos cenários regionais elaborados para Minas Gerais (PLAC-MG e estudos acadêmicos), indicando aumento da frequência de eventos extremos, estiagens mais prolongadas e maior risco de inundações. Essas informações ajudaram a priorizar ações de adaptação, como gestão de recursos hídricos, infraestrutura verde, controle de drenagem urbana e programas de saúde pública.

Consistência entre setores: A análise conjunta dos cenários permitiu relacionar vulnerabilidades locais (áreas sujeitas a alagamentos, ilhas de calor, insegurança energética) com oportunidades de mitigação (eficiência energética, mobilidade sustentável, gestão de resíduos).

Integração com planejamento municipal: Os cenários foram incorporados às políticas setoriais — como Plano Diretor, planos de mobilidade e saneamento — garantindo coerência entre os instrumentos de planejamento urbano e o plano climático.

Dessa forma, os cenários climáticos e de emissões serviram como base técnica para a priorização das ações, para o monitoramento dos resultados e para a atualização periódica do plano, garantindo alinhamento às melhores práticas internacionais (ICLEI, GCoM, C40).

The Energy Masterplan has been developed with the vision and strategic goals acting as
guiding principles. Energy reduction and decarbonisation opportunities have been identified
for the city based on eight key sectors. The sectors encompass activities across Galway City
which need to be targeted to reach the 51% emission reduction target. The scale of change
required across all sectors is not to be underestimated, and this plan recognises the need for
fundamental transformation to deliver on the level of ambition.
The key sectors; residential, municipal, commercial and industry, social housing, waste and

column23: A Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMAAC) foi fundamentada por cenários relacionados ao clima. As projeções climáticas apresentadas nesta estratégia foram elaboradas com base em dois modelos regionalizados para a Europa pelo projeto CORDEX5 a partir de dois modelos globais:• Modelo 1: SMHI-RCA4 (regional), a partir do MOHC-HadGEM2 (global);• Modelo 2: KNMI-RACMO22E (regional), a partir do ICHEC-EC-EARTH (global).A elaboração de projeções climáticas pressupõe a utilização de cenários de emissões de GEE como dados de entrada (inputs) nos modelos climáticos, designados por Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) (IPCC, 2013). Estes cenários representam possíveis evoluções socioeconómicas e respetivas emissões de GEE.A partir de uma concentração atual de CO2 que ronda as 400 ppm (partes por milhão) dois RCPs foram utilizados nesta estratégia:• RCP4.5: uma trajetória de aumento da concentração de CO2 atmosférico até 520 ppm em 2070, aumentando de forma mais lenta até ao final do século;• RCP8.5: uma trajetória de crescimento semelhante ao RCP4.5 até meio do século, seguida de um aumento rápido e acentuado, atingindo uma concentração de CO2 de 950 ppm no final do século.Os dados simulados a partir dos modelos climáticos são geralmente representados recorrendo a grelhas com uma resolução espacial associada à capacidade de cada modelo em representar adequadamente os variados fenómenos atmosféricos e as massas terrestres e oceânicas. No caso dos modelos utilizados nesta estratégia esta representação foi de aproximadamente 11 km (0,11°).Foi selecionado um ponto da grelha dentro do município de Guimarães para o qual foram obtidos os valores diários das seguintes variáveis climáticas: Temperatura (máxima, média e mínima); Precipitação (acumulada); Velocidade do vento (máxima). De forma a apoiar o desenvolvimento da EMAAC, as projeções destas três variáveis foram analisadas até ao final do século, para os seus valores médios anuais e anomalias (potenciais alterações), relativamente ao clima atual.Desta forma, para cada uma destas variáveis climáticas foram calculadas médias mensais, sazonais e anuais, assim como alguns indicadores relativos a eventos extremos. De forma a identificar as potenciais alterações (anomalias) projetadas entre o clima atual e futuro, todos os cálculos foram simulados para três períodos de trinta anos (normais climáticas): 1976-2005 (clima atual); 2041-2070 (médio-prazo); 2071-2100 (longo-prazo).

column30: Guimarães preserva o património cultural e natural, reforçando a resiliência, caminhando para a neutralidade climática e pretendendo ser uma cidade-planeta com um futuro seguro para o clima. No âmbito da Governação do Ecossistema de Guimarães 2030, Guimarães tem uma Política Climática desde 2015, que inclui a Estratégia Municipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas (EMACC). Recorrendo a evidência científica, compreende uma avaliação sistemática dos riscos e vulnerabilidades climáticas, considerando vários cenários: frequência e intensidade de eventos extremos, conjunturas geopolíticas e socioeconómicas. Guimarães é uma referência nacional e europeia na Adaptação Climática, um exemplo inspirador para outras cidades. Membro da Missão da UE: Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas e Missão Cidades da UE: 100 Cidades Inteligentes e com Impacto Neutro no Clima até 2030. Os efeitos das alterações climáticas globais já são evidentes a nível local, sendo necessária uma adaptação mais rápida e abrangente. A nossa equipa climática adquiriu aptidões e competências relevantes para avaliar os riscos e as vulnerabilidades climáticas sistemáticas (metodologia ADAM). A última avaliação foi efectuada em 2023. A ação climática é dinâmica e pró-ativa. Através da reavaliação de 2022, a seca e os deslizamentos de terras foram acrescentados aos impactos anteriores. Paralelamente à avaliação técnica, os cidadãos foram inquiridos sobre os eventos e impactos climáticos que mais os preocupavam. Os resultados foram coerentes com a avaliação técnica. A ação climática é sistémica. Todos os sectores económicos foram avaliados. Através do Climate City Contract, co-criado com as partes interessadas e os cidadãos locais, promovemos um sentimento inclusivo de pertença e responsabilidade. Os projetos económicos incluem novas iniciativas empresariais que, estruturalmente, complementam o desenvolvimento endógeno sustentável e são apoiadas por regulamentação específica. Continuaremos a fornecer uma abordagem holística e sistémica à mudança, melhorando as nossas capacidades de adaptação, antecipando a ação climática, dando prioridade à inovação não tecnológica e à co-criação, construindo uma adaptação inteligente e baseada na ciência, integrando as lições aprendidas, capitalizando soluções vantajosas para todos e integrando os dados à medida que estes ficam disponíveis.

No Plano Intermunicipal de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas e Prevenção e Gestão de Riscos do Ave (PIAAC) assume-se um novo e alargado conceito de adaptação, nomeadamente a capacidade de “navegar” os processos de transformação, construindo ativamente uma sociedade pós-carbono e reforçando a resiliência sócio ecológica do território: “Ave em Transição”.
Estratégia: neste plano o desígnio da Neutralidade carbónica é assumido simultaneamente com a necessidade de reduzir vulnerabilidades, integrando-se mitigação e adaptação às alterações climáticas. Promove-se desta forma a antecipação face à necessidade anunciada de estabelecer roteiros intermunicipais de redução de emissões de gases com efeito de estufa.
Assume-se a inevitabilidade de um colapso (planeado ou não), traduzido na mudança rápida e profunda dos modelos sociais e económicos, procurando-se criar as condições para reforçar a resiliência do território, incluindo a sua autonomia enquanto bio-região e o potenciar dos recursos endógenos. A emergência climática é plenamente integrada, assumindo-se a radicalidade das ações exigidas.
Aposta-se num modelo de cocriação, assente num amplo processo de capacitação e mobilização social que reforce e amplie as dinâmicas em curso. Assume-se o otimismo e a imaginação como ferramentas essenciais para atingir os objetivos propostos e ultrapassar os atuais impasses. Para além da transformação ao nível técnico e político, assume-se a necessidade de mudanças ao nível pessoal.
Procura-se responder ao desafio de reduzir desigualdades e reforçar a justiça climática, em particular ao nível do território e da defesa dos que se encontram em situações de maior fragilidade. Pretende-se explorar oportunidades de financiamento e sinergias entre atores e suas iniciativas.

column23: O combate às alterações climáticas foi definido como sendo de elevada prioridade e importância pela União Europeia. Para o período pós 2012, Portugal comprometeu-se com o objectivo de limitar o aumento das emissões de gases com efeito de estufa, para os sectores não abrangidos pelo Comércio Europeu de Licenças de Emissão (CELE), em 1% em relação a 2005 no período entre 2013 e 2020. Este compromisso foi definido no âmbito do Pacote Energia - Clima, lançado pela União Europeia em 2008. Neste Pacote foram definidas as metas 20-20-20. Em 2008 a Comissão Europeia lançou o movimento do Pacto de Autarcas. Este movimento tem como principal objectivo subscrever e apoiar os esforços desenvolvidos pelas autoridades locais na implementação de políticas de energia sustentável. Os signatários do Pacto representam os municípios que de forma voluntária assumiram o compromisso de reduzir em pelo menos 20% as suas emissões de gases com efeito de estufa até 2020 alinhados com o Pacote de Energia - Clima da União Europeia. O plano surge nas ações decorrentes da implementação do Pacto de Autarcas a nível local, neste contexto Águeda tem aderido às iniciativas e desafios que a nível internacional são colocados aos municípios no sentido de promover a sustentabilidade ambiental de uma forma mais abrangente e compatível com a promoção da boa qualidade de vida dos seus habitantes.
