Neste contexto, destacam-se quatro fatores que devem ser reconhecidos e orientar qualquer processo de adaptação:▪ É um processo contínuo;▪ É um processo específico;▪ É um processo que deve envolver múltiplos agentes, compreender perspetivas e contextos individuais;▪ É um processo que deve ser ajustado temporalmente.A metodologia de referência a utilizar na elaboração do plano para as alterações climáticas é uma metodologia baseada e adaptada à realidade portuguesa a partir do modelo UKCIP Adaptation Wizard. Este modelo foi desenvolvido e testado pelo UK Climate Impacts Programme (UKCIP)1, entidade integrada no Environmental Change Institute na Universidade de Oxford, por forma a providenciar um instrumento robusto para planeamento em adaptação, constituindo uma ferramenta de apoio à decisão.Esta metodologia pressupõe a utilização de princípios básicos de tomada de decisão e análise de risco e permite determinar quais os riscos climáticos que devem ser tidos em conta aquando de uma decisão, assim como que opções de adaptação serão necessárias implementar para fazer face a esses riscos.As principais etapas deste processo são:▪ Etapa 1. Preparação▪ Etapa 2. Identificação de vulnerabilidades climáticas atuais▪ Etapa 3. Vulnerabilidades climáticas futuras▪ Etapa 4. Opções de adaptação▪ Etapa 5. Monitorização- Avaliação (multicritério, participativa) das opções de adaptação em relação aos objetivos inicias;- Integração da adaptação na estratégia intermunicipal;- Definição do processo de implementação, monitorização e revisão. Quanto ao custo e dado o alargado horizonte temporal, assim como o elevado número de medidas incluídas no plano, não se prevê o custo global, já as medidas têm uma definição qualitativa quanto ao investimento que representa a sua implementação. O custo indicado é o de elaboração do plano.

column23: As Alterações Climáticas são uma realidade com impactos ambientais, sociais e económicos. Neste contexto, reduzir significativamente as emissões de Gases com Efeito de Estufa (GEE) através da construção de uma economia de baixo carbono é uma prioridade. Uma aposta em inovação e no investimento em tecnologias verdes permitirá alcançar uma sociedade de baixas emissões e, simultaneamente, impulsionar a economia, criar empregos e reforçar a competitividade do município. O Município de Águeda tem conduzido projetos inovadores na temática da sustentabilidade ambiental e climática, a par de um desenvolvimento evidente ao nível social e económico. No dia 12 de novembro de 2008, o Município de Águeda aderiu ao Pacto de Autarcas, assumindo o compromisso de reduzir as emissões de CO2 no seu território em 33% até 2020. Atualmente, o Município pretende atualizar este compromisso, adotando uma abordagem integrada à atenuação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas e assumindo o objetivo de ultrapassar a meta de redução de 55% de emissões de CO2 até 2030, a redução da pobreza energética e a criação de uma visão a longo prazo para alcançar a neutralidade climática até 2050, através de uma transição justa. De modo a alcançar as metas propostas o município desenvolveu o presente Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e o Clima (PAESC), o qual define diversas medidas de mitigação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas. O objetivo de redução de emissões de CO2 no território concelhio deverá ser alcançado através de um aumento da eficiência energética e de uma produção e utilização mais limpa da energia, tal como formulado no Pacote de Medidas da União Europeia sobre o Clima e as Energias Renováveis. Na vertente de adaptação às Alterações Climáticas são propostas ações com o objetivo de adaptação ou mitigação dos efeitos destas alterações. Estas ações vão desde ações de educação e sensibilização ambiental, adoção de sistemas de monitorização, avaliação e vigilância, reforço de infraestruturas verdes e gestão sustentável da floresta, ordenamento e gestão dos recursos fluviais e espécies florestais e agrícolas, controlo de pragas e doenças, entre outros. Assim, há um conjunto de medidas transversais e específicas que são planeadas de forma a maximizar os resultados, criando-se sinergias entre os vários atores, planos, atividades e intervenções previstas.Plano em aprovação

column30: A adoção de uma estratégia de mitigação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas é um elemento central no planeamento urbano, quer com o objetivo de promover um desenvolvimento mais sustentável, com menores impactes, quer com o objetivo de aumentar a resiliência local aos impactes das Alterações Climáticas, atuais e a médio-longo prazo. Com a elaboração e implementação do Plano de Ação para a Energia Sustentável e o Clima do Município de Águeda pretende-se identificar políticas e medidas de mitigação e de adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, de modo a alcançar uma redução de GEE, redução da pobreza energética e neutralidade climática. Como ações de mitigação referem-se a iniciativas de melhoria da eficiência energética, de aumento de produção renovável e outras com potencial de redução das emissões de GEE. Estas ações devem abranger os diversos setores consumidores de energia e com potencial de intervenção no território concelhio, tais como edifícios públicos, de serviços e residenciais, indústria, transportes e agricultura e pecuária, entres outros que se revelem relevantes. Ao nível das ações de adaptação, as mesmas são definidas de acordo com as especificidades e necessidades de cada território, tomando como referência os riscos e vulnerabilidades às Alterações Climáticas a que o município estará sujeito. Destacam-se, assim, como áreas prioritárias de intervenção, no âmbito da estratégia de adaptação, os setores da agricultura, florestas e pescas, a indústria, a proteção da biodiversidade, a gestão de infraestruturas de energia e de transportes, o turismo, o ordenamento do território, a gestão de recursos hídricos, serviços de saúde humana e segurança de pessoas e bens. Adicionalmente, e considerando que esta é uma problemática com impactes não só ambientais, mas também sociais e económicos, é essencial o envolvimento de toda a comunidade (empresas e serviços públicos, instituições financeiras, cidadãos, associações e cooperativas, instituições de educação e investigação, pólos de inovação e desenvolvimento, ...) no desenvolvimento de um plano de ação e politicamente endossado e participado. O Município de Águeda pretende mobilizar atores locais e contribuir para a mitigação e adaptação às Alterações Climáticas do seu território e melhorar a sua resposta às vulnerabilidades atuais e futuras. Pelas medidas e horizonte temporal não se define o investimento.

Os cenários relacionados ao clima desempenham um papel fundamental na construção da consistência e relevância do Plano de Ação Climática de Braga (PMAC-Braga). Ao considerar as projeções climáticas e os impactos esperados, o Município de Braga tem a capacidade de elaborar estratégias informadas que não apenas respondem aos desafios atuais, mas também se antecipam a futuras adversidades.

A base do PMAC-Braga é construída a partir de uma análise detalhada dos riscos climáticos específicos que afetam a região, como ondas de calor, inundações, secas e eventos meteorológicos extremos. Essas análises são realizadas com o auxílio de modelos climáticos que projetam diferentes cenários futuros, permitindo identificar vulnerabilidades e priorizar ações de adaptação e mitigação. Por exemplo, as projeções indicam um aumento nas temperaturas médias e uma maior frequência de eventos climáticos extremos, o que torna essencial a implementação de medidas de resiliência nas infraestruturas urbanas e na gestão dos recursos hídricos.

Além disso, a consideração de cenários climáticos permitiu que o PMAC-Braga fosse alinhado com as metas nacionais e internacionais, como os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e os compromissos do Acordo de Paris. O plano não apenas define metas ambiciosas de redução de emissões de gases com efeito de estufa, mas também estabelece ações concretas para aumentar a capacidade de resposta da cidade aos impactos das mudanças climáticas.

A utilização de cenários climáticos também contribui para a sensibilização da comunidade e para o envolvimento dos cidadãos. Ao comunicar claramente os riscos climáticos e as ações necessárias para mitigá-los, Braga fomenta uma maior participação pública e um senso de responsabilidade coletiva na luta contra as alterações climáticas.

Assim, a análise de cenários climáticos não só fornece a base científica para as decisões do PMAC-Braga, mas também garante que o plano seja dinâmico e adaptável. Com esta abordagem, Braga posiciona-se como uma cidade proativa, preparada para enfrentar os desafios climáticos de forma eficaz e sustentável, promovendo um futuro resiliente e sustentável para todos os seus habitantes.

O PMAC-Braga representa uma atualização significativa da estratégia do Município para enfrentar as alterações climáticas e promover a mitigação através da eficiência energética. Este plano, que é o quarto desenvolvido nos últimos 12 anos, reflete o compromisso contínuo da cidade em adaptar e aprimorar suas abordagens. O PMAC-Braga abrange setores estratégicos essenciais para enfrentar as alterações climáticas e promover o desenvolvimento sustentável.
1. Energia
Este setor concentra-se na promoção de fontes renováveis, como solar e eólica, e na eficiência energética. O objetivo é aumentar a utilização de energias limpas e reduzir a dependência de combustíveis fósseis para diminuir as emissões de gases com efeito de estufa.
2. Transporte e Mobilidade
Braga visa promover alternativas sustentáveis, como transporte público e bicicletas. A criação de infraestruturas para veículos elétricos e o incentivo a modos de transporte não poluentes são fundamentais para reduzir a pegada de carbono do setor.
3. Gestão de Resíduos
O plano inclui ações para minimizar a geração de resíduos e aumentar a reciclagem. Programas de compostagem e campanhas de sensibilização buscam envolver a comunidade na gestão eficiente dos resíduos.
4. Agricultura e Uso do Solo
A promoção de práticas agrícolas sustentáveis e a gestão adequada do solo são vitais para aumentar a resiliência climática. O reflorestamento e a proteção de ecossistemas contribuem para o sequestro de carbono.
5. Água
A gestão dos recursos hídricos é uma prioridade, focando na conservação e eficiência. O plano busca garantir a resiliência a eventos climáticos extremos, assegurando a disponibilidade de água potável.
6. Saúde e Bem-Estar
O PMAC considera os impactos climáticos na saúde pública. Medidas para melhorar a qualidade do ar e a segurança alimentar são essenciais para proteger a saúde dos cidadãos.
7. Infraestruturas Urbanas
A adaptação e melhoria das infraestruturas urbanas são cruciais para resistir a eventos climáticos extremos, garantindo a segurança e funcionalidade da cidade.
8. Edudação e Sensibilização
A educação e sensibilização sobre sustentabilidade e alterações climáticas visam promover uma cultura de responsabilidade ambiental.
9. Biodiversidade e Ecossistemas
A proteção da biodiversidade e a recuperação de habitats naturais são essenciais, promovendo o uso sustentável dos recursos naturais e seu papel na resiliência climática.

column30: The Resilient Cambridge Plan is the City's roadmap to reduce the risks from climate change and prepare the community for impacts that cannot be avoided. The Plan focuses on the threats from increasing temperature, precipitation, and sea level rise. Using projections to 2030 and 2070 based on the best available science, the City conducted a \'climate stress test\' -- the Climate Change Vulnerability Assessment (CCVA) -- to understand the potential impacts on the community if no action is taken. Starting with the CCVA as the technical foundation, two neighborhood plans for the Alewife area and The Port were developed to inform the citywide plan. Public meetings, workshops, focus groups, and surveys and a range of technical studies were conducted to generate the content for the Plan.Resilient Cambridge is organized around four categories of strategies: Closer Neighborhoods, Better Buildings, Stronger Infrastructure, and Greener City. The strategies are meant to work together and complement each other. Strategies are also recommended at the scales of sites and buildings, neighborhoods, city, and region. And there are roles for all parts of the community -- residents, institutions, government, and businesses. To be successful, everyone must do their part and collaborate.Please find more information about Resilient Cambridge here: https://www.cambridgema.gov/Departments/communitydevelopment/resilientcambridgeplan

column30: The City of West Palm Beach's \'Rethink Paradise: Sustainability Action Plan\' was first developed in 2012 and has since been updated in 2017 and 2020. The 2020 update provides a detailed report of what the City has done since the Plan was last updated in 2017. For the 2024 update, the City organized the mitigation and adaption recommendations using the LEED for Cities and Communities as the central organization theme for its sustainability program. For this Plan, the City and its team reviewed and analyzed over 400 adaptation and mitigation recommendations from five sources: (1) LEED for Cities guidance; (2) the Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy requirements; (3) the existing Rethink Paradise Recommendations last updated in 2017; (4) the Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact \'Climate Action Plan 2.0\', and (5) the City of West Palm Beach's \'Climate Resilience Vulnerability Assessment and Plan\'. The final list of recommendations was organized to identify overlaps across all the plans/recommendations evaluated and the City's overall goals to make one holistic and comprehensive guiding document that addresses climate change adaptation and mitigation strategies. \n\nThe 2024 update of the Rethink Paradise Plan will be taken to City Commission for formal adoption. The update is designed to address areas of need through 2050 to align with the City's Net Zero GHG Emissions goal, with a plan to review the plan every 3-5 years to make modifications as needed.

In the preparation of this report, the actual population growth rate of New Taipei City from 1996 to 2020 was referenced, and the population growth trend projected by the National Development Council was adopted to estimate the 2050 population. Considering the continuous expansion of the city's transportation network and its integration with neighboring cities into a shared living circle, a high-growth population scenario was selected.

According to the plan, by 2050, the residential and commercial sectors in New Taipei City will reduce natural gas and fuel oil consumption through full adoption of electronic stoves and electric water heaters. In the agriculture and fishery sectors, diesel used in fishing vessels will be replaced with biofuels and hydrogen energy. Waste treatment will achieve zero landfill by adopting biological decomposition methods such as black soldier flies and by utilizing biogas for power generation. The industrial sector will reduce emissions through energy transition strategies, including the conversion of coal-fired equipment to natural gas and the electrification of systems currently using natural gas or fuel oil. In the transport sector, decarbonization will be promoted through the electrification of vehicles and the use of clean energy. In the non-fuel combustion sector, hydrogen and biomass energy will be deployed to replace traditional fossil fuels.

As equipment becomes increasingly electrified, electricity demand in New Taipei City is expected to rise significantly by 2050, making power sector decarbonization a key to achieving net-zero emissions. However, realizing zero-carbon electricity will require the development of mature carbon capture technologies. Assuming that by 2050 the city's electricity generation mix consists of 80% renewable energy, 16% natural gas, and 4% hydrogen, the power emission factor is projected to decrease to 0.056 kg CO₂/kWh.

Taking into account the city's carbon sink capacity, emissions from both electric and non-electric sources, and future electricity demand, the city has analyzed the electricity usage patterns in the residential, commercial, industrial, and transportation sectors. The energy efficiency potential of various equipment types has been assessed in order to estimate future electricity consumption and carbon emissions, and to develop net-zero strategies and phased targets for all sectors leading up to 2050.

This report outlines strategies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 30% by 2030 and achieve net-zero by 2050 across five major sectors: residential and commercial, industrial, transportation, agriculture and forestry, and waste. Implementation is supported by four core enablers: (1) organizational governance - the New Taipei City Climate Change Response Steering Committee; (2) legal framework - the Autonomous Regulations for Climate Change Response Actions; (3) industrial development - smart city industrial clusters; and (4) financial support - green budgeting and the Climate Fund. These measures aim to build net-zero capacity and accelerate its progress.

Climate-vulnerable groups in the city include the homeless and elderly living alone. To protect them from extreme weather impacts, the city activates care mechanisms during high and low temperature periods.

New Taipei City's climate adaptation strategy is based on eight key adaptation areas and includes cross-analysis of future impacts such as extreme rainfall and temperatures. Relevant departments conduct monitoring, research, surveys, and implement locally appropriate adaptation actions. At the spatial planning level, zero-carbon concepts are integrated into national land use, regional, and urban development plans. The city also enhances disaster prevention and recovery capacity of essential infrastructure to build a resilient, livable New Taipei City.

A “Bali Net-Zero Demonstration Zone” has also been planned to implement 2030 net-zero strategies across the industrial, transportation, residential/commercial, and energy sectors. In addition to mitigation, the city will accelerate climate adaptation by prioritizing risk assessments and response measures for climate-vulnerable groups—such as the elderly and low-income households in the Bali Sanatorium—to ensure no one is left behind in the transition.

To strengthen policy alignment and international engagement, New Taipei City compiled the 'New Taipei 2050 Net-Zero Pathway and Climate Action White Paper 2024 Progress Report' in early 2025, ,based on existing climate policies and international urban net-zero blueprints. The report updates three key areas—overview, achievements, and future strategies—incorporating 2024 policy outcomes, with consolidated bilingual content and optimized layout to enhance communication and global engagement.

1. Enhancing Risk Assessment Based on Climate Change Simulation Data
The New Taipei City Adaptation Implementation Plan utilizes climate data provided by the Taiwan Climate Change Projection and Information Platform (TCCIP), integrating it with local baseline information for analysis. Spatial risk interpretation is conducted through geographic overlay techniques to assess potential risks under climate change scenarios.
In addition, the plan references the Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) released by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in 2021, incorporating Global Warming Levels (GWLs) and Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) as scientific foundations for improving the city's risk assessment and adaptation planning.

2. Prioritizing Adaptation Actions Based on Quantified Scenarios
The plan comprehensively evaluates three key factors—hazard, exposure, and vulnerability—while integrating projected changes in the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events based on climate simulation data. These results serve as the core basis for disaster risk assessment.
By quantifying future climate scenarios into specific risk levels, the city establishes priorities for adaptation actions. This approach strengthens the systematic and forward-looking nature of decision-making and facilitates the deployment and integration of cross-sector adaptation strategies.

3. Establishing a Rolling Adjustment and Monitoring Mechanism
Given the high uncertainty of climate change, the city has established a rolling mechanism for regular review and adjustment. Action items are revised in a timely manner based on the latest climate simulation results and disaster experiences.
In line with Article 20, Paragraph 2 of the Climate Change Response Act, the progress, inventory, and adjustment results of the adaptation implementation plan shall be compiled annually into an “Adaptation Action Plan Performance Report,” to be reviewed by the Climate Change Response Steering Committee and made publicly available.

column23: The annual average temperature of Easton is currently 49.36°F (based on data from 1981-2010) with an observed change of 1.2°F (compared to historical data from 1951-1980). With the effects of climate change, projected changes are expected to range from 2.15°F to 5.91°F (these are based on the difference between current conditions and the projected period 2041-2070). Easton could see an increase of 40 to 50 days with temperatures exceeding 90°F. It is expected that extreme heat events that have been observed every 20 years could happen as often as every two to four years. Impacts will continue into the foreseeable future due to the buildup of emissions in the atmosphere that last for hundreds of years, thus it is important to take action as soon as possible. The City of Easton used the U.S. Climate Explorer to identify likely changes from today through 2090 and included a graph to indicate that average daily temperatures have been increasing and will continue to rise through 2100 under both lower and higher emissions scenarios but much more dramatically under higher emissions, which could impact agriculture, public health, and other sectors of the community.

column30: This Climate Action Plan demonstrates the progress already made the actions that are being taken and will evolve to include more actions and more citywide involvement to deliver our ambition. The actions identified cover the eight priority themes of the Climate Change Strategy and have formed the basis for the developing Action Plan which sits alongside the Climate Change Strategy to deliver on its goals and targets. The actions identified are based on the work carried out by Leeds University (Net Zero Roadmap for York), pathway modelling by Anthesis, best practice guidance from the Local Government Association, recommended actions for Local Authorities by Friends of the Earth, stakeholder workshops and officer engagement. The Action Plan is a live document, which will be formally reviewed annually. It will change over time in response to the reporting and feedback mechanisms that track progress against our ambition, as well as changes in technology and Governmental policy. Our Action Plan has now been reviewed, receiving input from York Climate Commission, Council Teams and other stakeholders. From the previous list of 160 actions, 29 have been completed and 86 have been consolidated or removed. New actions have been added, with particular emphasis to include even more adaptation actions following our commitment to be a 'Climate Ready' city. The current Action Plan attached covers both adaptation and mitigation actions, however in the new plan they are designated 'A' for adaptation, 'M' for mitigation' or 'A/M' for both ensure this is explicit. Overall, the Action Plan is more concise, but with a broader scope, individual actions have been assessed for deliverability and assigned a responsible owner. The updated Action Plan will be published later this year. The decarbonisation of York and associated actions in the Action Plan have been calculated with the support of the Local Area Energy Plan (3.8 billion). The complete cost of the plan has not been calculated, however as seen in the attachments, each action has been designated a high to low cost score in order to illustrate the relative cost of each action.

column23: Climate-related scenarios have substantially informed the Vijayawada Climate Resilient City Action plan (CRCAP) through both quantitative and qualitative approaches. The CRCAP utilized Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) to assess future climate projections across multiple temperature scenarios, including RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5, with time horizons extending to 2079. These scenarios analyze temperature increases ranging from 0.9-2.2°C for maximum temperature and 0.8-2.0°C for minimum temperature, effectively addressing pathways aligned with varying degrees of global warming including scenarios both within and exceeding 1.5°C and 2°C targets. The plan also employed Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) methodology adapted from the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report to forecast population growth and urbanization patterns, examining three urbanization scenarios—rapid, moderate, and slow—with Vijayawada adopting the moderate pathway based on comparative analysis of historic and projected growth trends.\n\nFor emissions scenario planning, the plan developed three different quantitative pathways using ICLEI South Asia's Net-zero GHG Emissions Tool: a Business-as-Usual (BAU) projection showing emissions rising to 5.32 million tCO2e by 2047, a Progressive Action Scenario achieving 56% reduction from BAU, and a Net-zero Pathway targeting 89% reduction by 2047. These scenarios integrate composite economic and population growth rates, sector-specific assumptions for energy, transportation, residential, commercial, industry, and municipal services, with interim milestones set for 2030 and 2040. The scenario analysis was both quantitative—relying on numerical modeling of emissions, temperature projections, and precipitation changes—and qualitative, incorporating climate fragility statements that assess how various RCP scenarios would impact urban systems such as water supply, wastewater management, stormwater management, built environment, solid waste management, transportation, urban greening and biodiversity and health through likelihood and consequence assessments.

column30: Vijayawada's climate action prioritization employed a multidimensional assessment framework that incorporated climate resilience benefits, feasibility considerations, and implementation timelines to systematically rank proposed interventions across eight sectors. The plan identifies and prioritizes actions based on three primary factors: their benefits for climate resilience, feasibility including technical, political, and financial aspects, and the time required for these actions to yield results (short-term by 2030, medium-term by 2040, and long-term by 2047). The feasibility assessment evaluates each intervention based on technical aspects, financial aspects, and political aspects. The plan further prioritizes actions that offer significant climate resilience benefits, have high feasibility, and deliver quick impact timeframes, especially those supported by readily available technology and financing options. The Stakeholder Committee was instrumental in this prioritization process through participatory consultations, analyzing and ranking sectoral strategies and actions.\n\nAdditionally, the plan incorporates a targeted prioritization matrix that assesses climate resilience potential by evaluating actions' capacity to contribute to urban system redundancy and flexibility, their role in informing future planning, their responsiveness to sudden shocks or stresses, and their potential to reduce GHG emissions. This systematic assessment established the priority of various actions across different sectors, with actions evaluated for their \'climate resilience benefits,\' characterized as \'High,\' \'Very High,\' or \'Medium,\' and periods to realize impact classified as \'Short,\' \'Medium,\' or \'Long\'. For instance, in the water supply sector, actions such as local water resource management are prioritized as short-to-medium-term interventions with high climate resilience benefits, while reducing non-revenue water is prioritized as a medium-term initiative with very high climate resilience benefits. The plan demonstrates how feasibility assessments across technical, financial, and political dimensions influence prioritization, with sectors where city power and capacity are assessed as low to high, such as energy and public transportation, recognized as requiring enhanced collaboration and coordination across multiple institutions for effective implementation.

The Beşiktaş Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2024) has been directly shaped by climate-related scenarios assessing the district's vulnerabilities and risks. These scenarios, supported by national and metropolitan-level data, informed both mitigation and adaptation measures.

Temperature Increases & Heatwaves: Climate models projecting rising average temperatures and more frequent heatwaves have guided strategies such as improving energy efficiency in buildings, promoting green roofs and facades, and expanding urban green spaces to mitigate the urban heat island effect.

Flooding & Sea Level Rise: Scenarios of more intense rainfall and potential sea level rise have influenced infrastructure planning. Key measures include upgrading drainage systems to manage stormwater more effectively and reinforcing coastal areas to address long-term flood risks.

Drought & Water Stress: Anticipated risks of seasonal drought and water scarcity have informed water efficiency policies, rainwater harvesting initiatives, and the improvement of wastewater treatment facilities, ensuring more sustainable water use.

These scenarios were used not only to guide emissions reduction targets but also to prioritize adaptation actions that strengthen resilience. By embedding these climate projections into the SECAP and aligning them with the 2025-2029 Strategic Plan, Beşiktaş Municipality ensures that its policies, infrastructure investments, and community engagement strategies are robust against future climate risks.

The Beşiktaş Climate Action Plan (SECAP, 2024) provides a comprehensive strategy to mitigate climate change and adapt to its impacts. The plan focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, promoting energy efficiency and renewable energy, supporting sustainable transportation, and making the district's infrastructure more resilient to climate risks. It also emphasizes public engagement and awareness-raising as cross-cutting elements to ensure the inclusiveness of climate action.

Mitigation Strategies:

Energy Efficiency Projects: Actions to improve energy performance of residential, commercial, and municipal buildings through insulation, efficient lighting, and smart energy systems.

Renewable Energy Use: Installation of solar panels on municipal and other buildings, with policies to encourage wider adoption of renewable energy across the district.

Sustainable Transportation: Expanding electric vehicle charging infrastructure, supporting the transition to electric municipal fleets, and promoting active mobility solutions such as cycling.

Adaptation Strategies:

Resilient Infrastructure: Upgrading drainage systems and reinforcing coastal areas to address flood and sea-level rise risks.

Water Management: Enhancing water efficiency, wastewater treatment, and drought preparedness measures.

Public Awareness and Capacity Building: Community trainings, awareness campaigns, and participatory activities to engage residents and stakeholders.

Emergency and Disaster Preparedness: Integration with the Beşiktaş Disaster and Emergency Plan (BADOP) to strengthen readiness against climate-related hazards.

Energy-Related Strategies:

Reducing overall energy consumption by conducting energy audits in public facilities.

Promoting sustainable energy practices across sectors to ensure long-term reductions in emissions and reliance on fossil fuels.

column30: El documento, “Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático 2025-2030 de la Comuna de Independencia” (PACCC), constituye una herramienta clave para enfrentar los desafíos climáticos del territorio. En él se realiza un diagnóstico actualizado de los riesgos climáticos presentes en la comuna, se presenta la versión más reciente del Inventario Comunal de Gases de Efecto Invernadero y se proponen medidas concretas de adaptación y mitigación frente al cambio climático. Esta actualización se enmarca en la implementación de la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático, que establece en su artículo 12 la obligación de los municipios de incorporar un diagnóstico climático, identificar fuentes de financiamiento, describir detalladamente las medidas propuestas y asegurar su monitoreo, reporte y verificación. Asimismo, el documento responde al nuevo escenario climático actual, considera los proyectos recientemente implementados en la comuna y se articula con los lineamientos del Plan de Acción Regional de Cambio Climático de la Región Metropolitana de Santiago. \nEste documento actualiza el “Plan de Acción para el Clima y la Energía Sostenible: Estrategias de Mitigación y Adaptación al Cambio Climático 2020-2030” (PACES), elaborado en 2020 como una evolución del “Plan Local de Cambio Climático”, desarrollado en 2015 con el apoyo de la Asociación Adapt Chile. La actualización de 2020 fue posible gracias al respaldo de Adapt Chile, en representación de la Red de Municipios ante el Cambio Climático (RedMuniCC), en el marco del Programa Internacional de Cooperación Urbana para América Latina y el Caribe (IUC-LAC), específicamente bajo el componente 2: “Acción subnacional bajo la iniciativa del Pacto Global de Alcaldes por el Clima y la Energía (GCoM)”.\n

El Plan de Desarrollo Comunal (Pladeco) es una herramienta estratégica que orienta la gestión del territorio, funcionando como guía para coordinar las acciones del sector público y orientar la participación del sector privado. Su propósito central es articular las decisiones sobre proyectos y acciones específicas con los objetivos de desarrollo comunal a mediano y largo plazo, asegurando coherencia entre la planificación y la ejecución. En este sentido, se entiende como un instrumento político y técnico que define lineamientos estratégicos y establece un marco de acción común para todos los actores involucrados.
El proceso de elaboración del Pladeco combina información proveniente de fuentes secundarias —como estudios, investigaciones, cuentas públicas y documentos oficiales— con insumos primarios obtenidos a través de un diagnóstico participativo comunal. Este último se construyó mediante encuentros con habitantes de los cuatro territorios de la comuna, representantes de 26 unidades vecinales y 14 sectores poblacionales, además de funcionarios y funcionarias municipales. Este enfoque permite integrar distintas perspectivas y realidades en el diseño de las acciones, fortaleciendo la pertinencia y legitimidad del plan.
En el área de Medio Ambiente, se estableció el desarrollo de diversos proyectos relacionados con la adaptación al cambio climático, tales como la construcción y mejoramiento de áreas verdes, plazas, platabandas y centros deportivos, la consolidación y mejoramiento de la gestión de residuos, con énfasis en la disminución de su generación, y el fortalecimiento de la conciencia ambiental.
En el caso de Independencia, el Pladeco 2023-2028 se apoya en la experiencia del plan anterior (2015-2020), evaluando la vigencia de sus principales elementos y adaptándolos a los desafíos actuales. De esta manera, el nuevo plan se sustenta en un análisis integral que sistematiza información cualitativa y cuantitativa, garantizando que las estrategias y acciones propuestas respondan a las necesidades reales de la comunidad y orienten el desarrollo comunal hasta 2028.

column23:
The Concord Citywide Climate Action Plan (CAP was prepared in response to mandates from the State of California intended to reduce the emission of greenhouse gases statewide, because of their contribution to global climate change. 

Because the Concord Reuse Project Area Plan for the former Concord Naval Weapons Station would have allowed the City to meet GHG reduction targets in the short- and medium- term through development of the CRP area, the Citywide CAP focuses on actions that meet GHG reductions in the long- term, and additionally, provide community benefits. 

Arup consultants, the authors of the City's CAP detailed actions that addressed the projected climate change impacts in California and in Concord. Those projected impacts include direct, such as higher average temperatures, more frequent and intense heatwaves, more severe storm events, and sea-level rise; and secondary impacts, including increased air pollution, wildfires, droughts, flooding, higher electricity demand, disruption of native ecosystems, rising costs for agricultural, marine, and forest products, loss of Sierra snowpack, and intrusion of saltwater into groundwater supplies. 

Additionally, the consultants named projected impacts on human health and wellbeing, wildlife and habitat, infrastructure, food, electricity, insurance, and water quality and supply. 

The City prepared a baseline Greenhouse Gas Emissions Inventory for 2005, and forecast emissions inventories for 2020, 2030, and 2035. The purpose of the inventories was to understand the major sources of Concord's GHG emissions so that the CAP was able to target its approach to emissions reductions appropriately.

column23: Only sea level rise (SLR) and (more recently) water supply climate adaptation planning included scenarios. The former is included in this plan. The California Coastal Commission Guidance Document17 recommends evaluation of SLR impacts using a “scenario-based analysis.” This method seeks to understand how SLR and other drivers interact to threaten health, safety, and resources of coastal communities. Briefly, “the best available science (currently the 2012 NRC report) is used to identify a range of sea level rise scenarios including high, low, and intermediate projections.” Regional factors such as El Niño and extreme storm events that affect ocean levels, precipitation, and storm surge are then added to the model. For clarity, the SLR analysis focuses the hazard analysis on a subset of those scenarios, recommended by local and state experts (Table 3.1). Resulting sea levels are overlaid on geographic data including coastal elevation, infrastructure, and population information to produce hazard zones. The coastal climate vulnerability maps used for this study identify hazard zones for each climate scenario for the three planning horizons (2030, 2060, & 2100) under three different regional emissions scenarios (High, Medium, and Low). The resulting model allows planners to understand the range of impacts that may be expected and build an understanding of the overall risk posed by SLR. The Coastal Commission recommends all communities evaluate the impacts of the highest water level conditions that are projected to occur in the planning area. Local governments may also consider including higher scenarios (such as a 6.6 ft. [2m] scenario) where severe impacts to Coastal Act resources and development could occur from SLR. In addition to evaluating the worst-case scenario, planners need to understand the minimum amount of SLR that may cause impacts for their community, and how these impacts may change over time. CCWG's SLR hazard evaluation is intended to provide a predictive chronology of future risks to benefit local coastal planning and foster discussions with state regulatory and funding agencies. Estimates of the extent of assets at risk of various climate hazards were made using best available regional data. This approach allows planners to understand the full range of possible impacts that can be reasonably expected based on the best available science and build an understanding of the overall risk posed by potential future SLR.

column23: The Greenhouse Gas Reduction Program was developed based on current and projected communitywide greenhouse gas emissions for the City of Mountain View. The City developed a baseline emissions inventory for the 2005 operational year that addresses the following emission sectors: residential and nonresidential energy use, transportation, solid waste, water use, wastewater treatment, and off-road transportation. The baseline emissions inventory identified a communitywide emissions total of 796,987 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions (MT CO2e) in 2005. The Greenhouse Gas Reduction Program also provided business-as-usual emissions projections for the years 2020 and 2030 to understand the scale of reductions needed to achieve reduction goals. These emissions projections assume that historic trends describing energy and water consumption and waste generation will remain the same in the future, and that the only factor that will change is land use. According to these scenarios, communitywide emissions would increase by approximately 115,627 MT CO2e/yr (15%) between 2005 and 2020, and by approximately 204,035 MT CO2e/yr (26%) between 2005 and 2030. The magnitude of communitywide GHG emissions increases from 2005 to 2020 and 2030 is due primarily to anticipated future population and employment growth (and related consumption activity) in Mountain View, as well as land use changes recommended in the General Plan.
column30: The Greenhouse Gas Reduction Program includes strategies for into the following sectors: energy, transportation, solid waste, water, and carbon sequestration. Energy: The Energy Strategy recommends ways to increase energy efficiency in existing buildings, enhance energy performance for new construction, and increase use of renewable energy. The Waste Strategy increases waste diversion and recycling, reducing consumption of materials that otherwise end up in landfills. The Water Strategy promotes the efficient use and conservation of water in buildings and landscapes. The Transportation Strategy encourages transit, carpooling, walking, and bicycling as viable transportation modes to decrease the need to drive. The Carbon Sequestration Strategy uses street trees and urban forestry to capture and store carbon emitted from other sources. The GHG reduction measures impact various audiences, including the City of Mountain View, residents and community members, businesses and organizations, and industry.

column23: A 2050 emissions forecast was developed to inform development of the Climate Protection Roadmap. The 2050 emissions forecast was estimated by extrapolating from the 2020 and 2030 emission forecasts developed for the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Program and included a business-as-usual forecast, which accounted for activity growth and constant emission factors, and an adjusted business-as-usual forecast, which reflected a reduction in building sector emissions as a result of the implementation of the State of California's Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard. After the 2050 emission forecast was completed, an activity-based emissions impact analysis was performed to identify the types of macro-level changes in emissions generating activity that could create sizable reductions in community emissions. This high-level analysis provided insights into the ways emissions in the Energy, Transportation, and Solid Waste sectors could be reduced and the importance of different technology and other system transitions (e.g., energy efficiency improvements, fuel switching, increased waste diversion, etc.). In this analysis, it became clear that fuel switching and enhanced low-carbon and renewable energy generation would be critical to achieving the 2050 GHG emission reduction target. The Sustainability Action Plan 4 (SAP-4) was developed to help the City achieve its greenhouse gas emission reduction goal of 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. Staff developed SAP-4 based on the recommendations in the Environmental Sustainability Task Force 2 Final Report and Sustainability Strategic Plan, both of which used intensive stakeholder processes involving outreach to the Mountain View community and City staff. Among its proposed 81 new actions and 79 already-approved actions, SAP-4 contains both smaller projects that provide GHG reductions in the near term, and larger, longer-term infrastructure projects that may not have immediate impact but will yield significant GHG reductions over time. While achieving the City's short- and long-term GHG reduction targets remains the overall focus of the City's sustainability program, the proposed SAP-4 actions encompass the broader spectrum of sustainability. SAP-4 actions are organized around high-level goals in each sector, to highlight the synergies between different actions across City departments and to recognize the broad array of interdependent policies and programs needed to achieve the City's sustainability goals.

column23: The Shoreline Regional Park Community Sea Level Rise Capital Improvement Program (2022) is based on a \'High Sea Level Rise Scenario\' that will develop improvements to provide 100-year flood protection with 42 inches of sea level rise by Year 2070. This scenario is based on sea level rise projections developed by the California Ocean Protection Council (OPC). The 2018 State of California Sea Level Rise Guidance (OPC 2018) by the California Ocean Protection Council (OPC) presented updated sea level rise projections for various global greenhouse gas emissions scenarios bounded by a “business-as-usual” (high emissions) scenario and a “significant emissions reductions” (low emissions) scenario. The OPC 2018 guidance projected a 66% probability that the sea level rise in year 2070 will be at or below 23 inches and considered this to be a low-risk aversion scenario. It also projected a 0.5% probability that the sea level rise in 2070 will be at or above 42 inches and considered this to be a medium-to-high risk aversion scenario. The increased sea level rise projection is a reflection of the increasing rate of ice loss from Greenland and the Antarctic ice sheets, improved scientific understanding and modeling of sea level rise, and change in sea level rise with consideration of different greenhouse gas emission scenarios.
column30: The City of Mountain View (City) developed a Sea Level Rise Capital Improvement Program (SLR CIP) for the Shoreline Community in 2012, documented in the Shoreline Regional Park Community Sea Leve Rise Study Feasibility Report and Capital Improvement Program report (2012 Study). The SLR CIP presented a program to address long-term flood inundation impacts to the City due to a combination of the projected sea level rise, coastal flooding from South San Francisco Bay, and fluvial flooding from Permanente Creek and Stevens Creek. The program is designed to provide a coastal barrier to reduce the risk of Bay tide flood of the City shoreline, and minimize flooding due to overtopping and backwater from Permanente Creek and Stevens Creek. Based on the SLR CIP developed in 2012, the City has been working on projects in the SLR CIP. In addition, the City has been coordinating closely with members of other agencies working on regional efforts that affect the City's sea level rise adaptation efforts.The Shoreline Regional Park Community Sea Level Rise Capital Improvement Program Update (2022) is an incremental update of the 2012 Study. It updates the sea level rise projection and vulnerability of the City, and the projects in the SLR CIP, planning level cost estimates and implementation plan. With the latest projections, the planning year was updated from 2067 to 2070, which equates to an approximately 50-year planning horizon. The CIP includes fourteen projects to be initiated within 5-10 years that will help the City balance flood risk management needs of the City and the region as well as restore and preserve tidal marsh and wildlife habitats. The SLR CIP and sea level rise assessment will be monitored and updated every 5 years. More information can be found in the two attachments. The 2022 update to the CIP estimates that costs would range from $25.87M in a low-SLR scenario to $30.98M in a high SLR scenario.

column30: The Climate Action and Resilience Plan calls for carbon neutrality by 2050, 100% clean and renewable electricity by 2030, zero waste by 2050. CARP aims to reduce emissions across every sector and create a more livable community for all. It plans to increase the amount of public trees, protect private trees, maintain tree longevity across both sectors, diversify tree planting selection (to take into account anticipated future climate zone shifts due to a warming climate), and increase planting of native species, natural habitats, and green infrastructure, especially in areas where environmental justice issues have been identified. CARP aims to efficiently utilize public land to increase stormwater infiltration and detention while enhancing the primary use of the property. Per CARP, the City of Evanston is tracking and addressing energy and water usage through its Benchmarking Ordinance, and aims to increase water efficiency, decrease water usage, increase building efficiency, and decrease GHG emission in its Green Building Standard and passage of Building Performance Standards legislation. Water quality will be improved through the CARP goals to reduce emission and waste contaminants. The plan has aided in creating programs to begin to address residential and commercial building retrofits that encourage building electrification and other means of emission reductions, such as more energy efficient HVAC and appliances, better insulation, and other methods. It also supports updating the Green Building Ordinance to increase building performance standard and thus reduce stationary energy usage. CARP advises the transition to a circular economy, greatly reducing the amount of materials going to landfills and creating methane emissions. This comes in the form of bolstering recycling and compost capacity for the Evanston community. This includes diverting and recycling materials from the construction sector. Green space and biodiversity preservation are detailed in the CARP, in order to reduce urban head effects, provide access to natural areas for community members, and maintain a healthy ecosystem for all species. CARP aims to reduce vehicle miles traveled, while increasing trips made by walking, bicycling and transit. It also calls to increase use of electric vehicles, which decreases carbon emissions from vehicles and equipment.

column23: The Batangas City LCCAP was informed by climate risk and hazard scenarios generated from national and local assessments, including PAGASA climate projections, hazard maps, and vulnerability studies integrated into the CLUP and DRRM plans. These scenarios include sea-level rise, increased rainfall intensity, stronger typhoons, and temperature rise up to 2050, which guided the prioritization of coastal protection, flood control, and health-related adaptation actions. While the plan does not explicitly use global emission pathways (e.g., RCPs/SSPs), it applies medium- to high-emission scenario assumptions by planning for worst-case hazards such as 1-in-100-year floods and intensified storm surges. The LCCAP also uses qualitative scenario analysis by identifying future land use pressures, population growth, and industrial expansion that may amplify climate risks. These scenarios were applied in designing ecosystem-based adaptation, resilient infrastructure siting, and greenhouse gas mitigation pathways to ensure that the plan is robust under different future climate conditions.

column30: The Batangas City Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) serves as the city's primary framework for mainstreaming climate change adaptation and mitigation into local governance, development, and sectoral planning. It identifies the city's climate risks such as flooding, sea-level rise, coastal erosion, and extreme weather events, and outlines actions to protect vulnerable populations, strengthen disaster preparedness, and promote ecosystem-based adaptation. On the mitigation side, it integrates measures from the GHG Management Framework Plan, SEPPP, and LEECP, focusing on renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable transport, and waste management. The LCCAP also institutionalizes monitoring and evaluation mechanisms through the City ENRO and partner offices, and emphasizes multi-stakeholder engagement with barangays, civil society, academe, and the private sector. By aligning with national climate policies and international commitments, the LCCAP positions Batangas City as a resilient, low-carbon, and sustainable urban center.

column23:
The CLUP explicitly integrates Climate and Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA) into its land use policies and zoning decisions. Key climate-related hazards addressed include:
•	Seismic risks: microzonation to guide safe building heights, mandatory structural assessments, and stricter building permit enforcement.
•	Landslides and sinkholes: geotechnical validation, public building inspections, and relocation when engineering solutions are not feasible.
•	Flooding: use of rainfall projections (2023-2050), declaration of waterways as zones, drainage master plan, relocation of informal settlers, and nature-based solutions like Blue Walks (urban canals, stream restoration) and Green Walks (green streets).
•	Forest fires: integrated in multi-hazard strategies.
•	Urban heat islands & GHG emissions: creation of a Net Zero Zone in the central business district, energy efficiency measures, public mass transport promotion, and conversion of 95.8 ha of roads into greenbelts.
•	Life-support systems under stress: addressing deficits in forest cover, water resources, air quality, soil, green cover, and open spaces through stricter land use policies, hydrological studies, rainwater harvesting, and expanded agricultural areas.
In short: climate-related scenarios directly shaped zoning, density management, housing relocation, infrastructure safety, mobility planning, and environmental restoration.

The CLUP applies climate-responsive strategies across multiple sectors:
•	Housing & Settlements: Relocation of informal settlers from waterways, sinkholes, and hazard zones; provision of 28,123 housing units.
•	Infrastructure: Smart mobility infrastructure, green building standards, district-level facilities, and resilient public infrastructure.
•	Environment & Natural Resources: Forest expansion (29-30% cover by 2034), open and green spaces (60% goal by 2043), watershed protection, greenbelts, river rehabilitation, and urban agriculture.
•	Disaster Risk Reduction: Microzonation, multi-hazard indicators, evacuation areas, and redundancy in lifeline systems.
•	Energy & Transport: Energy efficiency, renewable energy, low-carbon mobility, mass public transport, and transit-oriented development.
•	Social Services: Education infrastructure (classroom deficits addressed by 2026), barangay facilities, healthcare, recreation, and cultural centers.
•	Tourism & Economy: Sustainable tourism carrying capacity, cultural mapping, creative districts, and MSME support.

Baguio City's community-level GHG (Greenhouse Gas) inventory has played a crucial role in informing and shaping its Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) by providing a clear, data-driven understanding of local emissions sources, trends, and mitigation opportunities. The inventory assessed emissions at the community level across major sectors such as transport, energy, waste, and land use and forestry. Transport emissions were measured from private vehicles, public transportation, and jeepneys, while energy emissions came from electricity consumption in households, commercial establishments, and government buildings. Waste-related emissions focused on methane from solid waste and open dumpsites, and land use and forestry emissions were analyzed in terms of deforestation, land conversion, and loss of green cover. By quantifying emissions from these sources, the inventory pinpointed priority areas for intervention in land use planning.

With sector-specific data, the CLUP incorporated strategies that directly address high-emission areas. Zoning for green spaces ensured that areas with high potential for carbon sequestration, like parks and forested zones, were prioritized and protected. Compact urban development was promoted to reduce vehicle emissions by re-evaluating sprawling residential areas and high-emission transport corridors.

Bacolod City, like other local government units in the Philippines, mainstreams climate-related scenarios into its Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) by conducting a thorough and science-based risk assessment. This process involves identifying climate hazards, assessing the city's vulnerability, and then developing targeted strategies for both adaptation and mitigation. The city's LCCAP is guided by national frameworks and policies, and its effectiveness is bolstered by partnerships and capacity-building initiatives.

The foundation of Bacolod City's LCCAP is a Climate & Disaster Risk Assessment (CDRA). This crucial step systematically analyzes the city's exposure and susceptibility to climate-related hazards. It helps planners understand which areas, sectors, and populations are most at risk from climate impacts, which focuses on key hazards like Flood, Storm Surge, Induced Landslide, and other geohazards.

By using science-based tools and data, including climate projections and historical disaster records, the city can create a risk profile that informs its planning, mainstreamed in LCCAP.

The Enhanced Local Climate Change Action Plan (ELCCAP) is a strategic roadmap 
designed to guide Cagayan de Oro City in addressing the challenges posed by climate 
change. 
The ELCCAP begins by recognizing the urgent need to address the adverse impacts of 
climate change on the community. It highlights the increasing frequency of extreme weather 
events, hazards such as floods, rain-induced landslides, storm surge and droughts, and the 
risks they pose to our infrastructure, ecosystems, and vulnerable populations in the present 
and future. These impacts require swift action to avert losses and reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions and adapt to a changing climate. 
At the core of the ELCCAP is a highlight of the city's vision for a sustainable environment 
and a resilient, progressive, and inclusive future. This vision guides our goals, relayed in a 
sectoral manner (Social, Economic, Environmental, infrastructure, and Institutional) with priorities for adaptation and mitigation measures. 
To achieve these goals, this action plan integrates a range of PPAs (Programs, Projects and 
activities that will be implemented across said sectors. In its implementation, we emphasize 
the importance of collaboration, engagement with local and national government agencies, 
community organizations, the academe, the private sector, and the residents. 
We recognize that climate change is a dynamic challenge; the ELCCAP underscores the 
city's commitment to adapt to the present and future evolving circumstances.

column23: Climate-related scenarios have substantially informed the Kakinada Climate Resilient City Action Plan (CRCAP) through both quantitative and qualitative approaches. The CRCAP applied Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) to assess future climate projections under RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5, with time horizons extending to 2080. These scenarios indicate temperature increases of 1.7-2.1°C for maximum temperature and 0.4-1.3°C for minimum temperature, capturing warming trajectories that align with and exceed 1.5°C and 2°C global thresholds. The plan also incorporated Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from IPCC AR6 to estimate population growth and urbanisation patterns, analysing rapid, moderate, and slow scenarios; Kakinada adopted the moderate pathway based on historic and projected demographic trends.\nFor emission scenarios, the CRCAP modelled three quantitative pathways using ICLEI South Asia's Net-zero GHG Emissions Tool: a Business-as-Usual (BAU) scenario projecting emissions rising to 1.4 million tCO₂e by 2047; a Progressive Action Scenario achieving a 54% reduction from BAU; and a Net-zero Pathway targeting an 83.8% reduction by 2047. These pathways integrate population and economic growth rates, sector-wise assumptions for energy, transport, residential, commercial, industry, and municipal operations, and include interim milestones for 2030 and 2040.\nThe scenario analysis combined numerical modelling of emissions, temperature and precipitation projections with qualitative assessments through climate fragility statements that evaluate how different RCP futures may impact urban systems such as water supply, wastewater, stormwater, solid waste management, built environment, transport, health, and biodiversity using likelihood and consequence assessments.

Kakinada's climate action prioritization follows a multidimensional assessment framework that evaluates climate resilience benefits, feasibility, and implementation timelines to systematically rank interventions across eight sectors. Actions were assessed using three primary dimensions: (i) climate resilience benefits, (ii) feasibility, considering technical, financial, and political factors, and (iii) time required to deliver impact, classified as short-term (2030), medium-term (2040), and long-term (2047). The feasibility analysis examined the maturity of technology, financial viability, institutional capacity, and political acceptability for each intervention.
Priority was given to actions offering high or very high climate resilience benefits, strong feasibility, and shorter impact horizons—particularly those supported by available technologies, existing programs, or accessible financing. The Stakeholder Committee played a key role through participatory consultations, reviewing and ranking actions across sectors to ensure alignment with local priorities.
A targeted prioritization matrix further strengthened this process by evaluating each action's potential to enhance system redundancy and flexibility, inform long-term planning, address acute climate shocks and chronic stresses, and reduce GHG emissions. Based on this assessment, actions were categorized by climate resilience benefit (Very High, High, or Medium) and expected timeframe for impact (Short, Medium, Long).
For example, in the water supply sector, local water resource management emerged as a short-to-medium-term priority with high resilience benefits, while reducing non-revenue water was identified as a medium-term action with very high benefits. The plan demonstrates how feasibility assessments across technical, financial, and political dimensions influence prioritization, with sectors where city power and capacity are assessed as low to high, such as energy and public transportation, recognized as requiring enhanced collaboration and coordination across multiple institutions for effective implementation.

column30: 31 of our actions came from the recommendations of our Climate Assembly. A Climate Assembly was held because we wanted to make sure that the local community were able to have a real say in decisions and were involved in shaping climate change projects that were right for them. FutureGov ran the assembly for us in Blackpool. This ensured the process was independent. Around forty Blackpool residents took part in the climate assembly, which was run entirely digitally due to the pandemic. An “open access” survey was created to gather intelligence from the population generally, giving the opportunity from those with various protected characteristics to give their view, with the intelligence gathered being used to develop the plan. An equality analysis ensured that consideration was given to those with vulnerabilities as part of the initial development phase. A separate youth climate group has been set up to bring together young people across Blackpool. A youth assembly was held by the group and this fed into the climate assembly sessions to make sure young people's voices are heard in the fight against climate change. A link to further information on Blackpool's Climate Assembly can be found here: https://www.blackpool.gov.uk/Residents/Planning-environment-and-community/Climate-emergency/Climate-assembly.aspx

The Local Area Energy Plan (LAEP) is aligned with the Scottish Government's Climate Change Targets (https://www.legislation.gov.uk/asp/2019/15/enacted). These targets are aligned with the Paris Agreement (keeping global temperature rise under 1.5 degrees or well below 2 degrees Celsius).

Climate scenarios have provided the analytical foundation for Dundee's LAEP, guiding the selection of technologies, timing of interventions, and prioritisation of actions. By stress-testing different futures, the plan ensures that Dundee's energy transition is resilient, equitable, and aligned with long-term climate goals.

1. Scenario-based modelling to 2045
The LAEP uses whole systems modelling to explore multiple decarbonisation pathways for Dundee's energy system, with scenarios covering: local resilience; high electrification; hydrogen integration; widespread hydrogen; business as usual; regulatory standards; and public-sector led. Each scenario tests different assumptions about technology uptake, energy demand, and policy implementation, helping to identify the most viable and resilient pathways for the city.

2. Climate scenario impacts on energy systems design
The modelling incorporates uncertainties from climate scenarios such as future energy demand shifts, technology cost trajectories and hydrogen readiness. These factors influence the feasibility and timing of interventions like heat networks, rooftop PV, EV charging infrastructure and building retrofits.

3. Integration with national climate policies
The LAEP is aligned with key Scottish climate strategies, including the Heat in Buildings Strategy, National Transport Strategy and the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2019. These policies provide the legislative and strategic context for the climate scenarios used in the LAEP.

column23: Dundee's Biodiversity Action Plan 2020-2030 is shaped by the city's recognition of the climate emergency and the interdependence between biodiversity and climate resilience. The plan acknowledges that climate change is a major driver of biodiversity loss, but also highlights how healthy ecosystems contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation. This dual role of biodiversity—as both vulnerable to and protective against climate impacts—is central to the plan's strategic approach. It positions biodiversity enhancement as a key component of Dundee's broader Climate Action Plan, aiming to build ecological resilience through better planning, habitat connectivity, and green infrastructure.\n\nClimate scenarios have informed the plan's emphasis on creating a resilient urban environment. For example, the strategy promotes the expansion and connection of species-rich greenspaces to buffer against climate-related stresses such as extreme weather and habitat fragmentation. It also integrates biodiversity considerations into local development frameworks, ensuring that future urban growth supports ecological sustainability. By aligning with national and international biodiversity targets—such as the Aichi Targets and Scotland's post-2020 biodiversity framework—the plan ensures that Dundee's local actions contribute meaningfully to global climate and biodiversity goals.

The Dundee Local Heat and Energy Efficiency Strategy (LHEES) Delivery Plan has been shaped by an understanding of climate scenarios in several key ways:

1. Alignment with Net Zero and Climate Emergency Goals
The LHEES is explicitly designed to support Dundee's response to the climate emergency and its commitment to achieving net zero emissions. Climate scenarios—particularly those projecting future emissions pathways and temperature increases—have informed the urgency and scale of interventions proposed in the plan.

2. Heat Decarbonisation and Energy Efficiency
The strategy prioritises heat decarbonisation and improved energy efficiency in buildings, which are central to mitigating climate impacts. These priorities reflect scenario-based modelling that shows the need to transition away from fossil fuels and reduce energy demand to meet long-term climate targets.

3. Health and Wellbeing Co-benefits
Climate scenarios often highlight increased risks to public health due to extreme weather and poor air quality. The LHEES responds to these risks by aiming to improve thermal comfort and indoor air quality, thereby enhancing residents' health and wellbeing.

4. Fuel Poverty and Economic Resilience
Understanding future climate risks also informs the plan's focus on alleviating fuel poverty and creating economic opportunities. By improving building performance and supporting local energy systems, the strategy aims to build resilience against energy price volatility and climate-related economic shocks.

Thessaloniki's pathways towards climate neutrality cross various sectors for which the Municipality of Thessaloniki has a specific vision with specific measurable targets been set. The sectors chosen for Thessaloniki are Electricity, Buildings and Heating, Transport & Logistics, Water & Waste management, Land Use and Green Infrastructure, as well as the one related to Smart Cities and Governance, which contribute reaching climate neutrality horizontally.
The objective of the Action Plan is the overall reduction of emissions from all the aforementioned sectors in 2030 at a level of 80% (taking into account 20% of residual emissions). Regarding residual emissions, the Municipality of Thessaloniki includes in the plan an integrated strategy in cooperation with stakeholders and plans/ implements mitigation actions, such as small-scale biogas energy production, carbon capture agriculture, as well as nature-based actions, such as the densification of urban green areas and the development of new urban areas.
Reaching the goal of climate neutrality requires, apart from finding financial programmes and tools, the creation of a Transition team to orchestrate the process of collaboration and coordination actions of multiple actors across sectors. Besides, the goal of transition to climate neutrality by 2030 does not consist only the vision of the Municipality but is the output of co-creation and cooperation between all stakeholders of the quadruple helix model (Public, Private, Research Community and Citizens) in planning and decision-making. Particular attention must be paid to interacting with civil society and consulting with them, so that the actions implemented have the
maximum possible acceptance, thus multiplying their impact and making society itself the agent of this transition. It is also proposed that an open forum for dialogue be set up to involve citizens in the decision-making process and monitor progress in implementing the actions.

The Nakuru County Energy Plan continues to provide a comprehensive framework to improve access to clean, affordable, and reliable energy while promoting sustainable energy practices across sectors. The plan emphasizes cross-cutting interventions, including household energy use, renewable energy adoption, energy efficiency, and clean technologies, targeting a shift away from traditional cooking, heating, cooling, and lighting practices in both households and institutions.

Complementing this, a county-wide clean cooking awareness campaign has reached households and communities, promoting improved jikos, low-emission cookstoves, and other sustainable cooking practices. The County is also exploring biogas investments to provide affordable and renewable energy options in rural areas, reducing dependence on firewood and charcoal.

These initiatives are further strengthened by the installation of 22 air quality monitors across the County, which provide real-time data on ambient pollution levels and inform the effectiveness of energy interventions. Combined, these actions not only advance climate mitigation and adaptation objectives but also improve public health, reduce emissions, and support community resilience. Ongoing collaborations with development partners, NGOs, and the private sector are critical for scaling these interventions, ensuring long-term sustainability and alignment with both national and county energy priorities.

Nakuru County has made significant investments to strengthen the Participatory Climate Risk Assessment (PCRA) process, with KES 309 million allocated to support capacity building, administrative functions, and the implementation of climate actions. A key component of this funding has been the training and capacity development of Ward Climate Change Planning Committees (WCCPCs), with 11 members per ward across all 55 wards. These capacity-building initiatives have equipped committee members with the knowledge, tools, and skills needed to identify, plan, and implement effective climate actions tailored to their local contexts.

In addition to capacity building, a portion of the funding has supported administrative operations and office infrastructure, ensuring the smooth coordination and oversight of climate initiatives at the ward and county levels. The financial resources have also enabled the execution of 52 climate actions across agriculture, water, and environment sectors, which include activities such as river riparian rehabilitation, promotion of climate-smart agriculture, clean water interventions, and forest restoration. These actions have strengthened local resilience, enhanced adaptive capacities, and fostered community-led climate solutions.

By investing in both people and projects, Nakuru County has created a foundation for evidence-based decision-making, monitoring, and adaptive management, ensuring that climate adaptation and mitigation strategies are effectively implemented, scaled, and aligned with county development priorities. The continued engagement of WCCPCs and community stakeholders ensures ownership, sustainability, and the potential for future partnerships to expand and deepen the impact of climate actions.

Debido a las precipitaciones, la comuna enfrenta impactos por inundaciones, manteniéndose
un mayor riesgo en dos tipos de terreno. Estas zonas incluyen los cauces y áreas aledañas, así
como las terrazas bajas y cauces estacionales que emergen ante eventos de lluvia más
intensos. Entre los cauces destacados se encuentran los esteros Quilapilún, Chacabuco,
Peldehue y Colina, además de las áreas de inundación generadas por la confluencia de los
esteros Lampa y Colina (Ilustre Municipalidad de Colina, 2015).
Se consideran también los procesos de remoción en masa, los cuales provocan derrumbes,
deslizamientos, flujos de detritos, rocas y/o corrientes de barro. Estos eventos ocurren
principalmente cuando hay precipitaciones muy intensas o desborde de los canales,
afectando los terrenos situados al borde de las laderas y sus alrededores. En la comuna, las
zonas que presentan peligro de remoción se ubican en zonas de relieve montañoso, conos
coluviales y de deyección, donde comúnmente se han presentado desprendimientos y flujos
de detritos y/o barro.
Los desprendimientos están vinculados a la pérdida de resistencia en los planos de
discontinuidad que se asocia tanto a la presencia de agua como al congelamiento que
incrementa la abertura de las superficies en la roca. Estos eventos se ven favorecidos por los
relieves de fuerte inclinación, fracturamiento superficial y disposición estructural inestable.
Los riesgos de este tipo se han observado en la laderas Occidentales del Cerro Las Moscas, en
dirección al pueblo de Colina, en la parte norte de los cerros Las Tórtolas y Tres Orejas y el
cerro Las Canteras en la parte sur de la comuna.

En el marco del Plan de Acción Comunal de Cambio Climático (PACCC) para Colina, se han
definido los medios de implementación necesarios para garantizar la efectividad de las
acciones propuestas, considerando las particularidades territoriales, sociales y ambientales de
la comuna. Estos medios se articulan con los instrumentos de gestión local, como el Plan de
Desarrollo Comunal (PLADECO), la Ordenanza Ambiental y las iniciativas de certificación
ambiental municipal, asegurando coherencia y pertinencia en la respuesta al cambio
climático.
Colina enfrenta desafíos específicos asociados a la escasez hídrica, la rápida expansión
urbana, la presión sobre los ecosistemas nativos y la necesidad de fortalecer la gestión de
riesgos ante eventos extremos como olas de calor, incendios forestales e inundaciones. Por
ello, los medios de implementación han sido diseñados para ser flexibles y adaptativos,
permitiendo responder a las contingencias y aprovechar las oportunidades que surgen del
desarrollo tecnológico y la colaboración público-privada.
La definición de estos medios se basa en la capacidad de la comuna para movilizar recursos,
coordinar a los distintos actores locales —incluyendo juntas de vecinos, organizaciones
rurales, empresas y servicios públicos— y fomentar la participación ciudadana en la toma de
decisiones. Las medidas propuestas integran soluciones de adaptación y mitigación, tales como la gestión eficiente del recurso hídrico, la promoción de energías renovables, la
restauración ecológica y el fortalecimiento de la educación ambiental.
Los medios de implementación se presentan organizados en fichas de medidas, detallando
su vinculación con las áreas estratégicas del PACCC, los responsables de su ejecución, los
plazos y las posibles fuentes de financiamiento, incluyendo fondos municipales, regionales y
alianzas con el sector privado. Este enfoque busca fortalecer la gobernanza local, mejorar la
calidad de vida de la comunidad y proteger el patrimonio natural y cultural de Colina,
promoviendo la resiliencia y el desarrollo sostenible frente a los desafíos del cambio climático.

EL plan se realizo en base a una caraterizacion territorial (geografia, socioeconomica, medio ambientales), un analisis de las evoluciones pasadas y futuras prevista que sea vinculados al clima, tal como a los motores socio economicos.
Los escenarios climaticos para la comuna de Talca fueron desarollados en base al trabajo al ministerio de Medio Ambiente lo cual elaboro una plataforma / visor climatico. A partir de la plataforma Web ARClim (Atlas de Riesgos Climáticos para Chile) del Ministerio del Medio Ambiente, se analizo las proyecciones futuras que dan cuenta de los efectos del cambio climático en la comuna. El “explorador de amenazas climáticas” es una herramienta que permite visualizar y descargar índices para un período histórico reciente (1980-2010) y uno futuro cercano (2035-2065). En este caso, se comparan las temperaturas medias anuales y las precipitaciones acumuladas. www.arclim.mma.gob.cl. Esta plataforma permite visualizar un escenario histórico actual v/s un escenario futuro. Apunta precipitaciones, temperaturas, ocurencias de olas de calor entre otro. Esta plataforma permitio destacar que para Talca el escenario climatico apunta menos agua en el invierno y más lluvias torrenciales. Aumento de días muy cálidos y disminución de capa de hielo en la cordillera, lo cual afectará el ciclo del agua y las capacidades de recarga de los acuíferos, entre otros.
